member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Application
member.summary: The composition root and main loop.
member.remarks: Startup order is fixed by Plan/01-architecture.md section 3: paths and logging, then content manifest and locale validation, then window, then renderer device and feature tier, then audio endpoint, then game state. Each step must fail with an actionable message rather than proceeding in a broken state.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Application.CaptionFonts
member.summary: The fonts the interface will draw with, best first.

remarks.para: Order matters and so does the set. The three F_CAPTION sizes are GK3's own caption font at 16, 20 and 26 point, which cut to 20, 26 and 33 pixel letters; F_CAPTION_DEFAULT is the 14-point Goudy the game used for its own subtitles. All four carry the full 181-character set, including the 52 accented letters.

The F_ARIAL fonts at the end carry 94 characters and not one of them is accented, which is why the interface used to draw H?tel de Rennes-le-Ch?teau in a game set in France. They stay as a last resort for an installation missing the caption sheets; nothing else should reach them.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.Showing(GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi,GK3Reborn.Game.MoviePlayer)
member.summary: Lets the scripts play a movie.
member.param: The host.
What plays them.

remarks.para: All three are waitable, and what they wait for is the movie's own length — which is why has to answer for them as well as performing them. A script that plays a cutscene and then speaks would otherwise speak over it.

A movie that will not play returns nothing to wait for, so the script carries on. The original does the same: its callback runs whether or not the video played, and a missing cutscene should cost the cutscene rather than the rest of the game.

PlayMovie is the windowed form and the other two are full screen. Both are drawn the same way here — fitted to the window, letterboxed — because a window inside a window is a decision about the interface that nothing else in this port has made yet.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.Beside(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: A sibling of the enhanced textures directory.
member.param: Where the enhanced colour textures are.
The sibling's name.
member.returns: Its path.
member.remarks: The generated maps sit beside the colour textures rather than among them, because a surface may have a better colour and no normal map, or the other way round, and they are judged separately.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.WantedGlyphHeight(System.Int32)
member.summary: How tall the interface's letters should be for a given display.
member.param: The framebuffer's height in pixels.
member.returns: A wanted glyph height, which the ladder is matched against.
member.remarks: Proportional to the display rather than fixed, because a bitmap font does not scale: the same 17-pixel sheet that is comfortable on a 480-line screen is a third the apparent size on a 1440-line one, which is exactly the complaint. 2.8% puts a 1080-line display on the 26-point rung and anything above it on the 26-point rung too, that being the largest the game shipped.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.TextPixels(System.Int32,System.Boolean)
member.summary: How tall an em should be, in pixels, for a window of a given height.
member.param: How tall the window is.
Whether this is the menu rather than the room's interface.
member.returns: The em size to draw the outline font at.
member.remarks: A share of the window rather than a fixed size, so the interface is the same apparent size on every display. The menu is drawn larger than the room's captions on purpose: captions must not cover the room, and a menu is the only thing on screen.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.InterfaceFont(System.String,System.String,GK3Reborn.Foundation.Diagnostics.DiagnosticBag)
member.summary: Finds the typeface the interface draws with.
member.param: A file named on the command line, or null.
The content workspace's enhanced set, if any.
Where a font that will not read is reported.
member.returns: The font, or null to fall back to GK3's own sheets.

remarks.para: Three places, in the order somebody working on the game would want them: --font-file, then any .ttf or .otf in the workspace's enhanced/fonts, then the one carried inside the assembly. The last is what a shipped game uses and is why this never comes back empty on an installation that has no workspace at all.
The embedded face is Noto Serif under the SIL Open Font Licence 1.1 — a serif, because GK3's own captions are one and a sans-serif menu in front of this game would look like somebody else's.

member.summary: Where to look for a typeface, best first.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.Magnification(GK3Reborn.Formats.Ui.FontFile,System.Int32)
member.summary: How many screen pixels one pixel of the chosen sheet should cover.
member.param: The rung that was picked.
The height that was asked for.
member.returns: A whole number, at least one.
member.remarks: The ladder runs out at 33-pixel letters, which is the largest sheet the game shipped. Past about 1,600 lines that is small enough to be the original complaint again, and the only thing left is to draw each sheet pixel as more than one. Whole numbers only: a fractional one lands glyph edges between pixels and the sampler averages neighbouring letters into each other.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.Complete(GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi)
member.summary: Asks whether this point in the story is over, and moves the clock on if it is.
member.param: The game.
member.returns: The room to open instead, or null to open the one that was asked for.

remarks.para: The rules are , one method per timeblock, each a run of conditions. They are checked on every change of location and nowhere else, which is the original's own arrangement (LocationManager::ChangeLocationInternal) and the reason a timeblock ends as you walk through a door rather than the moment you finish the last thing in it.

A timeblock change decides where the player goes, so it outranks the door they walked through: 110A ends on the way into RC1 and starts 112P in RC1, but several of the others put the player somewhere else entirely.

member.remarks: Once, before the first room. A fifth of the corpus's action statements are CallSheep, and a script that is not loaded is a call that does nothing — most visibly the ones that take the player from one room to the next.

member.param: The game's own barns.

The block-compressed build or a pack, if there is one.
Where a picture that will not decode is reported.
Its file name, with the extension.
member.returns: The picture, or nothing when no source has it.
member.remarks: Three places, in the order that gives the best-looking answer: the enhanced set, the compressed build, and then the archives, which is all a shipped game has. Missing is not a failure — a card without its painting still says what time it is, and a game that would not start because a decorative bitmap is malformed would be worse than either.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Application.CardSeconds
member.summary: How long the card stands there on its own, in seconds.
member.remarks: Long enough to read twice and short enough that nobody waits for it. The player can end it sooner, and the original's own card has no timer at all when it is not being used to cover a load — it sits until Continue is pressed. This ends by itself as well, because a card that needs dismissing is a card that can be missed by somebody who has walked away from the keyboard.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.Announce(GK3Reborn.Platform.SilkGameWindow,GK3Reborn.Rendering.Vulkan.VulkanRenderer,GK3Reborn.UI.MenuPage,GK3Reborn.Game.GameStrings,GK3Reborn.Game.Timeblock,GK3Reborn.Application.TitleScreen)
member.summary: Says that the story has moved on to another part of the day.
member.param: The window, for the click or key that ends it.
What draws the picture and the words.
The menu's own typeface, which is the big one.
What the game calls this part of the day.
Where the clock has got to.
The painting for it, or nothing.

remarks.para: The original has this screen and the port did not. A timeblock ending was a line on the console and nothing on the screen: the room dissolved, another one built itself, and two hours of story had passed with nothing said about it. TimeblockScreen in the reference shows a painting for the point in the story with its name lettered over it, and every one of those paintings is in the archives as TBT110A.BMP and its fifteen siblings.

The painting is kept and the lettering is not. The original draws the name as a fifteen-frame sprite animation whose position it has to hard-code per timeblock because the artists placed each one differently; the name itself is already in ESTRINGS.TXT as Day110a = Day 1, 10am - 12pm, and setting it in the port's own face costs nothing and is legible at any window size. That is the same division the title screen makes: the picture is art and the words are a widget.
It sits over a black screen when the archives have no painting, which is what an installation without the art gets and is still better than the room simply changing.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.ShowMenu(GK3Reborn.Platform.SilkGameWindow,GK3Reborn.Rendering.Vulkan.VulkanRenderer,GK3Reborn.UI.MenuPage,GK3Reborn.UI.FrontEnd,System.Action{GK3Reborn.Game.Settings},GK3Reborn.UI.MenuBehind,System.Func{GK3Reborn.Rendering.OverlayAtlas},System.Int32,System.String)
member.summary: Shows the menu until the player leaves it.
member.param: The window.
What draws it.
The drawn page.
What the pages hold and what choosing a row does.
What to do with a setting the moment it changes.
What is behind it, and so what it has to draw itself.
Cuts a fresh sheet of letters when the window changes size.
Leave after this many frames, or zero to wait for the player.
Where to write the last frame, if anywhere.
member.returns: What the player asked for.

remarks.para: A loop of its own rather than a mode of the room's. Nothing of the room advances while it runs, which is what pausing means, and the frame it draws is the same picture the room left on screen with the menu over it.
Three ways to work it, all live at once: the arrow keys and Enter, the pointer, and dragging a slider. A menu that can only be used one way is a menu somebody cannot use.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.MenuMagnification(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: How much to draw the menu's letters at.
member.param: How tall the window is, in pixels.
How tall the sheet's letters are.
member.returns: A whole-number magnification, one or more.
member.remarks: A menu is not a caption. Captions are sized to be readable without covering the room; a menu is the only thing on screen, and one drawn at caption size on a large display reads as a dialogue box from another decade. A row comes out at about a twenty-second of the window's height, which is roughly what the original's own buttons were on the screen they were drawn for.

member.remarks: Down in the left-hand corner over the title art, whose lettering is to the right of the angel: a menu that covers the name of the game it is the menu for is not a title screen. The settings pages are taller and wider, and centre themselves again.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.ShowIntro(GK3Reborn.Platform.SilkGameWindow,GK3Reborn.Rendering.Vulkan.VulkanRenderer,GK3Reborn.Game.MoviePlayer,GK3Reborn.UI.MenuPage,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.String})
member.summary: Plays the films the game opens with.
member.param: The window.
What draws them.
What plays them.
What draws the way out, or null when there is no font.
Which films, in order.

remarks.para: Enter, or the left button held. A click is what somebody does by accident while the machine is still settling down, and losing the opening of the game to a stray mouse is worse than holding a button for half a second. Escape works too, on the grounds that it is the first thing half the world will try.

Skipping ends the film showing and not the sequence. The logo and the intro are two different things to sit through: somebody who skips the publisher's logo has said nothing at all about whether they want to watch the opening of the game. So a cold start is two skips, and the button has to be let go between them — a hold that carried across the join would take the second film with the first.
Missing films are passed over in silence, because an installation that has none should still reach the menu.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.LoadMapArt(GK3Reborn.Content.GameArchives,GK3Reborn.Rendering.Vulkan.VulkanRenderer,GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter,GK3Reborn.Content.EnhancedTextures)
member.summary: Hands the driving map's own pictures to the interface.
member.param: The game's data, which is where the art is.
What holds the pictures.
What draws them, and needs to know how big each one is.
Upscaled textures to prefer, or null to use the archives'.

remarks.para: Seventeen pictures — the map and its sixteen markers — read once at startup and kept. A 640-by-480 painting reloaded every time somebody opens the map would be a stall the player can feel, and together they are under a megabyte.

The size recorded is always the archive's, whatever is drawn. The map is laid out in the 640-by-480 pixels the original was built in, and every marker's position is a coordinate in that space; an upscaled marker is the same marker at more samples, not a bigger one. Recording the enhanced size would put the markers in the wrong places by a factor of thirty-two.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Application.Playable(GK3Reborn.Content.GameArchives,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Makes sure the scene is loaded at a point in the story, not merely at a time of day.
member.param: The game's archives.
The scene's name.
What the player asked for.
member.returns: A request with a story behind it, where the room has one.

remarks.para: 202P is a point in the story and N is an asset suffix meaning night. Both are legitimate — see — and the render tooling wants the second, because looking at a room's night lighting should not require inventing a story to justify it.

A game is different. With no story state the scene's conditions go undecided, no action files come into scope and no soundtrack is chosen: every object in the room answers to nothing and nobody says a word. That is a room, not a game, and it looks exactly like a broken one. So the launcher takes a real timeblock instead and says which, rather than running a version of the game where nothing can be done.

member.summary: Where the game's own archives are, when nobody has said.
member.returns: The first directory holding a .brn, or where one should be put.

remarks.para: A published game is a directory somebody has copied the original archives into, so the executable's own Data is looked at first and the executable's directory after it, for anybody who dropped the barns straight in beside the game.

The walk up the tree is the development convenience it always was: the checkout keeps the installation six directories above bin/Debug, and copying eight hundred megabytes into every project's output to save the walk would be the wrong trade. It is looked at last so that a published tree never reaches past itself and quietly runs on whatever an unrelated directory above it happens to hold.

A directory only counts when it actually holds a barn. An empty Data beside the executable is the shape of an install somebody has started and not finished, and stopping there would report it as the answer.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Audio.AudioSpace
member.summary: Turns GK3's world into the one the sound device thinks in.

remarks.para: GK3's world is left-handed and OpenAL's is right-handed. The renderer already knows this — screen right is cross(up, forward) there, not the other way about — and the ears had never been told. Handing world coordinates straight to the device makes it work out its own right as cross(forward, up), which points the opposite way, so every sound in the game came from the wrong side: the fountain on your left was heard on your right.

One axis reversed is exactly what changes handedness, and reversing it is its own inverse. Z is the one turned over here — the choice is arbitrary, since any single axis gives the same result, and Z is the one graphics conventionally flips.

It must be applied to everything or to nothing. The listener's position, the way the head faces, which way is up for it, and every source's position are one geometry; mirroring some of them and not the others does not swap left and right, it puts sounds somewhere that does not exist. Distances are unaffected — a mirror is a rigid motion — so anything that only measures how far away a sound is stays in the world's own coordinates.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Audio.AudioSpace.Device(System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Puts a point or a direction into the device's coordinates.
member.param: Where it is, or which way it points, in the game's world.
member.returns: The same thing, in the right-handed world the device works in.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Audio.AudioSpace.RightOfListener(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Which way the device works out is to the right of a listener.
member.param: Where the head faces, in device coordinates.
Which way is up for it, in device coordinates.
member.returns: The direction the right ear points.
member.remarks: OpenAL's own rule, written down so that a test can check the whole chain against it rather than against my idea of it. The game's rule is the other order, which is the whole of the difference this file exists to bridge.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Audio.AudioSpace.Panning(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: How far to the right of a listener something is heard, from -1 to 1.
member.param: Where the listener is, in the world.
Where they face, in the world.
Which way is up for them, in the world.
Where the sound is, in the world.
member.returns: Negative when it is heard on the left, positive on the right, and zero when it is straight ahead, behind, above or below.
member.remarks: The whole chain in one line, so that "a sound on your left is heard on your left" is a thing a test can assert. Nothing in the game reads it; the device does this arithmetic itself, from what it is given.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Audio.OpenAlBackend
member.summary: The audio device, over OpenAL Soft.

remarks.para: One buffer per sound, uploaded the first time it is asked for and kept, and a pool of sources handed out as things play. GK3 never has many sounds going at once — a line of dialogue, a room tone, a door — so the pool is small and a sound that cannot get a source is dropped rather than queued. Dropping is the right failure: a footstep that arrives late is worse than one that never arrives.

Buses are gain multipliers applied when a source starts and when a gain changes. OpenAL has no bus concept, so this is the mixer: every voice remembers which bus it is on, so turning dialogue down turns down the line being spoken and not merely the next one.

Opening the device is allowed to fail. A machine with no sound card, or a headless run, gets no backend and a diagnostic saying so, because refusing to start the game over it would be worse than running it quietly.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Audio.OpenAlBackend.Muffle(GK3Reborn.Audio.OpenAlBackend.Voice)
member.summary: Takes the top off a sound that is far away.

remarks.para: Distance does two things to a sound and OpenAL only does one of them by itself. It makes it quieter, which the rolloff handles, and it takes the high frequencies out of it, which is most of what tells a listener that something is far off rather than merely quiet. A fountain across a square is a hiss; the same fountain turned down is still a fountain at your feet.

A low-pass through EFX, opened once and skipped where the device has no EFX at all. The curve is a straight line from no filtering at the sound's own minimum distance to a quarter of the high frequencies at its maximum — a stand-in for air absorption rather than a model of it, and nothing to do with what is in the way.

member.summary: The language whose dialogue is loaded.

remarks.para: Spoken assets are localised by prefixing the language's letter to the name, so the English recording of the line 0NQIB44QR1 is E0NQIB44QR1.YAK. Scripts never write the prefix; the engine adds it, which is why a plate taken straight from an action file matches nothing on disk.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.Authoring.EditLayer
member.summary: Composes a derived baseline with hand-authored corrections.

remarks.para: Converters guess. Lightmap-derived light positions and inferred material roughness are starting points, not answers, and the person looking at the scene in-engine will always know better. The problem is that regenerating the baseline would throw their corrections away.

So corrections live in their own file and are replayed over whatever the generator most recently produced. Deleting a derived light, nudging one that sits in the wrong place, dropping in a light the lightmap never implied, or making a material less glossy are all the same mechanism, and none of them is lost when the converter improves and reruns.
An edit that no longer applies - because the item it names is gone - is reported and skipped, never silently dropped and never fatal.

member.summary: The game's vertex animation clips, read on demand.

remarks.para: 5,796 of them and 399 MB, so they are read when something asks and kept afterwards — and read without their vertex data by default. The shapes are 92 million samples across the corpus and only skinning needs them; a door swinging needs its mesh transforms, which are a rounding error beside the rest.

A clip names the model it targets in its header, and the filename is not reliable: 12.9% of the corpus is named for something other than what it animates. Anything pairing a clip to a model must use .

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.CompressedTextures
member.summary: Block-compressed textures, standing in front of everything else.

remarks.para: The same enhanced textures as , compressed to BC7 and their normal maps to BC5 by the content pipeline. It is the cheapest form there is: the file goes to the device without being decoded, the mip chain is already built, and it takes a quarter of the video memory. `PbrLab` measures the pilot set at 13.71 GiB uncompressed against 3.43 GiB compressed, at 45.5–47.0 dB, which nobody can see.

One thing it cannot do is carry a colour key. works on texels and these are blocks, so a texture whose original uses GK3's magenta has to take the decoded path — three of the 324 in the pilot set do. Deciding that is the loader's business, because only the loader has the original to look at.
Names are matched without their extension and without regard to case, the same as every other texture layer: a surface refers to R25WALLS, the archive holds R25WALLS.BMP, and this holds R25WALLS.dds.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.EnhancedTextures
member.summary: Higher-resolution textures, standing in front of the archives.

remarks.para: The originals are 213 megapixels across 6,657 textures, and the surfaces a player looks at most — tier 0 in docs/texture-enhancement.md — are 5.8 megapixels of that between them. Replacing one is a matter of putting a PNG under the name the geometry already uses: the UV layout does not change, so nothing else has to.

A layer rather than a rewrite. The archives stay exactly as they are, and asking for a texture that has no enhanced version gets the original, so a partial set is a perfectly good set. That also makes it possible to render a scene with and without and put the two side by side, which is the only way to judge this work.
Names are matched without their extension and without regard to case, because a surface refers to R25WALLS while the archive holds R25WALLS.BMP and the enhanced set holds R25WALLS.PNG.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.FontLibrary
member.summary: The game's 137 bitmap fonts, read on demand.

remarks.para: A font is two files that have to be found together: the .FON that lists its characters and the bitmap they are cut from. Most name their bitmap outright; the nine that do not are called the same thing as the definition.

The definition is read as Latin-1 rather than UTF-8. The Font= line is a run of characters in the sheet's own order, and a third of them are above 127 — read as UTF-8 they become replacement characters, and every accented letter in the game maps to the wrong picture.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Content.FontLibrary.Nearest(System.Int32,System.String[])
member.summary: Finds and decodes the bitmap a font is cut from.
Reads a ladder of fonts and returns the one whose letters are nearest a wanted size.
member.param: How tall a capital should be, in pixels.
The ladder, in any order.
member.returns: The nearest one that loads, or null when none of them does.

remarks.para: A bitmap font has one size and there is no scaling it: drawing a 17-pixel sheet at 34 pixels is a blurry 17-pixel sheet. So "make the text bigger" means picking a different sheet, and GK3 shipped the ladder to pick from — its caption font exists at 16, 20 and 26 point, which cut to 20, 26 and 33 pixel letters.

Reading a candidate to measure it is the only way to know how tall it is: the height is not in the .FON, it is the sheet divided by the row count. They are a few kilobytes each and the answer is cached, so the ladder costs one read per rung for the life of the process.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.GameArchives
member.summary: Every barn archive of an installation, searched as one.
member.remarks: The game does not record which archive holds a given asset, and several archives can hold the same name, so the only reliable way to open one by name is to search them all in a fixed order. Doing that in one place keeps the order identical between the toolchain and the game, which matters because a name resolving differently in the two would make a tool's output describe something the game never loads.

member.remarks: The default and the honest one. Plan/02 section 1 requires human review before anything derived from the originals is distributed, so a candidate that passes every check a machine can make is still a draft.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Content.Manifests.TextureVerdict.Kept
member.summary: Sound, and not written, because there is already a texture under that name.
member.remarks: The enhanced set is hand-corrected work, not whatever a generator last left on disk. Textures in it have been redone by hand, and a rerun of an import that wrote over them would destroy that silently — the set lives outside the repository, so there is no history to get anything back from. An import leaves what it finds alone. --force is the only way past it and it is never the default.

member.summary: What an import of enhanced textures produced.

remarks.para: The provenance record Plan/02 section 1 asks for: which tool made these, from what, under what settings, and what a machine could tell about the result. It is deliberately a record of a draft. Nothing here approves anything; a verdict of means only that no automatic check found it broken.

Rejections are kept rather than dropped. A candidate that lost its alpha or changed its aspect ratio is worth going back to the generator about, and a list of names that simply vanished from the manifest would not tell anybody that.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.MappedStream
member.summary: A read-only, seekable stream over memory somebody else owns.

remarks.para: A ReBarn pack is memory-mapped once and read through windows onto that mapping, which is what keeps a hundred-megabyte movie out of the heap. A decoder wants a , and the framework has no read-only stream over : MemoryStream takes an array, so handing it one means copying the whole file first, which is the one thing the mapping exists to avoid.

The memory is not owned here. It stays valid only as long as whatever owns the mapping does, so a stream over a pack must not outlive the pack. The engine keeps its packs open for the life of the process, which is what makes this safe there.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.Movie
member.summary: A movie, opened and decoded on demand.

remarks.para: Decoded by the engine's own H.264 and AAC decoders, so a movie plays wherever the engine runs — Windows, Linux, a Mac — with nothing installed beside the executable and nothing to version. FFmpeg used to do this; it was sixty megabytes of shared libraries per platform, a different set of names for every generation, and no build at all for Apple silicon. The managed decoders are compared sample for sample against FFmpeg's in the tests, so what is lost is speed, not pictures.

Video is decoded ahead of the clock on its own thread and pulled frame by frame as the clock asks; the sound is decoded whole when the movie opens. The two are treated differently because they are used differently: a frame is wanted once and thrown away, and the sound has to be handed to the audio device as one buffer for the device to be the clock. GK3's longest movie is three and a half minutes, which is forty megabytes of PCM — worth spending to have the picture follow the sound rather than the other way round.

The decode thread runs a few frames ahead and no further, so a 320x240 movie costs nothing to speak of and a 1440x1080 one keeps one core busy without piling up frames it will never show. A frame that is not ready when the clock reaches it is skipped, which the player treats as leaving the last one on screen.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.RebarnContent
member.summary: Every ReBarn pack beside the executable, searched as one.

remarks.para: The remake's own content — enhanced colour, normal, ORM and height maps, modernised models, imported video — in one or two files that ship with the game rather than in forty thousand loose ones. is the equivalent for the original installation, and the two are separate on purpose: GK3's archives are read from wherever the player installed the game, and these are read from wherever the executable is.

Packs are opened in file-name order and the last one wins, so a pack dropped in later overrides one shipped earlier: Reborn.rebarn, then RebornMaterials.rebarn, then a RebornPatch.rebarn somebody adds. That is the whole mod story, and it needs no support beyond a name that sorts last.
A missing directory, or a directory with no packs in it, is not an error. The game runs from a legally obtained installation and all of this is an addition to it — exactly the rule follows.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.SoundLibrary
member.summary: The game's sounds, decoded and read on demand.

remarks.para: Straight out of the archives. 97.5% of the game's sounds are an MP3 inside a RIFF header, and decodes those where it finds them, so there is nothing to import and no second place to look. A decoded copy of the corpus used to sit in the content workspace and cost 3.7 GB to save about eight milliseconds a sound.

Names keep their extension, and a script may not give one. A line of dialogue is A0NQIB44.QR1 — where the last characters are a sequence number rather than a type, so two sounds can differ only in them — while a soundtrack asks for R25Theme1 and means R25THEME1.WAV. Both spellings have to reach the same file, which is why an extensionless name is tried again with .WAV.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.TreeLibrary
member.summary: The modelled trees that stand in for GK3's foliage cards.

remarks.para: A tree in this game is a picture of a tree on one quad, or on two quads crossed. That was the right call in 1999 and it is the single most obvious thing left in an outdoor scene: the scene files place 431 of those cards and the rooms draw 5,760 more, and the moment the camera moves off the angle the artist framed, a wood becomes a row of cardboard.

The trees themselves are grown by tools/blender/grow_trees.py and read from disk here. Each is normalised — trunk base at the origin, exactly one unit tall — so a species is grown a handful of times and then fitted to whichever card it is replacing, which is what keeps a forest to a few dozen kilobytes instead of one mesh per tree.

A layer rather than a rewrite, in the same way is. A missing directory, a missing manifest and a tree that will not parse all leave the flat card exactly where it was, so a partial set is a good set and the two can be rendered side by side — which is the only way to judge this work.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Content.VideoLibrary
member.summary: The game's movies, from the packs or from the workspace beside them.

remarks.para: GK3 refers to a movie by name and never by file: PlayFullScreenMovie("212pBegin") and the disc holds 212pbegin.bik. G-Engine's VideoHelper strips the extension deliberately, because some locales ship AVI where others ship BIK — so the name is the identity and the container is an implementation detail. Forty of them survive the import as H.264 in MP4.

Two places to find one, and which of them is looked in is the player's decision. --rebarn means the packs and nothing else, which is the only way to measure what the shipped form does; without it the loose enhanced/video directory is read as well and wins, so a movie re-imported during a session plays without the pack having to be rebuilt. That is the same way round as the textures, and for the same reason: the looser and more recent thing wins while a set is still moving.

What comes back is a stream rather than a file or an array. A movie in a pack is a window onto a memory mapping and a long one is a hundred megabytes, so copying it into the heap to play it would cost more than decoding it does.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Actions.NvcFile
member.summary: Reader for GK3's action files.

remarks.para: 390 files defining everything the player can do. Each line is noun, verb, case followed by optional approach=, target= and script={…} fields, and a trailing [LOGIC] section names the cases as Sheep expressions.

This is the file the modern interaction model is built from. Asking "what can the player do to this object right now" means taking every rule for that noun and evaluating its case — which is exactly what the original engine did to decide whether a verb appeared on its verb wheel.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Formats.Actions.NvcFile.BuiltInCases
member.summary: Cases the engine answers itself rather than reading from a file.

remarks.para: ALL always applies. GABE_ALL and the rest depend on who the player currently is, which matters because GK3 switches between Gabriel and Grace. The _TIME family counts how often the player has already done this to this, and the two DIALOGUE_TOPICS_LEFT forms ask whether there is anything left to say.

TIME_BLOCK and TIME_BLOCK_OVERRIDE are simply true. They mark an action a timeblock's own file writes to override one the location's general file gives, and the second outranks the first where both could apply. Missing them is expensive and silent: TIME_BLOCK_OVERRIDE is used by 90 of the corpus's action files and written into the logic section of exactly one, so treating it as an undefined case takes 918 actions out of the game.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile
member.summary: A GK3 vertex animation.

remarks.para: 5,796 clips and 399 MB — the whole of the game's movement. GK3's characters have no skeleton: a clip stores, per frame, where each of a model's mesh groups sits and where every one of its vertices is. A walk cycle is a list of poses, not a set of bone angles.

The format and every constant here are the spec in Plan/06-c6-rig-solve.md §3, which was transcribed from G-Engine and validated by parsing the entire corpus. Its five invariants are checked as the file is read rather than assumed, because each one failing means the reader has lost its place and everything after is noise.

Vertex data is read only when asked for. gab alone is 50.2 million vertex samples across its 943 clips, so anything that only wants to know how long a clip is, or where a door swings to, should not pay for that.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.PoseAt(System.Int32,System.Single,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Where a mesh group is at a moment between two frames.
member.param: Which mesh group.
Which frame, with a fraction of the way to the next one.
Whether the clip runs straight back into itself, so that the last frame leads to the first rather than being held.
member.returns: Its transform, or null when the clip never places it.

remarks.para: GK3 records fifteen poses a second and a modern display shows sixty frames a second, so playing the recorded poses as they stand shows each of them four times over. On anything slow that reads as the original's stiffness; on anything fast it reads as strobing, and the lobby's ceiling fans — six degrees a recorded pose, ninety a second — are the clearest case in the game.

So a moment between two recorded poses is the two of them mixed — but only where the two are recorded on consecutive frames. A mesh that does not move is not written again, so a gap in the recording is a pose held for the length of the gap, and mixing across one would make a mesh that moves once every ten frames drift the whole way instead of waiting and then moving. is where that is decided. Rotation is a proper spherical mix rather than a mix of the matrices, because mixing two rotation matrices shrinks whatever is between them.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.ShapeAt(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Single,System.Boolean)
member.summary: The shape of a submesh at a moment between two frames.
member.param: Which mesh group.
Which submesh within it.
Which frame, with a fraction of the way to the next one.
Whether the clip runs straight back into itself.
member.returns: Its vertices, or null when the clip never shapes it.
member.remarks: The same rule as , straight down the line between the two recorded shapes. A vertex travelling a curve over several recorded shapes is drawn as the chords of that curve, which at fifteen recorded shapes a second nobody can see; what they can see is a character's arm arriving in four equal jumps.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.Before(System.Int32,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.Single)
member.summary: The last recorded entry at or before a frame, or -1 when there is none.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.Next(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.Boolean)
member.summary: Which recorded entry a moment is heading towards, and how many frames away it is.

remarks.para: Only ever the very next frame. A mix is between an entry and one recorded on the frame after it; a gap in the recording is a pose that is held, and there is nothing to head towards until the gap ends. That is the rule from G-Engine's VertexAnimationPose::GetForTime, whose own comment states it: if the next pose is not for the next frame, use the current pose with no interpolation.

A gap says the mesh does not move, because a mesh that does not move is not recorded again. Sliding across one instead sets the mesh off the moment the hold begins and lands it as the hold ends, which is the whole gap spent somewhere it never was. It shows worst on the thing that holds most: a planted foot. Gabriel's walk records his right shoe on frames 0 and 4 to 15 and his left on 0 to 5 and 14 to 20 — the gaps are the half of each stride that foot spends on the ground. The right one's runs off the end of the clip, so what it mixed towards was the opening pose a whole stride's travel away, and the shoe left his ankle by fifty units and snapped back at the loop.

Past the last recorded entry the pose is held — unless the clip cycles and that entry is on the clip's last frame, in which case the frame after it is the clip's opening one. That is what makes a fan come round rather than freezing for a fifteenth of a second at the top of every turn: its blades are recorded on every frame there is, so the wrap is a step of one frame like any other.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.Mix(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4,System.Numerics.Matrix4x4,System.Single)
member.summary: Mixes two mesh transforms, turning the shorter way round.

remarks.para: A rotation is mixed as a rotation and not component by component, because a component-wise mix of two bases shortens them — the halfway point between two a quarter turn apart is 71% as long — which shrinks whatever it is applied to as it turns and springs it back again.

Every basis in the corpus is mirrored. GK3's world is left-handed and its mesh transforms carry a determinant of −1, which Matrix4x4.Decompose deals with by picking an axis to call negative — and it need not pick the same one twice running. Decomposing these directly makes a fan blade turn inside out between one recorded pose and the next, which reads as the fan flickering in and out of existence rather than as a mistake about handedness. So the mirror is taken out first, the rotation mixed, and the mirror put back.

Anything that is not a rotation with a mirror on it — a basis squashed flat, and some of the fan housings are — falls back to a straight component-wise mix. At the step sizes involved, a fifteenth of a second of the fastest thing in the game, that costs about a tenth of a percent of length and cannot go wrong.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.Turn(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4,System.Numerics.Quaternion@,System.Boolean@)
member.summary: Reads a basis as a rotation, saying whether it was mirrored to get there.
member.param: The transform.
The rotation it amounts to, once any mirror is taken out.
Whether taking the mirror out was necessary.
member.returns: False when it is not a rotation at all, mirrored or otherwise.
member.remarks: Orthonormality is checked rather than assumed: a basis whose axes are not unit length or not at right angles carries a scale or a shear, and turning it into a quaternion silently throws that away.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.Mirror(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: Turns a basis inside out, or back again.
member.remarks: The third axis reversed, which flips the handedness and is its own inverse. Which axis is arbitrary — any one of the three gives the same answer once it is put back — and the point is that the same one is chosen every time, which is exactly what Matrix4x4.Decompose does not promise.

member.summary: Which submeshes of a mesh group the clip shapes.

member.summary: Reads every frame.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.Block(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Int32@,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary{System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.Numerics.Vector3[]},System.Boolean)

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.Shape(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary{System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.Numerics.Vector3[]},System.Boolean,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Reads a submesh's vertices, compressed or not.
member.remarks: Read even when the caller does not want the positions, because a compressed frame is a delta against the previous recorded one: skipping a frame's shape would make every later frame of that submesh wrong. What the flag saves is keeping them, not reading them — and the block's declared size means the file can still be walked either way.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.Basis(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Builds a mesh's transform from its three bases and its position.
member.remarks: The bases are the columns of the rotation, taken exactly as read. They are orthonormal but their determinant is −1, which is correct: GK3 authored a left-handed world and the renderer already draws it that way. "Fixing" the handedness here by negating or permuting mirrors every character in the game.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.FromByte(System.Byte)
member.summary: Decodes a one-byte delta.
member.remarks: One sign bit, two whole bits, five fractional. The whole part is masked with 0x7F rather than 0x60 — the sign bit is not cleared before the shift discards it anyway — and that quirk is reproduced rather than tidied, because tidying it is how a reader ends up almost right.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile.FromUShort(System.Int32)
member.summary: Decodes a two-byte delta: one sign bit, seven whole, eight fractional.

remarks.para: 208 of the corpus's animations carry an [MVISIBILITY] section, and it is how a character who is not in the room walks into it. EmlRc1ExitLobby is the plain case: Emilio is hidden until the moment he opens the hotel door, and frame 0 of the animation that swings the door is what turns him on.

Which way it faces there, in radians about the vertical.

remarks.para: An [ACTIONS] line may carry eight numbers after the clip's name: an offset and heading from the actor to the model, then a second pair from the world to the model. The spot is the second offset plus the first rotated by the second heading, and the facing is the difference of the two headings. That is as strange as it sounds and it is what the original computes.
502 of the corpus's 6,040 action lines carry them — 8.3%. The other 92% place nothing and mean "play this where the model is standing".

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationFile
member.summary: Reader for GK3's animations.

remarks.para: 6,831 .ANM and 7,403 .YAK files, the largest asset family in the game and the same format: an INI file whose [HEADER] is a frame count, and whose sections list what happens on which frame — vertex animations to start, sounds to play, lines to speak.

A YAK is a line of dialogue. StartVoiceOver("1LLJ644QR1", 1) names one: the last character is a sequence number and the rest is the plate, so a voice-over of several lines is several YAKs in a row. That makes this the thing that decides how long a conversation takes — 20,709 of the corpus's 26,552 action-script statements are a waited StartVoiceOver, and until something could say how long one lasts, every one of them was over the instant it began.

Reading is not playing. The frames here are a schedule; running one needs the vertex animation format and an audio device, neither of which exists. What it does give is duration, which is what a script waiting on one needs to know.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationFile.FramesPerSecond
member.summary: How many frames a second an animation runs at, unless it says otherwise.
member.remarks: Fifteen, from G-Engine's Animation::mFramesPerSecond. Nothing in the files says so, which is worth knowing: a reader that assumed thirty would make every line of dialogue in the game half as long as it is.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationFile.Rate
member.summary: How many frames a second this animation runs at.

remarks.para: unless an [OPTIONS] line says otherwise, which thirty of the corpus's animations do — anywhere from 5 to 580. They are the ones whose timing is nothing like the rest: a fan, a flicker, a clock.

The option carries a frame number, so in principle the rate may change part-way through. One animation in the game does that and nothing appears to play it, so the last rate named wins for the whole clip, as the reference implementation also does.

member.summary: The mouth shapes it puts on people, in frame order.
member.remarks: 98,410 of these in the corpus and they are the whole of GK3's lip sync: one shape out of eight, on the frames the mouth changes. A line of dialogue is a .YAK whose sound is the recording and whose LIPSYNCH nodes are what the face does while it plays, which is why they are read from the same file rather than derived from the audio.

member.remarks: Brows, blinks and set mouths. A blink is one of these and nothing else: gabblink is four frames of eyelid textures, which is why blinking needs no geometry and no separate system.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationFile.Switched(System.String)
member.summary: Reads an on/off field.
member.remarks: The corpus writes it eight ways between them — on, ON, ON with a leading space — so this is a case-insensitive comparison on the trimmed text rather than anything cleverer. Anything that is not recognisably "on" is off, which is the safe way round: a model wrongly hidden is a missing person, and a model wrongly shown is a person standing in a wall.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationFile.Placement(GK3Reborn.Formats.Ini.IniLine)
member.summary: Reads an action line's absolute placement, if it has one.

remarks.para: <frame>,<clip>,x1,y1,z1,angle1,x2,y2,z2,angle2. The first offset goes actor-to-model and is wanted the other way round, so it is negated; and y and z are swapped in both, because the assets came out of Maya. Both quirks are the original's and reproducing them is the difference between a character standing on the floor and one standing in a wall.

Carrying the numbers is what makes a clip absolute, not what the numbers say. A line written with eight zeros is an absolute clip whose offset happens to be nothing — it plays at the coordinates it was authored at — and a line written with no numbers at all is a relative one that plays wherever its model is standing. The corpus splits three ways: 4,984 lines carry no numbers, 3,931 carry eight zeros, and 502 carry a real offset.

Treating the eight zeros as "no placement" collapses two fifths of the corpus into the wrong half. It is invisible on props, which are placed by the identity either way, and it moves every scripted set piece a character performs to wherever that character happens to be standing. Mosely reads his newspaper in the hotel dining room through one of these: the paper is a prop and stayed on the table, and he was corrected onto his model's resting place out beyond the room.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationFile.Read(GK3Reborn.Formats.Ini.IniSection,System.Action{GK3Reborn.Formats.Ini.IniLine})
member.summary: Walks the lines of a node section, skipping the count they open with.
member.remarks: Every section states how many entries follow and then lists them. The count is ignored in favour of the lines actually present, which is what the original does and what survives a file whose count is wrong.

member.summary: Reads the spoken lines.

remarks.para: Two forms, and the rarer one is the one that reads like documentation. SpeakerCaption carries everything on one line — end frame, noun, text — and occurs 211 times, in the long cutscenes. The ordinary form is a SPEAKER node naming who is talking followed by a CAPTION node with what they say, and that is 7,380 of the game's lines. A reader that handles only the first understands three percent of the dialogue.
A caption is a sentence and contains commas, so everything past the fixed fields is put back together rather than taken as more fields.

LIPSYNCH is 98,410 of the corpus's nodes — a mouth shape on each frame the mouth changes — and FACETEX/UNFACETEX another 1,268, which are the brows and the blinks. All three name a region of a character's face and a bitmap to put there; see .

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationFile.PartOf(GK3Reborn.Formats.Ini.IniLine,System.Int32)
member.summary: Which region of the face a node names, or null when it is one nothing paints.
member.remarks: One letter: M mouth, E eyelids, H forehead. Two of the corpus's nodes leave it off entirely and both name a mouth bitmap, so a missing letter means the mouth.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationFile.Rest(GK3Reborn.Formats.Ini.IniLine,System.Int32)
member.summary: Puts the fields from an index onwards back together as one string.
member.remarks: The reader repeats a bare keyword as its own value, because the files that need it rely on the value never being empty. A caption is a sentence rather than a keyword, so putting it back means writing the key alone unless the two actually differ — otherwise every line of dialogue in the game is said twice.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.GasFile
member.summary: A .GAS script: what a thing does when nobody is asking it to.

remarks.para: GK3 gives some models and every character a script of their own — named on a scene's model line as type=gasprop, gas=lbyfan.gas, or on an actor line as idle=madrc1mapidle.gas, talk=madreltalk.gas, listen=madreltalk.gas — and runs it for as long as the scene is loaded. The lobby's ceiling fans turn because of one, and so does everything a person does while they are not being told to do anything: breathing, shifting their weight, gesturing while they speak.

The format is a line an instruction, a keyword and its arguments, with // comments. Arguments are separated by commas or by spaces and the content uses both, sometimes in the same file — ANIM AbeHe1FightFidget, FALSE 50 — so both are separators here and neither is significant.

The language has 25 keywords across 502 scripts. The half that matters most is the smallest: ONEOF is 1,559 of the corpus's 4,000-odd instructions, and a run of them is one choice, not several — which is what makes an idle read as a person rather than as a loop.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.GasFile.Continuous
member.summary: Whether the script is one animation that simply runs for ever.
member.remarks: ANIM lbyfan_spin and loop, which is the shape of nearly every piece of scenery in the game: the ceiling fans, the fountains, the fires, the flashing clock. Worth telling apart because it can be played as a looping clip rather than as a script that starts the clip again every time round. The difference is a fifteenth of a second of held pose at each seam, which on a fan going ninety degrees a second is a visible hitch every four seconds.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.AssetClassifier
member.summary: Identifies assets from their contents rather than their names.

remarks.para: Extensions cannot be trusted in this corpus. Of 7,852 audio assets in the retail archives, only 1,170 are named .WAV; the rest carry three-character codes as their extension - .N61, .6J1, .B61 and 2,744 others - which is why the archives appear to hold 2,775 distinct file types when they hold on the order of a dozen. Classifying by name would mishandle 85% of the game's audio.
Several binary formats write their tag in little-endian order, so a model reads as LDOM rather than MODL and a lightmap as TLUM. The tags below are written as they appear on disk.

member.remarks: GK3's text assets are Latin-1, and use CRLF - sometimes CR CR LF - line endings. Anything mostly printable is treated as text. A NUL in the middle of content is a reliable sign of a binary format, but a trailing NUL is just a terminator.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Audio.SoundtrackFile
member.summary: Reader for GK3's soundtracks.

remarks.para: A .STK is not a piece of music. It is a little script — an INI file of numbered steps the game walks in order and then repeats — that builds room tone out of clips: wait a second, play the room's theme, wait five to ten seconds, play a mood, wait one to four, play another. Repeating that with different waits each time is what keeps a hotel room from sounding like a loop. 269 of them, named by 554 scene files.

[PRS] is the one section that is not what it looks like. Consecutive ones are one step — pick one of these at random — rather than several steps in a row, so they accumulate until some other section ends the run. Reading each as its own step would play all three of the vampire's hisses at once instead of one of them.

Documented from G-Engine's Soundtrack::Load. Unknown keys and sections are reported and ignored, which is also what the original does, and there are four in the corpus worth knowing about — see docs/formats/soundtracks.md.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Audio.WavFile
member.summary: A RIFF/WAVE file, decoded to signed 16-bit samples.

remarks.para: GK3's 7,852 sounds are RIFF files, and 7,656 of them — 97.5% — are not really WAV at all: format tag 85 is an MP3 stream wrapped in a RIFF header. Only 196 are plain PCM. So a reader that handles PCM alone can play the footsteps and the fly loop and nothing anybody says.

Both are read here, in process. Plan/01 rules out an external process at runtime, which is a different thing from ruling out decoding — and the difference is worth 3.7 GB: keeping a decoded copy of the corpus on disk cost that to save a few milliseconds a sound, while the compressed originals are 347 MB and already inside the archives.

member.summary: Decodes the MP3 stream inside a RIFF header.

remarks.para: Which is 7,656 of the game's 7,852 sounds — everything anybody says and almost every soundtrack. The fmt chunk describes the MP3 and the data chunk is the MP3 itself, so the frames are handed to the decoder as they stand and the header's channel count and rate are ignored in favour of what the stream actually says.

In process, and not by shelling out. Plan/01 rules out an external process at runtime, which is a different thing from ruling out decoding: keeping a decoded copy of the corpus on disk cost 3.7 GB to save what turns out to be a few milliseconds a sound.

member.remarks: Eight-bit WAV is unsigned with 128 as silence, which is the one trap here: read it as signed and every sound is a loud square wave. GK3's PCM is all 16-bit, but the import writes what it is given.

member.summary: Reader for GK3's "Barn" asset archives.

remarks.para: Named for the animals: some asset types are called Sheep and Yak. The metaphor did not go much further.

The reader opens the file, parses the table of contents and directories, and then extracts entries on demand. It never loads a whole archive into memory - the eight retail archives total 822 MB, and the importer walks all of them.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.BitmapDecoder
member.summary: Decodes GK3's texture formats to RGBA.

remarks.para: GK3 stores textures three ways. Most are its own container - 6,330 of them - which despite G-Engine calling it "compressed" is a raw 16-bit RGB565 bitmap with a tiny header. Nothing outside the game can open those, which is the main reason to convert. The rest are ordinary Windows bitmaps (322 palettised, 6 truecolour) and a handful of PNGs that are already fine as they are.

Layout of the GK3 container, from G-Engine's Texture::LoadCompressedFormat: two bytes 0x3136, two bytes 0x4D6E, then height and width as 16-bit values - in that order - followed by width x height RGB565 pixels from the top-left. Rows of odd width are padded with two bytes.

Magenta is the transparency key. G-Engine treats a texture as alpha-tested when its top-left pixel is magenta, and that convention is preserved here: such images decode with magenta made transparent, so a PNG viewer shows what the game shows. Images without the marker keep every pixel opaque, magenta included, because in those the colour is just a colour.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.BlockDecoder
member.summary: Turns block-compressed levels back into eight-bit pixels.

remarks.para: The content pipeline compresses to BC7, BC5 and BC4 because that is what a desktop GPU reads without decoding anything. Apple's GPUs read none of them: Metal on Apple silicon offers ASTC and ETC2 and no BC at all, so textureCompressionBC comes back false through MoltenVK and creating a BC image there is illegal rather than slow. This is what makes the same packs work on that hardware — the blocks are expanded on the host and uploaded as ordinary pixels.

It reproduces the sampler exactly rather than approximately, which is what lets a screenshot from a machine that decoded be compared with one from a machine that did not. In particular BC4 returns (r, 0, 0, 1) and BC5 (r, g, 0, 1), because that is what the hardware returns for the channels those formats do not carry, and a shader rebuilding a normal's z from two of them must see the same thing either way.

Nothing here runs on a machine that supports BC. Where it does run it costs about a second per hundred megabytes of blocks and four times the memory of the compressed form, which is the price of the format not existing on that device.

member.summary: BC7's partition shapes: which subset each of a block's sixteen texels belongs to.

remarks.para: Sixty-four shapes for a two-subset block and sixty-four more for a three-subset one, chosen by the partition field the block carries. They are the format's own data, not a decision this decoder makes, and they are kept apart from the decoder because a thousand numbers in the middle of it would bury the twenty lines that matter.

Each entry holds the subset in its low bits and marks the subset's anchor texel with the high bit, which is where reads both. Texel zero is the first subset's anchor in every shape; the others move with the shape.

Transcribed from the BC7 specification's tables. Khronos's published copy of them is known to contain errors, so the values were checked against the shape they describe: every two-subset row uses exactly the subsets 0 and 1 and marks exactly two anchors, every three-subset row uses 0, 1 and 2 and marks three, and BlockDecoderTests pins that.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.BlockDecoder.DecodeChannel(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Span{System.Byte})
member.summary: Expands one eight-byte channel block, as BC4 and both halves of BC5 are.
member.param: The eight bytes.
Sixteen values, in raster order within the tile.

remarks.para: Two endpoints and a three-bit index apiece. Which ramp the indices name depends on the endpoints' order: the six-value ramp reserves two codes for exactly zero and exactly one, which is how a compressor spends a block on a mask.

The ramp is mixed in sixteen-bit fixed point and rounded, not divided by seven and truncated. The specification writes the values as fractions and hardware rounds them; truncating instead is one less over about a fifth of the ramp, which is invisible in a texture and not invisible in a normal map — it was worth 0.6% of a lit frame differing from the same frame drawn from the blocks themselves.

member.summary: Expands one BC7 block.

remarks.para: The mode is the position of the lowest set bit, and everything else about the block follows from it — how many subsets the sixteen texels are divided into, how wide an endpoint is, whether alpha is stored at all, and whether the texel indices come in one set or two.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.DdsFile
member.summary: Reads DDS textures.

remarks.para: A block-compressed texture is the one image format that costs nothing to load: there is no decode, the mip chain is already built, and it takes a quarter of the video memory an R8G8B8A8 copy would. `PbrLab` measures the pilot set at 13.71 GiB uncompressed against 3.43 GiB compressed, and 45.5–47.0 dB on colour, which is not visible.

As narrow as the PNG reader, and for the same reason. Two-dimensional, no arrays, no cube maps, and only the three block formats the content pipeline emits. Anything else is refused by name so that a pipeline which starts producing something new hears about it.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.HeightField
member.summary: A height map as a number the CPU can ask for, rather than a picture for the device.

remarks.para: Everything else a height field is for happens in a shader, which reads it from a sampler and needs nothing here. Displacement is the exception: it moves vertices, and vertices are built once at load on this side of the seam. So the same map has to be readable twice, in two forms.

Mid grey is the modelled surface, which is the convention the whole pipeline shares: PbrLab integrates a normal map into a field and high-passes it back to a half, the shader subtracts a half before offsetting, and returns the same signed quantity — minus a half to plus a half of the field's full depth.

It is deliberately small. The shipped maps are 512 pixels and the workspace's are 2,048, and displacement samples at whatever spacing its triangle budget affords — six units on a street, which is a dozen texels apart at best. Reading a level low in the chain costs a fraction of the memory and answers the same question, so takes the smallest level that still has more texels than the geometry can use.

member.remarks: Bilinear and wrapping. Wrapping because a floor tiles its texture dozens of times across a street and the sampler that draws it repeats; a clamped read would flatten the relief along every tile's far edge into a smear of its last row.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.HeightField.Over(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: The field averaged over a square, as a signed fraction of its full depth.
member.param: Horizontal coordinate of the centre; wraps.
Vertical coordinate of the centre; wraps.
Width of the square, in texture coordinates.
member.returns: Minus a half to plus a half, zero being the modelled surface.
member.remarks: What displacement wants rather than . A vertex stands for a whole cell of the surface, and reading one texel at its centre makes the geometry a point sample of a field with detail far finer than the cell: the same street tessellated twice at slightly different densities comes out a different shape, and that shape is noise as often as it is cobbles. Averaging over the cell takes the part of the field the geometry can carry and leaves the rest to the parallax and the normal map, which is the division of labour those two were always meant to have.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.PngReader
member.summary: Reads PNG images.

remarks.para: The originals are GK3's own bitmaps, which handles; everything the project produces or takes in afterwards is PNG, because that is what Plan/02-content-pipeline.md chose as the editable form for images. Enhanced textures arrive that way, so loading one needs a reader and not only the writer that already existed.

Deliberately narrow. Every PNG in the corpus and in the enhanced set is eight bits a channel, RGB or RGBA, and not interlaced — 6,658 normalised textures and every candidate produced so far — so that is what this reads, and anything else is refused by name rather than half-decoded. A generator that starts emitting sixteen-bit or palettised output should hear about it from a diagnostic, not from a texture that looks subtly wrong.

It is also on the critical path for showing a room. The enhanced textures are 2048², which is 16 MB of pixels each, and a room asks for dozens; at 80 ms and 75 MB of garbage apiece that was ten seconds and several gigabytes for one scene. So every size here is known before anything is allocated, rows are reconstructed in place, and the filter is chosen once a row rather than once a byte.

member.remarks: Materialised rather than yielded, because a span cannot cross an iterator. It is a few dozen entries and the bodies stay where they are. The CRC is not checked: a truncated or corrupt file fails in the inflater or the row arithmetic either way, and with a name attached, which is what a reader owes its caller.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.PngReader.Inflate(System.Byte[],System.Int64,System.String)
member.summary: Inflates the image data into a buffer of exactly the size it must be.
member.remarks: The header says how many rows there are and how wide each is, and PNG adds one filter byte a row, so the inflated size is known before a byte is read. Reading exactly that many also does the truncation check for free.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.PngReader.Reconstruct(System.Byte[],System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.String)
member.summary: Undoes the per-row filters and widens to RGBA.

remarks.para: Every row carries a filter byte and is predicted from the pixel to its left and the row above, so rows have to be walked in order and cannot be skipped to. The five filters are the whole of PNG's compression cleverness; the rest is zlib.

Reconstructed in place, and the filter chosen once a row. Choosing it per byte — which is what falls out of writing this the obvious way — puts an unpredictable branch in front of every one of a 2048² texture's sixteen million bytes, and stops the Up filter, which is what an encoder picks for most rows of a photographic image, from vectorising at all.

member.summary: Each byte is predicted from the one a pixel to its left.

member.summary: Each byte is predicted from the one above it.
member.remarks: Nothing in the row depends on anything else in it, so the whole row adds a vector at a time.

member.summary: Each byte is predicted from the mean of the one left and the one above.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.PngReader.Paeth(System.Span{System.Byte},System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Int32)
member.summary: Each byte is predicted from whichever neighbour the gradient points at.
member.remarks: 95% of the rows in the enhanced set are this one, so it is where the decode spends its time and the only filter worth taking trouble over. Each byte depends on the byte a pixel to its left, so a row cannot be split — but the four channels within a pixel do not depend on each other, which is a vector four lanes wide.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.PngReader.PaethVector(System.Span{System.Byte},System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Int32)
member.summary: The Paeth filter, a pixel at a time.

remarks.para: The pixel to the left is whatever the last turn of the loop just wrote, so it stays in a register rather than being read back; the same goes for the pixel above-left, which is the pixel above from the turn before.

Four lanes are loaded whatever the pixel is worth, because reading three bytes costs the same as reading four. On RGB the fourth lane holds the next pixel's red, computes a result nobody stores, and is overwritten on the next turn — so the loop stops while four bytes are still readable and the last pixel or two go the scalar way.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Compression.Lzo1x
member.summary: Decompressor for the LZO1X streams used by GK3's Barn archives.

remarks.para: This is a managed port of the classic lzo1x_decompress. That routine is written as a web of gotos between labelled states, and C# will not let a goto jump into a nested scope, so the labels become an explicit state machine here. The states and their transitions are named after the originals so the two can be read side by side — the format is defined by that code rather than by a specification, and silently "tidying" the control flow is an excellent way to introduce a corruption that shows up in one asset out of thousands.
Unlike the reference, every read and write is bounds-checked against the input and output spans. A corrupt archive produces a naming the offset, not an out-of-bounds write.
Decompressing in managed code rather than binding to native minilzo keeps the toolchain free of a native dependency that would need building and shipping for every target platform.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Fonts.GlyphRasterizer
member.summary: Turns an outline into pixels.

remarks.para: A scanline fill with the nonzero winding rule, sampled several times down each pixel row and exactly across it. Vertical accuracy comes from the number of samples and horizontal accuracy is free, because a span's ends are known to the fraction of a pixel — which is the right trade for text, where the strokes that matter are vertical.

No hinting. The outline is not snapped to the pixel grid, so stems land where the design puts them and are grey at the edges rather than crisp. That is the modern answer — it is what a phone does — and it is the only one that keeps a letter the same shape at every size. The alternative is a bytecode interpreter serving screens that no longer exist.

member.remarks: Five is where the eye stops noticing on a horizontal edge, and each one costs a pass over the edges. Atlases are built once, so this is not a frame cost.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Fonts.TrueTypeFile
member.summary: A TrueType font: the outlines, the metrics, and which glyph a character is.

remarks.para: Why this exists at all. GK3's own fonts are bitmap sheets drawn for a 640x480 screen. Magnifying one by a whole number is the best that can be done with it, and on a modern display the interface is visibly made of enlarged pixels. An outline font is rasterised at whatever size the window actually is, so the text is crisp everywhere and the caption ladder stops being a ladder.
Written rather than taken from a package, in the same way every other format in this project is: the game's own parsers are here and this is no harder than the BSP.

What is deliberately not read. Hinting instructions are ignored — they are a bytecode interpreter's worth of work to serve 96-dpi screens that no longer exist, and a well-made font at menu sizes reads perfectly without them. Kerning lives in GPOS in modern fonts and is not read either, which costs a little air around a few pairs and nothing else. CFF outlines — an OpenType font whose curves are cubic — are refused rather than half-read.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Ini.IniDocument
member.summary: Reader for the INI dialect GK3's text assets use.

remarks.para: Scene initialisation files, scene assets, cursors, fonts and several other asset types share this format, so it is parsed once here rather than once per asset type.

It differs from ordinary INI in three ways. A line may carry several comma-separated key/value pairs, and commas inside braces belong to the value rather than separating pairs — pos={1, 2, 3} is one pair, not three. A bare token with no = is a keyword whose value repeats its key, which is how flags like hidden are written. And a section header may carry a condition, [MODELS={IsCurrentTime("202p")}], so the same section appears repeatedly with contents that depend on the story's state.
Conditions are kept verbatim. They are Sheep expressions, and evaluating them belongs to the Sheep virtual machine rather than to a text parser.

member.remarks: Whether commas separate pairs or belong to the value is a property of the asset type, not something that can be inferred from a line. Scene initialisation files write pos={1, 2, 3}, heading=90 and need splitting; scene assets write Position=1,2,3 and must not be split, or every vector in them reduces to its first component. Guessing per line gets the second case wrong silently, which is how a scene ends up with no lights at all rather than an error.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Lightmaps.MulFile
member.summary: Reader for GK3's baked lightmaps.

remarks.para: The tag reads TLUM on disk, being MULT stored little-endian. The layout is a count followed by that many bitmaps packed back to back in the ordinary texture format, with no offset table — so each one has to be measured to find the next.

The count matches the corresponding scene's surface count, and so does the order: lightmap i lights surface i. That pairing is what makes stage C4b possible, since a surface knows its own geometry and its lightmap UV offset and scale, while the lightmap knows how much light landed on it (ADR 0002).

These are the whole of the original game's lighting. There is nothing dynamic to recover, which is why the rigs C4b proposes have to be derived from this evidence and then reviewed by a human rather than simply read out.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Models.GlbReader
member.summary: Reads models written as glTF 2.0 binary (.glb) back into the engine's own model type.

remarks.para: The counterpart of , and the reason enhanced geometry can reach the screen at all. Until this existed enhanced/models was an output and never an input: the toolchain could convert a model out to glTF, improve it in a DCC and write it back, and the engine had no way to read the result. Everything drawn came from a .MOD.

A deliberately small subset, because the documents this reads are ones the project's own tools wrote: a static mesh hierarchy with positions, normals and one set of texture coordinates. Skins, morph targets, animation, sparse accessors and external buffers are refused rather than half-supported — a silently ignored skin is a model that draws in its bind pose forever and looks like a different bug.

A material names a texture and nothing else. GK3 addresses every surface by a texture name that the archives or the enhanced set resolve, so what the engine needs from a glTF material is that name; the PBR factors alongside it belong to a material system this renderer does not have. The name is taken from the material, falling back to the image, because Blender's exporter keeps material names exactly and rewrites image ones.

Coordinates pass straight through, as they do on the way out. The GLB files the toolchain writes are the game's own axes wearing a glTF label, so a model that goes to Blender and comes back lands exactly where it started — which is the property the tree work depends on, since a generated tree has to stand where the card it replaces stood.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Models.GlbWriter
member.summary: Writes models as glTF 2.0 binary (.glb).

remarks.para: glTF is the plan's interchange format for geometry, and a single .glb opens in Blender, any web viewer and most DCC tools without a plugin — which is the whole point of converting: 1,878 models currently exist in a format nothing but the game can read.

Materials reference the converted PNGs by relative URI, so a model opens textured as long as the normalized tree is intact. That keeps the geometry and its textures linked without embedding several megabytes of image into every model.

Normals are transformed into mesh space on the way out. glTF requires positions and normals to share a space, and in the original data they do not: positions are mesh space, normals appear to be local space. G-Engine applies the same correction, but only to models whose name is three characters — its own comment calls that a hack and says untransformed normals look wrong on characters while transformed ones look wrong on props. Exporting a self-consistent document is the right call for an interchange format; if the distinction turns out to be real, it belongs in the material pipeline rather than here.
