member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Models.LoopSubdivision
member.summary: Loop subdivision, for rounding off a 1999 silhouette.

remarks.para: GK3's characters are already shaded smoothly — their vertex normals are welded and agree to within a rounding error, across texture seams included — so what makes a head read as low-polygon is not its shading but its outline. Grace's hair is twenty triangles and Madeline's is thirteen, and no amount of work in texture space moves the edge of a twenty-sided shape. Subdivision is the only thing that does.

Boundary vertices are pinned rather than smoothed. The textbook rule moves them along the boundary curve, and where two submeshes meet — the hairline, the ear — that would be fine, because both sides move identically and the seam stays shut. The rim at the neck is the problem: it is the edge of the head shell, nothing on the other side is being refined with it, and a rim that shrinks opens a hole in someone's throat. Pinning costs a slightly flatter surface within one row of triangles of a boundary and cannot open a gap anywhere.

Texture coordinates are interpolated linearly rather than subdivided. The face texture is a composited surface — FaceController blits eyes and a mouth onto it at coordinates CHARACTERS.TXT gives in pixels — so the mapping has to stay where it was put. Smoothing the UVs as well would move a character's mouth.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Models.ModFile
member.summary: Reader for GK3's model format.

remarks.para: Documented from G-Engine's Model::ParseFromData. Tags are stored little-endian, so they read reversed on disk: LDOM for the file, HSEM per mesh, PRGM per submesh — the game called those "mesh groups" — KDOL for level-of-detail blocks and XDOM for the trailing section.

Two oddities are handled rather than explained, because the reference implementation does not explain them either: each triangle carries a fourth 16-bit value of unknown meaning after its three indices, and each LODK block holds three counted arrays whose contents are unidentified. Both are skipped by size.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Rebarn.RebarnArchive
member.summary: Reads one ReBarn pack.

remarks.para:
The whole volume is memory-mapped once and never read into the heap. A 2048-pixel BC7 texture is 5.6 MB, a room wants dozens of them, and they are read on every core at once: copying each one out of the file into a byte array before uploading it doubles the high-water mark of a scene load to achieve nothing at all.
hands back a window onto the mapping instead.

That window is only valid while the archive is open, which is the one sharp edge here and the reason — which copies — is the default. The engine keeps its packs open for the life of the process, so the mapped path is safe there; a tool that opens a pack in a using and holds the bytes afterwards would read freed address space. says so on its own summary.

Mapping costs address space rather than memory. An eleven-gigabyte volume reserves eleven gigabytes of a 64-bit address space and pages in only what is touched, so a session that visits four rooms pays for four rooms.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Rebarn.RebarnBuilder
member.summary: Writes a ReBarn pack.

remarks.para: One streaming pass. Sources are added by path or by bytes, then copies each one into the volume in turn, recording where it landed, and finishes with the name table, the index and a rewritten header. Nothing is held in memory but the index — fifteen gigabytes of textures go through a one-megabyte buffer.

The order entries are written in is the order they were added, and the index is sorted by key hash afterwards, so a pack built twice from the same inputs is byte for byte the same file. That is what lets a build be compared, and what stops a rebuild looking like a change to anything watching the directory.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Rebarn.RebarnFormat
member.summary: The ReBarn container: constants, keys, and the header that opens every volume.

remarks.para: ReBarn holds the remake's own content — enhanced textures and their material channels, modernised models, imported video — in a file that sits beside the executable. It is deliberately not GK3's Barn format: Barn is a 1999 archive with 32-bit offsets and per-entry LZO, and what this has to hold is fifteen gigabytes of block data that must reach the GPU without being decoded on the way.

Which is the whole design. Every offset is 64-bit; entries are aligned so that a mapped view of one can be handed straight to a staging buffer; and block-compressed textures are stored verbatim, because a DDS is already compressed and running DEFLATE over one buys a few per cent for a decompression pass on the critical path of a room load. Time to display is what matters — see docs/formats/rebarn.md.

Layout, in order: a 64-byte header, the data section, the name table, then the index. The index is last so that a pack can be written in one streaming pass without knowing in advance how large it will be, and the header is rewritten at the end with the three offsets that pass discovered.
remarks.code: 0 header 64 bytes 64 data entries, each starting on a 256-byte boundary .. name table UTF-8, no separators; entries carry an offset and a length .. index entryCount records of 48 bytes, sorted by key hash

Bit 1 appears on walls, ceilings and floors, bit 2 on surfaces that are hard to make out, bit 4 on a mixture of light sources and hit tests, and bit 32 nowhere in the corpus; the three that carry meaning here are named below. Documented from G-Engine's BSPSurface.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.BspSurface.IsSelfLit
member.summary: Whether the bake lit this surface, or it carries its own brightness.
member.remarks: The original binds a white lightmap and a multiplier of one for these, which comes out as the texture at full brightness: a lit bulb, a glowing shade, the painted view through a window. Multiplying them by a bake instead leaves them as dim as the room they are supposed to be lighting.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.BspSurface.CastsShadows
member.summary: Whether this surface should block a ray-traced shadow.
member.remarks: Light fittings must not. The rig puts its emitters where the bulb is — inside the shade, behind the pane, under the sconce — because the 1999 bake did not trace the fitting against its own light. Tracing it now seals every one of those lights inside its fixture and the room goes dark, which is what R25's lamps and its window showed. The data says which surfaces those are, so they are left out of the acceleration structure exactly as alpha-keyed geometry is.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.BspFile
member.summary: Reader for GK3's scene geometry: the rooms themselves.

remarks.para: 110 files, 56 MB, holding every location in the game. Documented from G-Engine's BSP::ParseFromData. The tag reads NECS on disk, being SCEN stored little-endian.

Only what is needed to reconstruct the visible geometry is kept: names, surfaces, polygons, vertices, texture coordinates and the index array. The BSP tree itself — nodes, planes and bounding spheres — is read past rather than retained, because a modern renderer does not traverse it and an exporter has no use for it. The original navigation data lives elsewhere, so nothing here is load-bearing for collision.
Surfaces carry a lightmap offset and scale per surface, which stage C4b needs when it back-projects lightmap luminance to propose scene lights (ADR 0002).

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.SceneAssetFile
member.summary: Reader for scene assets: the geometry, skybox, model list and lights of a scene at one time of day.

remarks.para: This file answers the question ADR 0002 left open. The plan assumed the original lighting existed only as baked lightmaps and that light positions would have to be inferred from them. They do not: every scene asset carries the full rig the artists authored — position, direction, colour, cone angles, attenuation range, intensity, emitter radius and whether the light cast shadows in the bake. R25 at night alone declares 48 of them.

That is a far better starting point for a modern re-light than anything derived from lightmap texels. The derived rigs remain useful as a cross-check — a light in the file that leaves no trace in the bake was disabled or occluded — but the file is the source of truth.

Units need care. Cone angles are stored in radians and attenuation distances in scene units, but intensity and colour were tuned for a 1999 renderer with no exposure control, so they are hints rather than physical quantities.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.SceneGlbWriter
member.summary: Exports a parsed scene as glTF binary.

remarks.para: Reuses the model exporter by presenting the scene as a set of meshes: one per named object in the room, with a submesh per texture inside it. That grouping is the one the original data already carries — several surfaces make up a "door" — so a room opens in Blender as a named outliner tree rather than as one undifferentiated soup of triangles.

Scene geometry has no per-vertex normals in the original. They are computed from face winding and averaged across the vertices that share them, which is the best available reconstruction and enough for the geometry to shade sensibly in a viewer.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.SceneInitFile
member.summary: Reader for scene initialisation files.

remarks.para: A SIF says what a scene is: which scene asset to load for a given time of day, which models stand in it, which actors are present, where the cameras are and where the player may walk. Without it a BSP is a building with no way in and no indication of which way is the front.

Almost everything in one is conditional. The same scene has different geometry, different props and different lighting at each of the game's timeblocks, expressed as repeated sections whose headers carry Sheep expressions. Reading a SIF without evaluating those conditions gives the union of every state the scene can be in, which is right for tooling and wrong for the game — so which to include is the caller's choice.

member.remarks: It changes what a repeated declaration means. remarks.para: Every one that applies, rather than the last: camera bounds are the one general setting the original adds to instead of overriding, and the corpus relies on it. R25 names R25CameraBounds for the room and then r25_sidcm in the conditional block for the timeblocks where Sidney is out on the desk, fencing the camera out of the space the close-up needs.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.SceneInitFile.Models(System.Boolean)
member.summary: The models the scene places, deduplicated by name.
member.param: Whether to include conditional sections.
member.returns: The models.

remarks.para: The same model appears in several conditional blocks, and the later ones refine the noun and type of the earlier, so those come from the last occurrence.

Hiding does not work that way when the conditions have not been decided. A pair of blocks under complementary conditions — {!IsCurrentTime("202p")} and {IsCurrentTime("202p")} — describes two states of the scene, of which exactly one holds; the second is not a correction of the first. Taking the last occurrence would hide whatever any block hides, which is how the hall door in R25 disappeared and left its knob behind. So without a model is hidden only when every block that declares it agrees, and the rest are reported through . Erring towards drawing matches this reader's treatment of conditionals everywhere else: an object that should not be there is a smaller loss than a missing wall or door.
With the conditions decided the question does not arise. Only one of the pair applies, so the last declaration wins outright — hiding included — and nothing is ever in dispute.

member.remarks: Bare names on their own lines, no key= about them, and the name carries the meaning: r25_all.nvc applies to every timeblock, r25_23all.nvc to days two and three, r25202p.nvc to that afternoon alone. See for how that is read.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Ui.FontFile
member.summary: One of GK3's 137 bitmap fonts.

remarks.para: A .FON is a handful of keys and one long Font= line listing, in order, every character the sheet contains. The sheet itself is an ordinary texture. What is not written down anywhere is where each character starts and stops: the top row of the sheet carries a marker colour at the left edge of every glyph, and the width of a character is the distance to the next marker.

So reading a font means scanning a row of pixels. The first pixel of the sheet is the background; the first pixel along the top row that is not the background is the marker; and from there each run between markers is one character, taken in the order the Font= line gives them.
Some sheets stack several rows of glyphs, which Line Count gives. The top pixel of each row is the marker strip and not part of the letter, so a glyph is one pixel shorter than the row that holds it.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Formats.Ui.FontFile.Cut(System.String,System.Int32,GK3Reborn.Foundation.Diagnostics.DiagnosticBag)
member.summary: Walks the marker strip and cuts the sheet into characters.

remarks.para: The marker colour is whatever the first non-background pixel of the top row is — most fonts use pure red, but not all of them do, and a couple are a few units off it, so the comparison allows a little slack rather than demanding an exact match.

A row's last marker may be a terminator rather than a glyph. On a sheet with one row the last letter ends at the sheet's right edge and nothing has to say so; on a sheet with several, the rows are different lengths and each needs a mark saying where its last letter stops, with padding after it. Counting that mark as a glyph costs the row one character and shifts every character after it — which is why the caption sheets, the only multi-row fonts the interface draws with, wrote Gabqiel Lnnk where they meant Gabriel Look.

Which of the two a sheet is doing is decided by counting rather than guessing: the Font= line says how many characters there are, so a sheet with exactly that many markers has no terminators and one with that many plus a marker per row has one each. Neither, and each row is judged on whether there is any ink after its last mark. Across the corpus the count settles 112 of the 136 fonts outright.

member.summary: Where the markers along one row's top edge are.
member.remarks: The starts of runs, not every marked pixel: a marker two pixels wide is one marker. The scan begins where the first row's did, because a row whose first letter is narrower than another's still starts in the same column.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Ui.KeyedText
member.summary: The game's prose files: sections of key = the rest of the line.

remarks.para: ESIDNEY.TXT, ESIDNEYEMAIL.TXT and their neighbours look like the scene initialisation files and are not the same thing. A .SIF line is a list of comma-separated settings and splits it as one; these hold a single value that runs to the end of the line, and most of them are English sentences full of commas. Parsing one with the other reader turns a paragraph into forty settings.

So: sections in brackets, one key to a line, everything after the first = is the value. Comments start with ; or // — both appear, sometimes in the same file — and a key may repeat, which is how Body1, Body2 would work if the game had not numbered them; order is kept either way.

Two escapes are decoded, because the files are written for a renderer that understood them: \n and \t as the characters they name, and <space> as a paragraph break on a line of its own. Nothing else is interpreted — a %s in the Sidney text is a placeholder its caller fills, and this is not its caller.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Video.Aac.AacDecoder
member.summary: AAC-LC decoder for raw (non-ADTS) access units as stored in MP4 mp4a samples.

remarks.para: The port plays the game's cut-scene movies from MP4, whose audio track is AAC-LC. Decoding it in managed code keeps deployment a single self-contained build on every platform: no FFmpeg binaries to ship per OS and architecture, no native loader, no licence bundle. The whole decoder is a few thousand lines because AAC-LC without SBR is a small format: Huffman-coded quantised spectra, a handful of stereo tools, and an overlapped inverse MDCT.

Supported: single, pair and LFE channel elements, all window sequences and both window shapes, all spectral codebooks, pulse data, TNS, M/S, intensity and perceptual noise substitution, and the skip-over of data, fill (including SBR payloads) and program-config elements. Not supported: 960-sample frames, main profile prediction, LTP, SBR/PS reconstruction and more than two channels. The decoder is not thread-safe; use one instance per stream.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Video.Aac.HuffmanCodebook
member.summary: One AAC Huffman codebook prepared for fast decoding.
member.remarks: The standard lists each book as (length, codeword, values) rows. Scanning those rows per symbol, as the reference decoder does, costs tens of comparisons for every pair of coefficients. Instead a ten-bit direct lookup resolves the common short codes in one array read, and the rare longer codes (up to 19 bits in the scalefactor book) fall through to a binary tree walk.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Video.Aac.Imdct
member.summary: Inverse MDCT of 2048 or 256 points, evaluated through an N/4-point complex FFT.

remarks.para: The direct definition, x[n] = (2/N) sum X[k] cos(2pi/N (n + n0)(k + 1/2)), is an O(N^2) sum that would cost more than everything else in the decoder combined. The same values come out of a DCT-IV of N/2 points, which folds into an N/4-point FFT with a complex twiddle before and after, and the DCT-IV's symmetries give the four quarters of the IMDCT output.
The FFT is a plain radix-2 decimation-in-time on split real/imaginary arrays with precomputed twiddles; at 512 and 64 points it needs no cleverer scheme.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Video.H264.Deblocker
member.summary: The in-loop deblocking filter, 8.7, run over a whole picture once its slices are decoded.

remarks.para: Macroblock by macroblock in raster order, and within each: the vertical luma edges left to right, the horizontal ones top to bottom, then chroma the same way. The order matters because each edge is filtered in place and the next reads what the last wrote.

Boundary strengths come from the per-block state the slice decoder stored: intra, coefficients, and which pictures each block predicted from — compared by picture, not by index, since two indices can name one picture.

member.summary: An H.264 decoder for progressive 8-bit 4:2:0, 4:4:4 and monochrome video: the parts of the standard the game's cinematics use, with CAVLC and CABAC, all slice types, all intra modes, weighted and direct prediction, and the deblocking filter.

member.summary: Fractional-sample interpolation, 8.4.2.2, and weighted sample prediction, 8.4.2.3.

remarks.para: A block's reference window is copied into a local buffer with its coordinates clamped to the picture, which is how the standard defines reads beyond the edge; the block itself is then computed from that window without further bounds checks. Luma is quarter-sample with the six-tap filter, chroma of a 4:2:0 picture eighth-sample bilinear; 4:4:4 chroma is interpolated like luma, as 8.4.2.2 requires.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Video.H264.IntraPrediction
member.summary: Intra prediction, 8.3: builds a block from the reconstructed samples around it.

remarks.para: The 4x4 and 8x8 predictors share one implementation over an edge array laid out so that the standard's p[x, -1] and p[-1, y] are plain offsets from the corner: the left column bottom-up, the corner, then the top row. The formulas can then be written as they appear in 8.3.1.2 and 8.3.2.2, negative indices included.
Prediction writes straight into the picture; the residual is added on top afterwards.

member.summary: A sequence parameter set: what every picture of a coded video sequence has in common.
member.remarks: Only progressive 8-bit video is accepted. member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Video.H264.Picture
member.summary: A decoded picture: its three planes and everything later pictures and later macroblocks need to know about how it was coded.

remarks.para: Motion vectors, reference choices and coefficient counts are kept per 4x4 block in raster order within the macroblock — (y / 4) * 4 + x / 4 — rather than in the standard's block-index order, because prediction looks up "the block to the left" far more often than it looks up "block 5", and raster order makes that an offset of one.
Everything is flat arrays indexed by macroblock address so the decoder allocates nothing per macroblock, and the arrays are reused when the picture is.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Video.H264.SliceDecoder
member.summary: The CABAC half of macroblock parsing: 7.3.5 read with the contexts of 9.3.
member.remarks: Context index increments are derived from the neighbouring macroblocks exactly as 9.3.3.1.1 says, with the picture's stored per-macroblock and per-block state standing in for "the syntax element of mbAddrN". The conventions that make those lookups uniform — a skipped macroblock stores cbp 0, an I_PCM one stores cbp 0x2F and every coded block flag set — are chosen in .
member.summary: The CAVLC half of macroblock parsing: 7.3.5 read with Exp-Golomb codes and the coefficient coding of 9.2.
Decodes the macroblocks of one slice into a picture.

remarks.para: One object per picture, re-pointed at each slice: the scratch macroblock, the entropy decoders and the prediction buffers are allocated once. The slice loop is here; the entropy-specific parsing is in the CABAC and CAVLC partial files, motion vector prediction in the motion one, and the sample-level work — intra prediction, motion compensation, transforms — in static helpers that know nothing about slices.

Macroblocks are addressed in raster order and a neighbour is available when it is in the picture, has been decoded, and belongs to this slice — the last being what makes slices independently decodable and what the deblocking filter, which runs afterwards over the whole picture, does not care about.

member.summary: What each mb_type and sub_mb_type means, Tables 7-11 to 7-18, and the block geometry that follows from it.

Motion vector prediction, 8.4.1: turning differences into vectors, and inferring the vectors of skipped and direct-predicted blocks from their neighbours or from the co-located block of the first list-1 reference.
From a parsed macroblock to samples in the picture: prediction, then the residual on top of it.

member.summary: Ticks to subtract from every presentation time before it means anything.
member.remarks: The edit list. A file whose pictures are reordered, or whose sound has an encoder delay, says so by declaring that the presentation starts some way into the media rather than at its first sample; a player that ignores it shows the first few frames late and the sound early. Only the simplest and by far most common form is honoured — a single edit, possibly preceded by an empty one — which is what FFmpeg writes and what the import produces.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Formats.Video.YuvConverter
member.summary: Turns a decoded Y'CbCr picture into the RGBA a texture upload wants.

remarks.para: Limited-range BT.601 unless the stream's VUI says BT.709 or full range: the game's cinematics are standard-definition conversions of standard-definition sources, and nothing in the import tags them, which is the case BT.601 is the convention for. The same choice FFmpeg's scaler makes for untagged video, so a frame through this path looks the way it did through that one.

Fixed point with lookup tables, one multiply per channel per sample. Chroma of a 4:2:0 picture is used at its own resolution — each chroma sample covers a 2x2 block of luma — which is what a nearest upsampling is, and what looks right for material that was 320x240 to begin with.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Foundation.DeterministicRandom
member.summary: The engine's only source of randomness: explicitly seeded and reproducible.

remarks.para: Plan/04-execution-and-quality.md P4: GK3Reborn deliberately does NOT reproduce GEngine's random streams. GEngine seeds std::default_random_engine from the wall clock, declares it static in a header (so every translation unit gets its own generator), and uses std::uniform_*_distribution, whose output is implementation-defined. That stream is unreproducible even against itself, and it is not the 1999 executable's stream either.

Instead: one documented algorithm (xoshiro256++), one explicit seed, saved and restored with the game state. Differential tests compare RNG-dependent outcomes as equivalence classes, not exact streams.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Foundation.InstallPaths
member.summary: Where the game may read from and where it may write, given where it was installed.

remarks.para: Everything the game reaches for is derived from - content, saves, the shader cache. That works on Windows and Linux, where a game is a directory somebody unpacked and owns. It does not work on macOS, where an installed application is a signed, read-only .app bundle in /Applications: writing into it either fails outright or breaks the signature, and the executable does not even sit at the root of the tree but three levels down in Contents/MacOS.

So there are two roots rather than one. is the read-only half - the bundle's own Contents/Resources, where a packaged build puts whatever it ships. is the writable half, per user and outside any install, which is where settings have always gone and where saves and the shader cache go when the game cannot write beside itself.

Nothing here is macOS-only in effect. A Windows or Linux game still finds its writable directories beside the executable, because that is where they are writable; the fallback simply stops being hypothetical on a Mac.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Foundation.InstallPaths.UserData
member.summary: The per-user directory for anything the game writes that is not a saved game.
member.remarks: %AppData%\GK3Reborn on Windows and ~/.config/GK3Reborn on Linux, both of which are what gives. On macOS that same folder is also ~/.config, which is not where a Mac keeps per-application state - ~/Library/Application Support is, and a file put anywhere else is invisible to Time Machine's migration and to the user. Named explicitly for that reason rather than trusted to the BCL's Unix mapping.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Foundation.InstallPaths.BundleResources
member.summary: The Contents/Resources of the .app bundle the game is running from, or null when it is not running from one.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Foundation.InstallPaths.InAppBundle
member.summary: Whether the executable is inside a macOS application bundle.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Foundation.InstallPaths.WritableRoot
member.summary: The directory a loose file the game writes belongs in: the executable's own when that can be written to, and when it cannot.
member.remarks: The directory returned exists by the time it is returned.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Foundation.InstallPaths.WritableDirectory(System.String)
member.summary: A directory the game may write to, named beside the executable when that is possible and under when it is not.
member.param: Directory name, such as shader-cache.
member.returns: An absolute path to a directory that exists and can be written to.
member.remarks: Beside the executable first because that keeps an unpacked install self-contained: somebody who moves the folder takes their shader cache with them. The probe is a real write rather than a permissions check, because a permissions check answers a different question than the one being asked on a read-only volume, an unsigned bundle or a directory behind a consent prompt nobody is there to answer.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Foundation.InstallPaths.CanWrite(System.String)

member.param: Directory to probe. Created if it does not exist.
member.returns: True when a file was written there and removed again.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Foundation.InstallPaths.FindBundleResources(System.String)
member.summary: Recognises <name>.app/Contents/MacOS and returns the sibling Resources.
member.param: The executable's own directory.
member.returns: The bundle's resources directory, or null.
member.remarks: The shape of the path is the test, not the operating system: a bundle laid out on a Windows machine by the macOS publish profile is still a bundle, and being able to reason about one without a Mac is the difference between this being testable and not. Public for that reason - is the answer for this process, and this is the answer for any path.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionResolver
member.summary: Decides what the player can do to something right now.

remarks.para: This is the hinge between the original data and the modern interaction model. The game's action files list every noun, verb and the condition under which that pairing applies; the original engine used the same information to decide which verbs to put on its verb wheel. Asking it for one noun's currently valid verbs is the same query, answered for a different interface.

Plan/03-gameplay-ui-audio.md section 2.3 requires that modernising input must not change what an action does, so this resolver only ever *selects*: the script it returns is the original script, unchanged, and execution still goes through Sheep.
It also never mutates state. A resolver that evaluated a condition by trying the action would corrupt the save just by hovering the cursor.

member.summary: The nouns a click on one noun also answers to.

remarks.para: GK3 writes a handful of rules about two people at once and expects clicking either of them to find it. Nothing in the data declares the equivalence — the reference implementation hard-codes the same list and says so — so this is the shipped content's own shape rather than a rule anything can derive.
Without them, Lady Howard and Estelle answer to nothing they share, and the Armchair's two bodies lose every line written about their clothes and their throats.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionResolver.OpensTheTopicList(GK3Reborn.Formats.Actions.NvcAction)
member.summary: Whether a rule is the Talk that exists only to reach the topics.

remarks.para: TALK is a real verb with 127 rules of its own, and most of them do something no topic does: Larry has a line, Prince James has a conversation, and nine rules are guarded by NOT_DIALOGUE_TOPICS_LEFT and are what a character says once there is nothing left to ask them. Those all stay.

Thirty-two are guarded by DIALOGUE_TOPICS_LEFT, and that case means exactly "there is something to ask about". In the original, choosing Talk there opened the list of T_ verbs; this port puts them on the menu itself, so offering Talk beside them is offering the player a door into the room they are standing in.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionResolver.Find(System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Finds the rule a verb on a noun would run.
member.param: The thing being acted on.
What is being done to it.
Who the player currently is.
member.returns: The rule, or null when nothing applies.

remarks.para: Four sets of rules can answer, from the most general to the most particular, and the last one that does wins: the wildcard pair, the wildcard noun with this verb, this noun with the wildcard item verb, and finally the pair actually asked about. The two item forms are consulted only for an inventory verb, because ANY_INV_ITEM means "whatever is in hand" and there is nothing in hand otherwise.
Selecting still changes nothing; performing is 's job.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionResolver.Elsewhen(GK3Reborn.Formats.Actions.NvcAction)
member.summary: Whether an action belongs to a different point in the story than this one.
member.param: The rule.
member.returns: True when it cannot sensibly run now.

remarks.para: Reported as the church's four angels offering "Trace" on the first morning, two days before the puzzle that verb belongs to. The shipped data really does allow it: the case is VALID_TO_TRACE, which reads !GetFlag("LockedSquare") && GetNounVerbCount("Four_Angels","Trace") == 0, and both halves are true from the moment the game begins. The original offers it early too.

The rule says when it belongs, in its own script. Those actions end in CallSheep("chu205p", "Done") — they hand off to the compiled script of one point in the story, which is loaded at that point and at no other. An action that calls into a script the game has not got is an action that cannot finish, and offering it is offering a verb that does half of something.

107 distinct timeblock scripts are called this way across the corpus, so this is a general reading of the data rather than a patch for one statue. A rule that names no such script is not filtered by it at all.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionResolver.Now
member.summary: Where the story has got to, when anything told the resolver.
member.remarks: Null leaves filtering nothing, which is what the tools want: a sweep asks what a room can do across the whole story rather than at one moment in it, and a resolver with no clock must not quietly answer a narrower question.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionResolver.Approaching(GK3Reborn.Formats.Actions.NvcAction,System.String)
member.summary: Gives a topic the walk that the Talk it was hoisted out of would have made.
member.param: The rule that is going to run.
Who the player currently is.
member.returns: The same rule, or a copy of it carrying an approach.

remarks.para: In the original, asking somebody about something took two steps. TALK carried the approach — EMILIO, TALK, DIALOGUE_TOPICS_LEFT, approach=ANIM, target=GabEmlLbyShake walks Gabriel over and shakes his hand — and the topics it then opened carried none, because by that point he was already standing there.

drops that Talk and puts the topics on the menu directly, which is the improvement docs/screens.md asks for; it also dropped the walk along with the step it replaced, so Gabriel could hold a conversation with Emilio from the phone-room curtains on the far side of the lobby.

Only the approach is borrowed. The script a topic runs is its own and is untouched, which is what Plan/03 section 2.3 requires of anything that modernises input. A topic that states its own approach keeps it, and a noun whose Talk states none gains nothing.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionResolver.Best(System.String,System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: The one rule a noun and verb run, out of however many could.
member.param: The noun the rules are written about, which may be a wildcard.
The verb they are written for, which may be a wildcard.
The verb actually being done, which is what decides its kind.
Who the player currently is.
member.returns: The rule to run, or null when none of them applies.

remarks.para: Not the first one the files list. Several rules for one pair are ordinary — the lobby writes REGISTER, LOOK, GABE_ALL above REGISTER, LOOK, NOT_SEEN_REGISTER — and taking whichever came first gives Gabriel the line he says about a register he has already read, the first time he reads it.

The case decides, on the original's own ladder: the catch-alls are worth least, a timeblock's override more, a condition somebody actually wrote more still, and "the first time you did this" most of all. Where two hand-written conditions tie, the more specific file wins, and where that ties too the original falls back on comparing the case names — see , which is as strange as it looks and is what the shipped data was authored against.

member.returns: Its rank, higher being stronger.
member.remarks: The original's ladder, lowest first: the catch-alls, then the ego-specific ones, then a timeblock's plain marker, then "not the first time", then the two questions about whether there is anything left to say, then a timeblock's override, then any condition written in a logic section, and above everything the counted ones.

member.param: The case being considered.

member.remarks: Not an ordinal comparison. A digit beats anything that is not one and a smaller digit beats a larger; an underscore beats any letter; otherwise the earlier letter wins. member.summary: Whether anything is left to say to someone.

remarks.para: A topic is a verb: dialogue is written as actions whose verbs are named T_SOMETHING, so "are there topics left" is "is there a T_ action for this noun whose case holds and which has not been used up". The original tracks the topics played this conversation; this reads the count the story keeps, which says the same thing for everything except a topic said twice in one sitting.
Topic cases are not consulted recursively. A topic whose own case is DIALOGUE_TOPICS_LEFT would ask this question to answer this question, and the original does not define what that means either.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionRunner
member.summary: Runs the script an action names.

remarks.para: chooses; this performs. They are deliberately separate: choosing happens whenever the cursor moves and must not touch the story, while performing is what a click is for. Plan/03 section 2.3 requires that modernising input must not change what an action does, so the script executed here is the original's own text, unchanged, evaluated through the same Sheep host everything else goes through.

An action's script is a much smaller language than Sheep. Across the corpus's 5,872 scripts there are 6,842 statements, every one of them a function call, 5,824 of those prefixed with wait, drawn from 55 distinct functions of which StartVoiceOver alone is 4,314. There are no branches, no loops and no locals: the files put that in the case conditions and in the scripts the actions call into. So this reads statements rather than compiling a language, and refuses anything else out loud instead of guessing at it.

wait is recorded and not obeyed, because there is nothing yet for a script to wait on: calls run inline to completion, which produces the same observable order for anything that does not depend on real elapsed time. Keeping it in the record is what lets that stop being true later without the traces becoming incomparable.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionRunner.Finish(GK3Reborn.Formats.Actions.NvcAction)
member.summary: What the engine does once an action is over, whatever its script said.
member.remarks: Topics and chats count themselves; ordinary verbs do not. That asymmetry is the original's — a topic is used up by being raised, so the engine records it, while an ordinary action increments its own count only if its script says IncNounVerbCount, which 260 of the corpus's scripts do. Counting them all here would make every 1ST_TIME rule fire once and never again.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionRunner.Approach(GK3Reborn.Formats.Actions.NvcAction,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Reads a script into statements, or explains why it cannot.
Takes the player to the thing before doing anything to it.
member.param: The action, whose approach says how.

remarks.para: An action file says approach=WalkTo, target=TO_B25 beside the script, and it is not part of the script: it is what has to be true before the script runs. Nothing performed it, so Gabriel opened doors from across the room.

The walk is started here and how long it takes is handed back, so that the caller can hold the script until the player has arrived. That is what the original does: Scene::ExecuteAction walks the ego to the approach target and performs the action from the arrival callback. Running the script over the walk instead is what had Gabriel talking to somebody he was still crossing the square towards.
TurnToModel and TurnTo are approaches too and they are turns rather than walks, so they go through the same hook saying so. 394 of the corpus's 3,617.

member.param: Whether the player asked for it twice.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionRunner.Measure(System.String)
member.summary: Works out how long a waited statement takes without performing it.
member.param: The call, as the script wrote it.
member.returns: Seconds, or zero when the host cannot say.

remarks.para: How long a call takes depends on its arguments — which line of dialogue, which animation — so the arguments have to be worked out, and working them out means evaluating the expression. Reading a script is supposed to change nothing, so the evaluation is done against a host that does nothing, and the call is caught on its way in rather than being allowed to happen.

An argument that is itself a call — StartVoiceOver(GetVar("x"), 1) — comes out empty, because the inert host has nothing to return. There are none of those in the corpus; if there were, they would read as instantaneous rather than wrong.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionRunner.Inert
member.summary: A host that does nothing, for finding out what a script would call.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionRunner.NameOf(System.String)
member.summary: The function a statement calls, if it is a call at all.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionRunner.Split(System.String)
member.summary: Splits a script into statements on the semicolons that separate them.
member.remarks: Not every semicolon: one inside a string is part of the string, and one inside parentheses belongs to an argument list. Splitting on all of them works for nearly every script in the corpus and fails silently on the rest, which is the worst way for it to be wrong.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionSets
member.summary: Which action files are in scope in a scene, and in what order.

remarks.para: A scene's verbs do not all come from the scene. Four sets of files are in play at once: the timeblock file's own, listed in its [ACTIONS] section; the location's, listed in the general file and spanning days or the whole game; a dozen global sets that apply everywhere; and sixteen inventory sets that say what can be done with what the player is carrying. Without the last two most objects have no LOOK, because looking at things is a rule about the game rather than about the room.

Which of them apply is written in their names — R25_23ALL.NVC is days two and three — and reads that. The original checks the name for the files the general file lists and for the global and inventory sets, and does not check it for the timeblock file's own: that file is already the timeblock's, so anything it names is meant for now whatever it is called.

Order is priority, because keeps the first rule it finds for a verb. Most specific first, then, which is the opposite of the order the original inserts them in — it can afford general-first because it keeps every rule and separates them by case at the point of use, where this keeps one entry per verb so that a menu can be built from the answer.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionSets.Global

member.remarks: From G-Engine's ActionManager::kGlobalActionSets. The names encode their own timeblocks, so this is the whole list and the range decides.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionSets.Inventory

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ActionSets.For(GK3Reborn.Game.SceneDefinition,System.Nullable{GK3Reborn.Game.Timeblock})
member.summary: The files a scene brings into scope, most specific first.
member.param: The scene's initialisation files.

Where the story is, or null when the caller named no timeblock. With no timeblock there is no way to tell which of a location's files apply, so all of them are taken and the global and inventory sets are left out — the same union the rest of the loader falls back to when the conditions cannot be decided.
member.returns: File names, without duplicates, in the order they should be consulted.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actions.VerbLibrary
member.summary: VERBS.TXT — every verb the game knows, and which kind each one is.

remarks.para: One INI section holding 287 lines, each naming a verb and the icons that draw it. What matters here is the type at the end: Normal, Inventory, Topic or RecurringTopic. There are 88 topics and one recurring one.

The distinction is the whole of what separates talking from doing. An action file makes no distinction — a topic is written exactly like a verb, BUTHANE, T_TOUR_GROUP, CASE, script={...} — so without this file there is no way to tell "ask her about the tour group" from "open her". Guessing by the T_ prefix gets close and gets the recurring ones wrong, which is the difference between a topic that is used up and one that may be raised again.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.AnimationStart
member.summary: Where an animation expects somebody to be standing before it starts.

remarks.para: approach=anim is the third most common approach in the game — 398 of the corpus's 3,617 — and it is the only one whose target is not a place. It names an animation, and what it means is walk to where that animation begins, then play it. Pouring the coffee in the hotel dining room is the case: without this Gabriel starts pouring from wherever he is standing, and the pot is across the room.

The animation does not say where it begins in so many words. It says it in the clip: the first frame poses every mesh, and among a character's meshes are three that are not body parts at all — an axis triad at the hips and one under each shoe, which is the only thing in a GK3 character that stands for a skeleton. CHARACTERS.TXT names which mesh, group and point they are, per character. The hip triad's point is where the actor stands.

Which way they face has to be worked out rather than read, and this is the part that is not obvious. A character's model normally faces −Z, so a heading is the mesh's rotation plus a half turn — but the game is not consistent about it and a few animations are authored the other way round. The triads settle it: the three points make a triangle whose normal is the way the body is actually facing, and comparing that against the hip mesh's own Y axis says which of the two conventions this clip was authored in. Getting it wrong walks the actor to the right spot with their back to the thing.

remarks.para: The same measure takes, at any frame rather than the first: an actor stands where the triad under their hips is.

It matters wherever a position is read out of a clip rather than differenced across one. The average of a character's mesh-group origins moves with exactly the same rigid motion, so a difference of two averages is the same answer and much cheaper — but one average on its own is that answer plus a constant, and the constant is most of a torso. Emilio walked out of the hotel and then set off for his bench from a couple of feet behind where he was standing.

member.remarks: The shoes and the hips make a triangle, and its normal flattened onto the floor is the direction the body faces. Nearly every model in the game has that opposite the hip mesh's Y axis, which is what makes a heading "the mesh's rotation plus a half turn"; a few have it the same way round, and for those the half turn must not be applied. The dot product is the whole of the test, and it is the original's.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.CharacterHead
member.summary: Which part of a character is the head.

remarks.para: GK3's people have no skeleton. A character is a dozen or so separate meshes, each with its own transform, and an animation moves those transforms and the vertices inside them — Gabriel is thirteen meshes. That is worse than a skeleton for most purposes and better for this one: turning a head is moving one mesh, and the pivot it turns about is the mesh's own origin, which sits where the neck is because that is where the artist put it.

The meshes are not named — the format has no room for it — so the head is found by what it is painted with. Every character in the game has a face, eyelids, a mouth and a forehead as separate textures, named for them: GAB_FACE, GRA_EYELIDS, MOS_MOUTH00. A mesh wearing those is a head.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.FaceLibrary
member.summary: FACES.TXT — how each character's face is assembled.

remarks.para: GK3's people have no facial geometry at all. A head is one mesh painted with one bitmap, and everything a face does — talking, blinking, raising an eyebrow — is done by patching regions of that bitmap while the game runs. This file is the only place the regions are written down: where the mouth sits on the texture and how big it is, where the eyelids and forehead go, which blink animations a character uses and how often.

Thirty-two characters have an entry. Two of them — CON-XXX and EM2-xxx — carry the suffix the file's own header says to remove once the art exists, so they are not art that shipped and are skipped rather than half-read.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.Faces
member.summary: The faces in a room, and what each of them is doing.

remarks.para: GK3's characters have no facial geometry. A head is one mesh wearing one bitmap, and every expression the game has — a word, a blink, a raised brow — is a small picture pasted into a copy of that bitmap while the game runs. FACES.TXT says where each region goes; the animations say which picture and when.

So this is a compositor with a clock. Three regions are tracked per character — mouth, eyelids, forehead — and whenever any of them changes, the four bitmaps are pasted together into a face, given to the renderer under a name of its own, and the character's head is repainted with it. Compositions are cached by what they are made of, because a sentence comes back to the same eight mouth shapes over and over and a blink is the same two pictures every time.

Two things drive it. Lip sync comes from the line being spoken: a .YAK carries the recording in its [SOUNDS] and the mouth shapes in its [GK3], against the same frame numbers, so the mouth follows the words by construction rather than by analysis. Blinking runs on its own: every character has two blink animations and a frequency in FACES.TXT, and one is drawn at random every five to twelve seconds. Without that, a room full of people stares.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.Faces.CodeFor(System.String)

member.remarks: Not always the model name. The lobby places Simone as sim_ and her face is listed under SIM, so an animation built from the model name — sim_sleepon — names nothing at all. It is the same code the mouth and eyelid bitmaps use.

member.remarks: The cues are absolute frame numbers from the start of the line, so the last one at or before now is the shape — not the next one along. member.param: The face being built, which is written into.
The patch.
Where its top left corner goes.

A bitmap saying how much of the patch to show, or null for all of it. The resting eyelids have one: they are a soft edge against the skin rather than a cut-out, and pasted without it they read as a strip of paint across the eyes.
member.remarks: The patches are keyed rather than authored with an alpha channel — a forehead's corners are magenta — and the decoder has already turned that into transparency, so this is an ordinary blend. member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.FacingArrow
member.summary: Which way a character's model is built to face.

remarks.para: GK3 ships an invisible arrow per character — DOR_EML, DOR_EST, DOR_LH2, 23 of them — whose three vertices point the way that model faces. The original loads one beside every actor, hides it, keeps it turned with them, and reads the character's facing straight off it: GKActor::GetModelFacingDirection.

Why it matters more than it looks. Everything else in this engine assumes a character's model is built facing −Z, and turns it by "heading plus a half turn" — . That is true of most of them and is not a rule. The reference never assumes it: SetModelRotationToActorRotation measures where the model is currently facing and rotates it by the difference from where it should be. A model built the other way round is turned correctly there and is turned end for end here, which is the museum's Estelle and Lady Howard standing back to back.

The tip is the first vertex for nearly every character. The reference's own comment on the exception is worth keeping: "OF COURSE these points aren't consistent...Mosely uses different ones" — MOS and DEM put the tip third.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.FacingArrow.Reversed
member.summary: The characters whose arrow points from the other end.
member.remarks: Two of them, named in the reference and nowhere in the data. An arrow read from the wrong end is a character facing exactly backwards, which is the failure this whole class exists to stop, so the exception is worth carrying by name.

member.summary: What a model's arrow is called.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.FacingArrow.Of(GK3Reborn.Formats.Models.ModFile,System.String)
member.summary: Which way a character's model is built to face, as a heading.
member.param: The DOR_ model, already parsed.
The character's model name, for the two that are read backwards.
member.returns: The heading the model faces when its placement is the identity, or null when the arrow has no triangle to read.
member.remarks: In the model's own space, with no placement applied, so what comes back is a property of the character rather than of where they are standing. Turning that model to a heading is then a matter of the difference between the two, which is what the reference does every frame and what this lets a placement do once.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.FacingArrow.Rotation(System.Single,System.Nullable{System.Single})

member.param: Where they should be looking, as the game measures a heading.
Which way the model is built to face, from , or null when nothing says.
member.returns: The angle to turn the model about the vertical.
member.remarks: The difference between the two, which is the reference's own arithmetic. Without an arrow it falls back to the half turn every other part of this engine assumes, so a character with no DOR_ model behaves exactly as before rather than differently.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.Footsteps
member.summary: What a step sounds like: which floor, which shoes.

remarks.para: Three files between them. FLOORMAP.TXT maps a floor texture to one of six kinds of ground — carpet, tile, wood, concrete, dirt, grass — by listing every texture under each. FOOTSTEPS.TXT and FOOTSCUFFS.TXT map that and a shoe type to three sounds to pick between. CHARACTERS.TXT says which shoes each character is wearing.

The animations already say when: a walk clip carries <frame>,FOOTSTEP,GABRIEL nodes in its [GK3] section, three or four to a stride. Those were parsed and dropped, so every character in the game walked in silence across every surface.
The sound names in these files carry no extension, which the file itself points out.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.Glances
member.summary: Who is looking at what.

remarks.para: A glance is the smallest thing that makes a room feel inhabited: somebody turns their head when you come in, or looks at the thing they are talking about. GK3's scripts ask for it constantly — LookitActor, LookitModel, TurnHead — and in the reference implementation every one of those functions is an empty body that returns zero, so none of it has ever happened.
It is scene state, not story state. Who somebody is looking at means nothing once the room has changed, and there is no save in the game that records it.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.Glances.YawLimit
member.summary: How far round a head will turn, in radians.
member.remarks: Eighty degrees. A person can manage rather more with their shoulders, but a head on its own that goes past this reads as broken rather than as attentive, and the mesh has no neck to stretch. Anything further is simply looked at as far as possible.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.Glances.PitchLimit

member.summary: Points an actor at something.
member.param: Who is looking at what.

How long for, or zero to hold the look until something cancels it. The scripts say which they mean: LOOKAT GABRIEL EH 5 is a five-second glance, and dropping the five left Emilio watching Gabriel over his shoulder for the rest of the scene — through standing up, through the whole of his walk to the hotel door.
member.remarks: One at a time: an actor asked to look somewhere else stops looking where they were, which is what a person does.

member.param: How long has passed.
member.remarks: An expired glance is removed rather than zeroed, and the head then eases back to straight ahead on its own: the turning code aims at nothing-in-particular the same way it aims at a target.

member.param: Where the actor is.
Which way their body faces, in radians about the up axis.

What they are looking at.
member.returns: Yaw and pitch for the head, both already clamped to what a neck allows.
member.remarks: Relative to the body, because the head is a child of it: an actor already facing the thing turns their head not at all. Something directly overhead or underfoot gives no meaningful direction to turn towards, so the head stays where it is.

member.remarks: Without this, something a little to the left of an actor facing north reads as almost a full turn to the right, and the clamp then holds the head at its limit facing the wrong way.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.HeadRig
member.summary: A character's head as the clips address it, kept beside the head that is drawn.
member.param: Which of the model's meshes is the head.

The authored vertex positions, per submesh, in the order a .ACT shapes them. This is what a clip's vertices are compared against to recover the head's motion. Kept whole, including the axis triad, because its length is what says whether a clip is talking about this mesh at all.
Which of those vertices to actually fit with, per submesh.
How wide the head is, so a fit's leftover can be reported as a fraction of it rather than in scene units that mean nothing on their own.
member.remarks: The sample exists to drop the axis triad. Every mesh group in the game carries three extra vertices at (60,0,0), (0,60,0) and (0,0,60) — Plan/06 §4.3 — which are four times the size of a head and do not travel with it. Fitting them along with the head puts three points with enormous leverage on the wrong answer: it reported Mosely as deforming his head by 40% of its width on a tenth of his frames, and he does not.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.HeadRig.Sample
member.summary: Which of those vertices to actually fit with, per submesh.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.HeadRig.Span

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.HeadRefinement
member.summary: Gives a character a denser head without invalidating a single frame of animation.

remarks.para: .ACT is addressed by vertex index, so changing a character's topology normally throws away every clip that character has — which is why Plan/05 rules out any route that re-meshes the cast. The head is the exception, and it is the exception for a reason that was measured rather than assumed: heads do not deform. Fitting the authored head onto all 122,034 recorded frames of all 3,069 head clips, for all 56 models that have any, leaves 1.0% of head width at the median of medians and 4.1% at the worst model — the encoding's own quantisation noise rather than any deformation. Not one of the fifty-six fails. GK3Reborn.Tools head-solve is the survey.

So the head's vertex track carries a rigid motion and nothing else, and a rigid motion will drive any mesh at all. The clip keeps addressing the authored vertices, the fit turns what it says into a transform, and the transform carries a subdivided head that the clip has never heard of. Nothing is re-authored, no clip is invalidated, and the thirty-eight characters with no donor are treated exactly like the three with one.

This is the smallest useful piece of what Plan/06 calls the rig solve — one bone, no clustering, no weight fitting — and it is worth having on its own because the head is where the complaint is. Grace's hair is twenty triangles; Madeline's is thirteen.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.HeadRefinement.MaximumLevels
member.summary: The most levels worth applying.
member.remarks: Two turns Grace's twenty-triangle hair into three hundred and twenty, which is where the silhouette stops being a polygon. A third would be four times the vertices to round off something already round.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.HeadRefinement.Coincident
member.summary: Positions closer together than this are the same point.
member.remarks: Used only to weld normals across submeshes. The authored data agrees to a rounding error at those seams — measured at 0.0° of disagreement — and refining each submesh separately would introduce a shading seam at the hairline that the original does not have.

member.summary: Refines a character's head, and says how to drive it.
member.param: The character, as parsed.
How many times to subdivide. Clamped to .
member.returns: The model to draw and the rig to drive its head with, or the model unchanged and no rig when it has no head to refine.
member.remarks: The rig's rest positions come from the model as it was parsed, before refinement, because that is what the clips address. Reading them off the refined mesh would compare a clip's 307 vertices against 4,900 and fit nothing.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit
member.summary: The rotation and translation that best carries one set of points onto another.

remarks.para: GK3 animates by moving vertices, so a clip says where every point of a head is on every frame and never says that the head turned. This puts that back: given the head as the model authored it and the head as a clip shapes it, it recovers the single rigid motion between them — which is all the clip was ever expressing, because a head does not deform. Measured over the whole corpus — 3,069 clips, 122,034 recorded frames, all 56 models that have any — the leftover is 1.0% of head width for the median model and 4.1% for the worst. See docs/head-refinement.md.

That is what lets a character's head be replaced with denser geometry without touching the .ACT files: the clip keeps addressing the original 1,200-odd vertices, the fit turns what it says into a transform, and the transform will carry any mesh at all.

The method is Kabsch's, with the orthogonal factor found by Higham's Newton iteration rather than by a singular value decomposition, which System.Numerics does not have and which would be a great deal of code for a 3×3.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Steps
member.summary: How many Newton steps before giving up on convergence.
member.remarks: The iteration is quadratically convergent, so this is a backstop rather than a budget: well-conditioned input is done in five or six.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Settled
member.summary: Close enough that another step would not move it.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Solve(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Numerics.Vector3},System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Numerics.Vector3},System.Single@)
member.summary: Finds the rigid motion carrying onto .
member.param: Where the points are.
Where they should end up. Must be the same length.
Root-mean-square distance left over per point, in the space the points are given in. Zero means the two sets really are one rigid motion apart.
member.returns: The transform, or null when the points do not determine one.
member.remarks: Null rather than an identity, because the two answers mean opposite things: an identity says the head did not move, and a caller that cannot tell them apart draws a head that snaps back to rest on every frame the fit fails.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Middle(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Numerics.Vector3})
member.summary: The average of a set of points.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Orthogonalise(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: The nearest rotation to a matrix.
member.param: The covariance, with the 3×3 part in the upper left.
member.returns: The rotation, or null when there is not one to find.

remarks.para: Higham's iteration, R ← ½(R + R⁻ᵀ), which converges on the orthogonal factor of the polar decomposition — the same matrix an SVD would give as UVᵀ.

A negative determinant is refused rather than corrected. The nearest orthogonal matrix to a covariance with a negative determinant is a reflection, and the usual correction — flip the smallest singular value — needs the decomposition this is avoiding. It also should not arise: a head and the same head a frame later are a rotation apart, not a mirror. If it does, the points are degenerate and no answer is better than a mirrored head. GK3's world is left-handed, which is a property of the space these points are expressed in and not of the motion between two poses within it; the determinant here is of the motion.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Determinant(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: The determinant of the 3×3 part.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Half(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4,System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: Halfway between two matrices, in their 3×3 parts.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Distance(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4,System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: The largest element-wise difference between two 3×3 parts.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.RigidFit.Orthonormal(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: Whether a matrix's 3×3 part is a rotation, to a loose tolerance.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Binoculars
member.summary: The binoculars.

remarks.para: Two places in the game have them — the Armchair of the Devil and the tower at Château de Blanchefort — and from each, at each time of day, a handful of other places can be picked out and zoomed into. BINOCS.TXT describes all of it: twenty-one vantage points, forty-seven things to look at, and four spots that have a line of dialogue rather than a destination.

The panorama is the room, not a picture. The binoculars do not show a painted backdrop; they narrow the view and let the player pan the camera they already have. Each thing worth seeing is a rectangle in degrees — heading across, pitch up and down — and the file's numbers say so: they run from 1 to 189 across and from -7 to 11 up, which is an arc of hillside and a few degrees either side of the horizon rather than any kind of image coordinate.

Zooming in is a camera, and sometimes a room. Each sight carries the position and angle the camera takes when the player zooms — usually inside another room entirely, which is why it also names that room's floor. The enter and exit scripts are the original's own hooks for hiding and showing whatever has to be in place before the cut; they are recorded and run through the ordinary script host.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.ConversationCamera
member.summary: Which camera to watch a conversation from.

remarks.para: A scene's [DIALOGUE_CAMERAS] names one or more shots per conversation and marks one initial, and where a conversation says which one it is, that is the answer. Plenty of exchanges do not: the lobby's introduction to Emilio calls SetDefaultDialogueCamera and then starts talking, and never names a conversation at all — and SetDefaultDialogueCamera does nothing in the original either. So there is no faithful answer to fall back on, and the game was carrying on the conversation wherever the camera happened to be pointing, often at neither speaker.

The port decides, out of the artists' own cameras. Every camera the scene names is scored on whether it shows both speakers and how well, and the best is used. Nothing is invented: a shot that was never authored is never framed, which is what Plan/03 section 5 asks for. Where no authored camera can see both of them, the view is left alone — a bad cut is worse than no cut.

And from in front of them. Scoring on framing alone picked shots from behind, which is how a conversation ended up watching the back of Gabriel's head — reported as him turning round, because from the player's chair that is exactly what it looks like. A camera behind a speaker holds them in frame perfectly well; what it does not do is show their face, and a shot of two people talking is a shot of at least one face.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.ConversationCamera.Within
member.summary: How far off the middle of the view a speaker may be and still count.
member.remarks: Sixty degrees is the game's own default field of view, so half of it is the edge of the frame. Two thirds of that keeps a speaker off the very edge, which is where a shot stops reading as being about them.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.ConversationCamera.Far
member.summary: How far a camera may be from a speaker before it stops being about them.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.ConversationCamera.Ahead
member.summary: How far round from a speaker's own line of sight a camera may sit and still see them.
member.remarks: A right angle either side, so anything from a full profile forwards counts as a face and anything behind the shoulders does not. Generous on purpose: three-quarter views are most of the game's authored shots and a stricter rule would throw them away.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ConversationCamera.Framing(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.SceneCamera},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Numerics.Vector3},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Numerics.Vector3})
member.summary: Picks the camera that best shows everyone talking.
member.param: Every camera the scene names.
Where the people talking are standing.
Which way each of them is facing, in the same order. Optional: without it a shot is judged on framing alone, which is what picked the back of Gabriel's head.
member.returns: The camera's name, or null when none of them shows the conversation.

remarks.para: A camera scores by the worst-framed speaker rather than the average, because a shot that frames one person beautifully and leaves the other out of it is not a shot of a conversation. Ties go to the closer camera: two shots that both hold everybody make the tighter one the better one.
Heads rather than feet. A camera aimed at where somebody stands is aimed at the floor in front of them, and every one of these shots was framed for faces.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ConversationCamera.Scores(GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.SceneCamera,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Numerics.Vector3},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Numerics.Vector3})

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.DrivingMap
member.summary: The map the moped is ridden around.

remarks.para: A painting of the Rennes-le-Château countryside, 640 by 480, with sixteen places on it. Each place's marker is a lit copy of that patch of the map rather than a pin over it, which is why the markers look like part of the picture: dm_rlc is the village, painted brighter.

Where the positions come from. The retail engine builds this list in the constructor of its driving layer, sixteen calls with the coordinates as immediates. They are recovered from there and written down here rather than read at runtime: nothing this engine ships may depend on the original executable, and sixteen pairs of integers about where a village sits on a painting are a fact about the map rather than a thing that can be derived. The pictures themselves come out of the player's own .BRN archives, like everything else.

The road network is data. PATHDATA.TXT is in the archives and describes twenty junctions with their map positions and the roads between them, which is how the moped rides along the roads rather than flying between towns in a straight line.

What is open. Five places are on the map from the first ride — Rennes-le-Château, Larry Chester's house, Blanchefort, Rennes-les-Bains and the Couiza train station — and the rest arrive as the story finds them. The original keeps a flag per marker and sets it from its own script hooks; here a place is on the map once the player has been there or a script has said so, which is the same set arrived at from state the save already keeps.

remarks.para: The one piece of the game's story that lives in neither the scripts nor the scene files: the original's fingerprint screen carries this table in its own code, the same way the executable carried the score table and the starting inventory. Thirteen of the game's score events are awarded from here and nowhere else, which is why check-story reported every fingerprint in the game as unreachable: no script names them, and none is missing.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Foliage
member.summary: Finds the trees hiding in a scene's flat foliage cards.

remarks.para: GK3 draws a tree as a picture of one on a quad, or on two quads crossed at the trunk. The picture is the tree's whole description: how tall it is, how wide it spread, and which species it was meant to be. So a card is not thrown away and guessed at — it is measured, and what replaces it is grown to the size the artist drew.

The species comes from the texture rather than from the model's name, because the names do not agree with each other and the textures do. WOD_BIGDTREEFF, CSE_FFTREE03 and PL6_FFTREE01 are the same broadleaf under three conventions, and all three draw TREE00.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Foliage.Backdrops
member.summary: Foliage bitmaps that are a hillside rather than a tree.

remarks.para: Painted strips of distant woodland, whole ridges of it on one quad. There is no single tree in one to measure and nothing sensible to put in its place, so they are left drawn — but they must not stop the real trees beside them being replaced, which is what they were doing: an object holding two trees and one of these was refused whole, and nineteen objects across the corpus are shaped that way.

Named here rather than in the tree manifest because this is a fact about the 1999 corpus and not about anything that has been grown. A species says which sprites it stands in for; this says which sprites are nobody's job.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Foliage.SmallestTree
member.summary: The smallest card worth replacing, in scene units.
member.remarks: Gabriel is 76 units tall. Anything under half of him is a shrub or a scrap of undergrowth rather than a tree, and a grown trunk with a crown on it is the wrong shape for it.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Foliage.LeastSqueeze
member.summary: How far a grown tree may be stretched or squeezed to match a card's width.
member.remarks: A tree is not a rectangle and the two do not have to agree exactly, but a maple card is square where a grown maple is broader than it is tall, and left alone the crown would overhang the path the card kept clear. Clamped, because a tree squashed to half its width stops reading as that species at all.

member.param: The parsed prop.
The grown trees available to stand in for it.
member.returns: Where a tree goes, or null when this prop is not a tree.

remarks.para: Every submesh has to be foliage, and they all have to be the same species. A model that is a tree and something else — a lantern hung in one, a sign nailed to one — would lose the something else, and there is no way to put it back from here.

The box is the model's own, in its own space, because that is the space it will be placed in: GK3's props carry their scene position in their vertices rather than in a transform, so a card's box is already where the tree goes.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Foliage.Mix(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.String)
member.summary: A hash that is the same in every process, which is the whole point of it.
member.remarks: FNV-1a, written out, and deliberately not : that one is seeded randomly once per process, so a wood hashed with it would be a different wood every time the game was started. The property being protected is that a room comes out the same on every load — a stand that reshuffles itself when the player walks out and back in is worse than a stand of identical trees, and it makes two renders of one scene impossible to compare. The test for it can only see one process, so the reason has to be written down here.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Foliage.InGeometry(GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.BspFile,GK3Reborn.Content.TreeLibrary)
member.summary: Finds the trees in a room's own geometry.
member.param: The parsed room.
The grown trees available to stand in for its cards.
member.returns: One entry per object that is entirely foliage, largest first.

remarks.para: The rooms hold 5,760 drawn foliage cards, 3,790 of them inside 64 objects — wod_treeshadowcasters, lhm_treeshadowcasters, rc1_pleavesshadowcasters — that contain nothing else.

Most of those turn out to be the same trees the scene file places as props, drawn a second time, so what this actually adds is small: across the twenty-five outdoor scenes measured it is 24 trees, sixteen of them in BAL and two in LHE, where the room carries trees no prop does. It is worth having for those and it is not where the bulk of the foliage is.

Only objects that are nothing but foliage. An object that mixes cards with something else cannot be taken away, because a room is hidden by name and there is no way to hide half of one: wod_dectree01 draws its leaves on cards and its bole with TRUNK01, and hiding it to replace the leaves would take the trunk with them. 96 objects are mixed like that and they keep their cards.

A card is a surface, never a polygon. A room's geometry has been through a BSP splitter, and what that leaves is not the faces an artist drew: one 320-unit spruce card in LHM arrives as five polygons, sliced across at whatever heights the tree's planes happened to cut it. Clustering those directly turns a single tree into half a dozen — and a slice taken from between 300 and 378 units up is a tree that grows in mid-air, with its own trunk, above the real one. LHM's 1,023 polygons are 190 drawn faces, and 190 is the number this works from.

The clustering is then simple, because the reconstructed data is: one tree is two or three cards crossed at the same spot, and their centres agree to within about three units where the trees themselves stand a couple of hundred apart.
