member.summary: Gathers cards that stand over the same ground into one tree each.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Foliage.Standing(GK3Reborn.Game.TreeSite,GK3Reborn.Content.GrownTree)
member.summary: Where a grown tree has to be put to fill a site.
member.param: The site.
The variant chosen for it.
member.returns: A transform for the normalised tree.

remarks.para: A grown tree stands on the origin and is exactly one unit tall, so the height is the whole of the vertical scale. The horizontal scale starts there too and is then nudged towards the card's own width, within limits: a grown maple is wider than it is tall and the square card it replaces is not, and a crown that overhangs by half its width reaches over walls the card never touched.

The turn about the vertical is what stops four variants from looking like four copies. It comes from the site's seed rather than from a counter, so a wood is the same wood every time the room is loaded.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState
member.summary: The game's observable state: what scripts read and write.

remarks.para: Everything here is what the plan's differential harness compares between implementations. Presentation — camera cuts, animations, dialogue — is recorded as events rather than held as state, because two engines can draw a scene differently and still be equivalent, while disagreeing about a flag means the game diverges.
Names are case-insensitive throughout, matching the language: the specification says upper and lower case are the same, and scripts spell the same flag several ways.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState._sidneyScans
member.summary: Which inventory items have been through the scanner.
member.remarks: Beside the file names rather than derived from them. The story asks about the file — DoesSidneyFileExist("fileParchment1") — and Sidney's own store has to show the item it came from, with its name and what may be done to it. Reversing a file name back to an item would mean the naming rule had to stay invertible for ever, which is a promise not worth making for one set of strings.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.DefaultRandomSeed
member.summary: Where the game's luck starts.
member.remarks: Fixed, and the sequence is reproducible from it, because ADR 0004 forbids ambient nondeterminism in engine code and the differential harness compares two runs of the same story. A script asking for a random number is asking the state for one, and how many it has asked for is part of what makes two runs comparable.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.Inventory
member.summary: What each character is carrying.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.CameraAngle
member.summary: Which of the scene's cameras the view is at, or empty for the scene's default.
member.remarks: A name rather than a position, because that is what the scripts deal in and what survives a scene being rebuilt. Cleared on changing location, where the names belong to a room that is no longer there.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.Inspecting
member.summary: What the view is looking at closely, or empty when it is looking at the room.

remarks.para: Inspecting is a camera, not a screen. InspectObject moves the view to the close-up the scene declares for a thing and UnInspect brings it back — there is nothing drawn over the room and nothing modal about it, which is why modelling it as one of left the verb doing nothing visible at all.

It sits beside rather than replacing it, and that is what makes coming back free: the angle the story left the view at is still there underneath, so clearing this returns to it without anything having to remember it.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.CameraGliding
member.summary: Whether the last camera move was asked to take a moment.
member.remarks: A cut and a glide end in the same place, so this is the only thing that separates them once has changed. Not in the state hash: where the view ends up is a fact about the story, how it got there is not, and two runs that disagree only about that have not diverged.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.ForcedCameraCuts
member.summary: Whether the story may cut the camera about even with cinematics turned off.
member.remarks: SetForcedCameraCuts: a script about to show something the player has to see says so, and the preference gives way for as long as it holds.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.CinematicsEnabled
member.summary: Whether the player wants the story moving the camera at all.
member.remarks: A preference the original also has, and one that changes what a script does: CutToCameraAngle only cuts when this or is on, while ForceCutToCameraAngle ignores both. It is in the state hash for that reason — two runs made with different answers to it will diverge, and the harness should see why rather than wonder.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.EasterEggFlag
member.summary: The flag the game's own easter-egg content is written against.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.EasterEggs
member.summary: Whether the game's easter-egg content is switched on.

remarks.para: A player's preference kept as a story flag, because a flag is where the game itself looks: EGG is a built-in action case, and Sidney's sixth email is written against GetFlag("Egg"). Reading it through a property rather than leaving everybody to spell the flag gives it one name and one place.

Which means it can arrive in a save, and it must not: it is what this player asked for, not something the story earned. puts the current answer back over whatever the save had, so loading somebody else's game does not turn it on.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.Timers
member.summary: Actions the story has asked for later.
member.remarks: Story state rather than scene state: a minute set in the lobby has to still be counting in the hall, which is why the original saves them.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.Screens
member.summary: What is in front of the room.
member.remarks: State rather than presentation: scripts ask what is showing — IsTopLayerInventory is a real question in the data — and behave differently by the answer, so two runs that disagree about it have diverged.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.Timeblock
member.summary: The current timeblock, such as 110A.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.DefaultDialogueCamera
member.summary: The camera a conversation falls back to, or null for whatever the scene names.
member.remarks: A scene's [DIALOGUE_CAMERAS] marks one camera per conversation as the initial one, and a script may override it for the exchange it is about to start — SetDefaultDialogueCamera("GabMadWide") before a chat with Madeline. Clearing it puts the scene's own choice back.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.CameraFieldOfView
member.summary: A field of view a script has asked for, in radians, or null for the scene's own.
member.remarks: The original renders at sixty degrees and the scene files override it per camera — fov=20 on a close-up. This is the other override: a script narrowing the view for a moment. Null rather than sixty degrees, so that "nobody has asked" and "somebody asked for the default" stay distinguishable.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.BlockedHitTests
member.summary: Hit tests a script has switched off, by name.
member.remarks: A hit test is a volume the player can click and never see — a doorway's clickable area, the patch of desk a note lies on. Scripts turn them off while something else is happening and on again afterwards, which is how a scene stops the player clicking through a cutscene.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.Location
member.summary: Three-letter code of the current location.
member.remarks: Moving remembers where you moved from, whoever does the moving. A script says SetLocation("mop") and the room loop follows with the arrival, so two separate places set this — and each of them treating the other as the one that records the change is how stayed empty for ever.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.LastLocation
member.summary: Three-letter code of the location before this one.
member.remarks: Scenes are built differently depending on where the player came from — which door stands open, which backdrop is visible through it — so this is state a scene reads, not a breadcrumb. It is also what decides where the player is standing on arrival: a room's SCENE:ENTER asks WasLastLocation and stands them at the matching spot. Left empty, every arrival is the room's default.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.Ego
member.summary: Name of the actor the player controls.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.Score
member.summary: The player's score.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.MustChooseAnAction
member.summary: Whether the action chooser is insisting on an answer.
member.remarks: SetVerbModal in the data: the story has asked a question and wants one of the offered actions rather than a shrug. The flag is kept faithfully because scripts set and clear it around moments that depend on it.
member.seealso: Section 2.1 requires that no puzzle action fire because the engine guessed, so a chooser the player cannot leave must still offer a way out that chooses nothing — a modal question is a reason to keep asking, never a reason to trap somebody in a menu. Which of the offered actions is right is the player's to decide; whether they may walk away and come back is not the script's.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.RandomDraws
member.summary: How many random numbers scripts have drawn.
member.remarks: Observable state, not a statistic: two runs that have drawn a different number of times will disagree about everything random from then on, and a differential run should see that immediately rather than at the first visible consequence.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.GameState.SidneyFiles
member.summary: The files the player has gathered in Sidney, in a stable order.
member.remarks: Sidney is the in-game computer, and its files are evidence: a photograph scanned in, a shape traced off a map, a text translated. Scripts ask whether one is there before letting the story move on. Nothing puts them there yet — that is the analysis screen — so this reads as an investigation nobody has started.

member.summary: How many times the player has done a verb to a noun.

remarks.para: GK3 gates a great deal of dialogue on these counts — the second time you ask about something you get a different answer — so they are game state, not statistics.

Counted per character. Gabriel and Grace investigate the same places and what one of them has already looked at says nothing about the other, so 1ST_TIME means the first time for whoever is being played. The game has a function whose only purpose is to set both at once, SetNounVerbCountBoth, which is what gives the distinction away.

member.summary: Writes everything observable down, so that it can be put back.
member.param: What to call it.
member.returns: The save.

remarks.para: The composite keys go across whole rather than being taken apart and rebuilt. They are this class's own private encoding — an actor, a noun and a verb joined by a separator no name contains — and a save that decomposed them would have to agree with that encoding for ever. Copying them keeps the round trip exact by construction, which is what makes the hash test meaningful rather than circular.
Compare with : the two enumerate the same things, and they have to. Anything the hash counts as part of the game and this leaves out is something a loaded game would have lost.

member.summary: Puts a saved game back, throwing away whatever was here.
member.param: The save.
member.remarks: Everything is cleared first. Loading into a state that still holds the previous game's flags is the classic save bug: the story reads a flag nobody set in this run and takes a branch the player never earned, and it only shows up hours later. Setting is not enough; unsetting has to happen too, and a save records only what is set.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.GameStrings
member.summary: ESTRINGS.TXT — what the game calls things, in the player's language.

remarks.para: Three families matter here. loc_lby = Hotel Lobby names all 79 locations; Day110a = Day 1, 10am - 12pm names the seventeen timeblocks; and dm_rl1 names the driving map's stops. The engine had been showing the codes — LBY - 110A in the corner of the screen — and reading the third family with a hand-rolled parser inside the driving map.

It is what an exit should be called. RC1's four ways out are nouns the artists numbered rather than named: EXIT, EXIT1, EXIT2, EXIT3, EXIT4, EXIT5. Those numbers mean nothing to anybody — they are not even in a sensible order — and the interface was drawing them as "Exit3". What the player wants to know is where the door goes, and the rule behind the door says: its script calls SetLocation("rc3"), and this turns that into "Outside Church".

The file is Windows-1252 and full of French place names, which already decodes correctly. Missing keys are simply absent: an installation without the file gets the codes back, which is what the interface drew before this existed.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.GameTimers
member.summary: Actions the story has asked for later.

remarks.para: SetGameTimer(noun, verb, ms) is how a script arranges for something to happen by itself: a phone that rings a minute after you walk in, a character who gives up waiting. The action is an ordinary noun and verb, resolved and run when the time comes exactly as a click would resolve and run it, which is why this holds a *name* rather than a piece of work — the rule that applies is the one that applies then, not the one that applied when the timer was set.

Timers outlive the room. The original keeps them in a global list and saves them, because a minute set in the lobby has to still be counting in the hall, so they belong to the story rather than to the scene.
Nothing here runs anything. hands back what has come due and the caller performs it, because performing needs a resolver and a runner and the story's state has no business knowing about either.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi
member.summary: The GK3 API surface, bound to game state.

remarks.para: The specification documents 359 functions, of which 174 are development-only, leaving around 130 that gameplay needs. Those divide cleanly by what they do rather than by how common they are.

**State functions are implemented.** Flags, game variables, noun/verb counts, topic counts, score, timeblock and location are what determines whether the story can progress, and they are what a differential comparison between engines has to agree on.

**Presentation functions are recorded.** CutToCameraAngle is called 2,235 times across the corpus and StartAnimation 2,067, but neither changes what the game permits — and neither can be performed before the renderer exists. Recording them keeps the trace complete and honest: the call happened, in that order, with those arguments, and nothing was faked.
Anything not registered is reported once. Silence there would let a missing function look like a working one.

member.summary: How long the next lines of the conversation in progress take.
member.remarks: ContinueDialogue(2) means the next two of a run whose licence plate was given once, several statements ago, so only the thing doing the speaking knows which recordings those are. Null where nothing is speaking, which answers nought and is right: a continuation of nothing says nothing and takes no time.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi.Walks
member.summary: What sends an actor across the room, when there is a room to cross.
member.remarks: Given the actor, the place, how to get there and whether they are in a hurry; answers how long it will take. Set by , so a tool with no scene leaves it null and the walking calls stay recorded, as they always were.

Only the player is ever in a hurry. A script that sends somebody somewhere passes false, because a script's timings are written against the pace the game walks at and hurrying one leg of a scripted sequence would arrive an actor before their line.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi.ActingOn
member.summary: The noun of the action being carried out, or empty.
member.remarks:
Some functions take no arguments and mean "the thing this action is about". InspectObject() is the one that matters — REGISTER, INSPECT, ALL, script={wait InspectObject();} is the whole of that rule, and without a noun it has nothing to look at.
Set when an action starts and left there, rather than restored afterwards. An action's script may be deferred until its approach has finished, so the noun has to outlive the call that set it; and actions are serialised by their approach anyway, so the last one started is the one running.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi.ActionSeconds
member.summary: How much longer the action that is running has to run.

remarks.para: The reference keeps a whole mCurrentAction for this and asks it IsActionPlaying; what anything here wants to know is only whether the story is in the middle of something, so what is kept is the time left rather than the action. The runner writes the sum of an action's waits here as it performs it and the room counts it down.

It is a floor rather than a promise. A statement whose length the host cannot work out — wait CallSheep(…), whose length is another script — contributes nothing, so an action can still be going on after this has run out. Whoever asks has to be safe if it says no too early.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi.MovieSeconds
member.summary: How long a movie runs, asked before it is played.
member.remarks: A hook rather than a library lookup, because the length lives in the movie's own container and only the thing that can open one knows it. Null means no movies, which is a machine with no decoder: the scripts still run and wait for nothing.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi.WalksToAnimationStart
member.summary: Walks an actor to where an animation begins, and says how long it takes.
member.remarks: A hook of its own rather than another , because the name it is given is an animation rather than a place: working out where to go means reading the clip, and only a standing scene has the clips.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi.Defers
member.summary: What holds something back until the player has walked there, if anything can.
member.remarks: Given a number of seconds and the work; answers whether it took charge of it. An action's approach has to finish before its script runs — the original walks the ego to the target and performs the action from the arrival — and this is where a runner finds something with a clock to wait against. Null in a tool, where every action runs the instant it is asked for, exactly as it always did.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi.Plays
member.summary: What plays an animation, when there is a room to play it in.
member.remarks: Given the animation's name and whether it repeats; answers how long it will take. Null in a tool, where the animation calls stay recorded as they always were.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi.Animations
member.summary: The animations, for the calls whose length is a frame count.
member.remarks: Optional, because a tool sweeping the corpus has no clock and does not want one. Without it a line of dialogue is over as soon as it starts, which is what every waited call did before there was anywhere to read a duration from.

remarks.para: Only the calls whose length is knowable from what has been read. A timer is exactly its argument and a camera glide is as long as a glide, both of which the engine decides for itself. The rest is asset-shaped: an animation is a frame count at fifteen frames a second, and a voice-over is one animation per line of dialogue.
A call whose asset cannot be found answers zero rather than a plausible guess, so a missing file makes a line instant instead of inventing a pause that is not in the game.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Interaction.ScenePicker
member.summary: Answers what is under a point on the screen.

remarks.para: GK3 puts nearly everything clickable inside the room's own geometry. A door, a drawer, a notice board are objects in the BSP that the initialisation file names — model= with a noun= — and the handful of things that are not, the props and the people, are separate models standing in it. So resolving a click means casting one ray at the geometry and at the placed models together and keeping whichever it reaches first.

Some clickable things are not drawn at all. A hittest is ordinary geometry with an ordinary texture that the scene marks invisible: a slab across a doorway, a box over the area a note occupies on a desk, giving the player something forgiving to aim at. They are in the ray's world even though they are not in the picture, which is why a picture is not enough to check this against — hence the noun map.

Hidden objects are the opposite: a scene or hittest model the story has switched off is not merely undrawn, it is not there. The ray passes through it and hits whatever stands behind, exactly as the original does by clearing the interactive flag on those surfaces.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Interaction.ScenePicker.#ctor(GK3Reborn.Game.LoadedScene)
member.summary: Builds a picker for a loaded scene.
member.param: The scene, with its geometry and its placed models.
member.remarks: The triangles are gathered once, grouped by object with a box around each — the room's in world space, a model's in its own, since a model can still be moved. A room is fifteen thousand triangles and a click has to be answered between two frames; the box rejects nearly all of them before any arithmetic that matters happens.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Interaction.ScenePicker.TargetCount
member.summary: How many separately nameable things the ray can meet.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Interaction.ScenePicker.Blocked
member.summary: Things a script has switched off, by name.
member.remarks: Shared with the story rather than owned here, because a hit test switched off stays off across a camera cut and a reload of the same room. See GameState.BlockedHitTests.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Interaction.ScenePicker.Interactive
member.summary: Everything in the room the player can act on, and where it is.
member.returns: Each noun once, with the object it was found on and the middle of what it occupies in world space. The object comes back because what a noun should be called sometimes depends on it — a hotel door is named by the number in its model's name — and there is no pick to ask when every hotspot is being listed at once.

remarks.para: For showing them all at once while a key is held. A 1999 adventure game hides its hotspots and expects the player to sweep the pointer over the furniture until something lights up, which is the least interesting thing anybody does in one.

Each noun once, not each object: the church carves its four angels as four models and the hallway's hit tests double up on doors, and a room labelled twice for the same thing reads as a fault rather than as thoroughness. The first one found wins, and the middle is of that one's own box.

An actor walks: the sink is handed a new transform every frame and the triangles gathered here never hear about it, so baking them into the room would leave Gabriel's noun standing on the spot he set off from — the pointer finding him where he used to be and finding nothing where he is.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Interaction.ScenePicker.Into(GK3Reborn.Rendering.Ray,GK3Reborn.Game.Interaction.ScenePicker.Target,GK3Reborn.Game.Interaction.ScenePicker.Part)
member.summary: The ray as the target sees it, or null when the target is nowhere.

remarks.para: The room's own geometry is already in world space and comes back untouched. A model is asked where it is standing now and the ray is put through the inverse of that.

Distances survive the trip. An affine transform carries the point at t along the ray to the point at t along the transformed ray, so a hit found in a model's own space is at the same t in the room — which is what lets a scaled actor and a wall be compared for which one the ray reached first, and what lets the hit point be read off the original ray.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.MoviePlayer
member.summary: Plays one movie: the picture against a clock, the sound in one piece.

remarks.para: GK3 stops for a movie. PlayFullScreenMovie is waitable, the script that called it does not go on until the movie is over, and the room behind it is not being played — so there is no mixing to do and no world to keep in step with, only a picture to put on screen and a sound to put with it.

The sound is handed over whole and the picture chases it. That is the same arrangement as dialogue, and for the same reason: an audio device that has been given a buffer will play it at exactly the right rate whatever the display is doing, and a picture that is a frame late is invisible where a sound that is a frame late is a click. Frames are asked for by time rather than counted out, so a slow frame skips a picture instead of putting the whole movie behind.
One movie at a time. Nothing in the game plays two, and the second would have nowhere to go: the screen is the whole of the output.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds
member.summary: The shell that keeps the camera inside the room.

remarks.para: A room's own geometry is the wrong thing to collide against. It is a box seen from the inside with holes in it: doorways stand open, a wall meets a ceiling with a seam, and a backdrop hangs beyond the window with nothing between. A camera pushed against any of those finds its way through, and what it sees on the other side is the room turned inside out — walls from behind, a floor with nothing under it, the black between the scenery.

The game's artists solved this in 1999 and the answer is in the data. 114 models in the corpus are camera bounds: closed, invisible shells authored around the space the camera may occupy, named by cameraBounds= in the scene's initialisation file and drawn by nothing. Every one of the game's 78 locations names at least one. Colliding against those rather than against the room gives a camera that stops at the doorway it is meant to stop at and is allowed through the one it is meant to go through.

The movement is resolved rather than merely blocked. A camera that simply stopped dead on contact would be unusable along a wall — every wall would be flypaper — so what is left of the move is projected onto the surface and tried again, which is what makes a camera slide along a wall instead of sticking to it. Two passes: the first turns the move along the wall, the second stops it in a corner, and a third would only chase the last thousandth of a unit.

A shell is a few hundred triangles — the largest in the corpus is 2,233 — and there are one or two of them, so every triangle is tested every frame. A tree would save nothing worth the code at that size.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Radius
member.summary: How wide a berth the camera keeps, in scene units.
member.remarks: The reference implementation's radius. A camera treated as a point would put its near plane through the wall it is touching, which shows as the wall vanishing while the camera is still nominally inside the room.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Passes
member.summary: How many times a blocked move is redirected before what is left is dropped.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Skin
member.summary: How far clear of a surface a freed sphere is left, in scene units.
member.remarks: Settling it exactly touching leaves the next frame's arithmetic to decide whether it is a hair inside or a hair outside, and a hair inside is a step refused outright. A fortieth of a unit is under a millimetre of game world and puts the question beyond the reach of a float.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Nudges
member.summary: How many times a trapped sphere is pushed before best effort is accepted.
member.remarks: Out of one surface and into another is the ordinary case in a corner, so once is not enough; four clears a corner of three walls with a pass to spare. It stops rather than looping because somewhere in the game a gap is narrower than the camera and no number of pushes will satisfy both of its sides — there, moving it as far as one pass gets is better than hanging.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Still
member.summary: Below this a move is not worth resolving.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.#ctor(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{GK3Reborn.Formats.Models.ModFile})
member.summary: Builds bounds from the shells a scene names.
member.param: The bounds models, already loaded.
member.remarks: Every mesh's own transform is applied and nothing else. A bounds model stands at the world origin — the original notes the local-to-world matrix is the identity for these and the corpus bears it out — so a mesh's is the whole of the journey into the room.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds._shell
member.summary: How many triangles the scene's own shell contributed.
member.remarks: Everything past this came from a script, and unblocking one takes it back off. The shell itself cannot be removed: it is the room.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Block(System.String,GK3Reborn.Formats.Models.ModFile,System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: Fences the camera out of a model as well.
member.param: What to file it under, so it can be taken back off.
The model, in the space the room places it.
Where the room places it.
member.returns: True when it added anything.
member.remarks: CameraBoundaryBlockModel, 48 calls. The artists draw one shell per room and then a script adds a van, a lorry, a door that has swung open — anything that arrives after the room was authored and that the camera should not be able to see through.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Unblock(System.String)
member.summary: Takes a model back out of the shell.
member.param: What it was filed under.
member.returns: True when there was one to take out.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Rebuild
member.summary: Puts the shell back together after something was added or removed.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.TriangleCount
member.summary: How many triangles the camera is fenced in by.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.IsEmpty
member.summary: Whether there is anything to collide with.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Resolve(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Moves the camera as far along a step as the shell allows.
member.param: Where it is now.
Where it is trying to go, as an offset.
member.returns: Where it ends up.
member.remarks: A camera that has somehow got outside — placed there by a scene's own viewpoint, or left there by bounds that arrived after it did — is not trapped. Only a move towards a surface's front is refused, so the way back in is always open; this is the reference's rule and it is what stops a bad starting position from making a room unusable.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Free(System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Pushes the camera out of any surface it has ended up inside.
member.param: Where it is.
member.returns: Where it should be, clear of the shell.

remarks.para: Sweeping a sphere along a step decides what a move is allowed to do. It says nothing about a sphere that is already overlapping something when the step begins, and one arrives there often enough: a scene cuts to a viewpoint the artists placed against the room's own walls rather than against a shell sixteen units thick, CameraBoundaryBlockModel parks a van where the camera is standing, or a step settles a fraction inside and the fractions accumulate.

Once it overlaps, every step towards that wall is refused and every step along it is allowed, so the camera slides along inside the wall indefinitely — which is what being stuck in the geometry looks like from the player's chair. Pushing it back out is the whole of the fix, and it belongs at both ends of a step: at the start because that is where a bad position arrives from elsewhere, and at the end because that is where the sweep's own arithmetic leaves one.

Out of the deepest overlap first, then look again, rather than adding up every push at once. Summing them overshoots in a corner — two walls each asking for their own full clearance send the camera out through the third — where taking the worst one at a time converges on the point that satisfies both.

A camera on the far side of the shell is left where it is. It is outside and is meant to be able to come back in, which is the rule the sweep follows too, and pushing it "clear" of a surface it is already behind would only push it further away.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Deepest(System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: The push out of whichever surface the sphere is furthest inside.
member.returns: The offset that clears it, or null when nothing is overlapping.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Closest(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: The point of a triangle nearest to somewhere else.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.OnSegment(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: The point of a segment nearest to somewhere else.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Contains(System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Whether a point is inside the shell.
member.param: The point, in world space.
member.returns: True when it is enclosed.

remarks.para: Counted crossings along a ray: a shell is closed, so a line out of it meets an odd number of its surfaces from inside and an even number from outside. The direction is a fixed awkward one rather than an axis, because a shell built of axis-aligned walls has whole faces lying in the planes an axis-aligned ray would graze, and a graze counts once or twice depending on the last bit of a float.

Asked once when a room opens rather than every frame. It is what tells the player that a scene's own viewpoint sits outside its bounds, which is otherwise invisible until they try to move and find the walls behaving backwards.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Crosses(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Whether a ray meets a triangle in front of where it starts.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Sweep(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: How far along a step a sphere gets before it meets one triangle.
member.returns: A fraction of the step, or null when it never meets it.

remarks.para: Three things can stop the sphere and all three are tested, because the nearest of them is the one that matters: the face itself, one of its three edges, and one of its three corners. Testing only the face lets a camera slip through the seam between two triangles, which on a shell built of quads is every second join.

The face test moves the plane out by the radius and finds where the centre crosses it; the edges and corners are the classic reduction of a swept sphere to a ray against a cylinder and a ball. A fraction below zero means the sphere was already touching, which is reported as zero rather than as a move backwards.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Ball(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.CameraBounds.Cylinder(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Where a moving sphere first touches a line segment.
member.remarks: The infinite cylinder around the segment, then a check that the touch happened between the two ends. The ends themselves are the corners, tested separately.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.SceneSight
member.summary: Whether one point in a room can see another.

remarks.para: For WalkToSee, which is 2,120 of the corpus's 3,000-odd approaches and therefore the commonest thing anybody in the game does. It means "walk until you can see it", and without a sight test it can only mean "walk to it" — which is the same answer for anything standing in the open and much too close for anything on the far side of a wall, a counter or a doorway.

The room's own geometry and nothing else. Props and characters do not block a line of sight here, which matches the reference — a walker that stopped because somebody was standing in the way would stop in a different place every time the story moved somebody, and the walk is planned once before anybody sets off.

Rooms hold ten to twenty thousand triangles and a walk asks about thirty positions, six rays apiece, so the triangles are bucketed by where they stand on the ground plan and a ray visits only the buckets it crosses. Flat rather than three-dimensional because a room is wide and short: the height range of a whole scene is a few hundred units, so dividing it would gain very little and cost a dimension of book-keeping.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.SceneSight.Reach
member.summary: How far anybody is taken to be able to see, in scene units.
member.remarks: The reference's own figure. It is what stops "walk until you can see it" from meaning "do not walk at all" every time the thing is across an open room: Gabriel can see the far wall of the lobby from the door, and a walk that ended there would leave him describing a painting from thirty feet away.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.SceneSight.TriangleCount

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary
member.summary: Where an actor is allowed to stand, as a bitmap laid over the floor.

remarks.para: GK3 does not describe walkable ground with geometry. Each scene names a small palettised bitmap — boundary=R25wlkBnds, size={369.06, 386.20}, offset={39.95, -32.00} — stretched over the world's X/Z plane, and the palette index at a point says what is there. R25's is sixty-four pixels square for a room three hundred units across, so a texel is about five units: fine enough for a doorway, coarse enough that this is a navigation aid rather than collision.

The index is the region. Zero to seven is open floor, and the ascending values are a gradient away from the walls that the original's pathfinder used to keep actors from scraping along them. 255 is wall. Values from 128 up are named regions a script can open and close — a door that unlocks, a corridor that a guard blocks — which is why the unwalkable set is state rather than a constant. Across the corpus's 66 boundary bitmaps only 0-8, 229-238 and 245-255 ever appear.
Anything outside the bitmap is outside the room, and unwalkable.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary.ClosedByDefault
member.summary: The regions that are closed unless a script opens them.
member.remarks: 255 is wall. 8 and 9 are the far end of the gradient, close enough to a wall that the original treats them as wall too — 9 never appears in the corpus and is carried for the same reason the original carries it.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker
member.summary: An actor crossing a room.

remarks.para: finds a route across the walk boundary and nothing moved along it. This does: given the elapsed time it advances a position along the route's corners, turning to face the way it is going, and says when it has arrived.

Position and facing only. Playing the walk cycle needs the .ACT vertex animation format, so what crosses the room at the moment is an actor in whatever pose they were standing in — which looks odd and is still the difference between a game where the player goes places and one where they do not.

Turning is separate from moving and faster, so an actor rounding a corner turns into it over a few frames rather than snapping. Both are rates rather than durations, because a route's length is not known until it is found and a fixed duration would make a long walk and a short one take the same time.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Speed
member.summary: How fast an actor walks when nothing says otherwise, in units a second.
member.remarks: R25 is 369 by 386 units across, so this crosses it in about six seconds. It is a guess, and a walk that has a clip uses the clip's own pace instead — see . Gabriel's stride covers 49.9 units in 1.40 seconds, which is 35.6: this is nearly twice that, and the difference is a character whose feet slide.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.TurnRate
member.summary: How fast an actor turns, in radians a second.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.StandOff
member.summary: How far short of a thing an actor stops, when nothing says otherwise.
member.remarks: Gabriel's WalkerHeight, which is what a character with an entry in CHARACTERS.TXT uses instead. Standing a person's own height away from what they are looking at is about right for a picture on a wall and not obviously wrong for anything else.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Close
member.summary: How near the first corner an actor may already be standing.
member.remarks: Only for the route's opening corner, which usually puts where the actor already is. Walking to where you are is a wasted step and a turn towards nothing in particular.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.#ctor(System.String,GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkRoute,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Single,System.Nullable{System.Single},System.Nullable{System.Numerics.Vector3},System.Nullable{System.Single})
member.summary: Starts an actor walking.
member.param: Whose walk it is.
The corners to walk, in order.
Where they are standing now.
Which way they are facing now, in radians.
Which way to be facing on arrival, in radians, or null to keep whatever direction the last step was going.

A point to be facing on arrival. Taken from wherever the actor actually stops, which is not where they were sent: the boundary stops them short of anything solid, so a heading worked out in advance from the requested destination is a heading towards a place they never reach — and when the two coincide, no heading at all.
How fast they walk, in scene units a second, or null for . A walk with a stride to play should pass the stride's own pace, or the feet and the ground disagree.
member.remarks: Arriving facing something is the point of most walks. A scene's named spots each carry a heading — the way somebody standing there is meant to face — and walking to look at a thing means ending up looking at it. Without this an actor arrives facing whichever way the last corner of the route happened to point, which is usually a wall.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Actor
member.summary: Whose walk it is.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Pace
member.summary: How fast this actor walks, in scene units a second.
member.remarks: The stride's own speed where there is one, so that the ground covered and the feet covering it agree. Everything else about a walk is a rate rather than a duration for the same reason: a route's length is not known until it is found.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Ground
member.summary: How high the ground is under a point, when the room can say.

remarks.para: Set by whoever starts the walk, because the answer belongs to the room rather than to the actor. Null keeps the old behaviour — hold the height set off at — which is what a room with no floor object named has to do.

Applied after every move rather than baked into the route, and that is the point: a route is corners on a flat bitmap, so the only place the shape of the ground can get in is where the actor actually is.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Position
member.summary: Where they are now.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Facing
member.summary: Which way they are facing, in radians about the vertical.

member.remarks: A route that stopped short is still walked — getting as close as the floor allows is what the original does — but a caller that cares can tell the difference.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Walking
member.summary: Whether there is any walking left, or any turning after it.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Destination
member.summary: Where the route ends, which is not always where the caller asked to go.
member.remarks: A route that cannot reach its goal stops as near as the floor allows, and this is that spot rather than the unreachable one. IsWalkingActorNear asks about it: a script that wants to know whether somebody is on their way over means the place they will actually end up.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Turning
member.summary: Whether the route is done and only the arrival turn is left.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Arrival
member.summary: Which way to be facing once the walking is over, if it matters.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Remaining
member.summary: How far there is still to go, in scene units.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Seconds
member.summary: How long the whole walk will take, in seconds.

remarks.para: The ground and then the turn at the end of it. The turn was missing, and it is what an action is held back by: defers a script by exactly this number, so a walk that reported only its distance let the script start while the actor was still rotating to face what he had walked to.

Reported as the coffee pot: Gabriel is sent to the table, the pot's clip begins the moment his feet stop, and it plays out in the air beside a man still turning towards it. Anything an actor walks up to and then handles has the same shape.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Swing
member.summary: How far there is still to turn at the end of the walk, in radians.
member.remarks: Worked out for where the walk ends rather than for where the actor is standing now. Arriving along the last leg of the route is what they will be facing, and the last leg is known from the start — so this is an estimate only in that the route may be replaced, which replaces the walk and this along with it.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Advance(System.Single)
member.summary: Moves along the route.
member.param: How much time has passed.
member.returns: True while there is still walking to do.
member.remarks: A frame long enough to cross more than one corner crosses more than one corner, rather than stopping at the first and losing the rest of the frame. A slow frame should cost smoothness, never distance.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Grounded(System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Puts a point on the floor, if the room knows where the floor is.
member.remarks: The height that goes in is the one the actor is already at, which is what lets a floor covering the same ground twice answer with the storey they are on rather than the one above it.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Stop
member.summary: Stops where they stand.
member.remarks: For leaving the room, and for a script that asked for a walk and then asked for something else. An actor left mid-stride is better than one who goes on walking towards a corner of a room nobody is in.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Transform(System.Single,System.Nullable{System.Single})
member.summary: The transform to place the actor's model with.
member.param: The scale the model was placed at.
member.returns: The transform.
member.param: Which way the model is built to face, when its own arrow says. Null turns it by the half turn most models want, which is what this did before any of them were measured.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Rotation(System.Single)
member.summary: The rotation that points a character's model along a heading.
member.param: A heading, in radians, as the game's data measures one.
member.returns: The angle to turn the model about the vertical.

remarks.para: GK3 measures a heading the way it measures a camera's — zero along +Z, increasing towards +X — and models its characters facing −Z. Every heading in the engine is the first kind, and this is the single place the second is applied.

R25 is the case that settles it. The room stands an actor arriving from the hall at FR_HALL, heading=180, which under that convention faces −Z: away from the door, into the room. Its neighbour TO_HALL is at heading=-5.12, facing +Z at the door — and the door's own action is approach=walkto, target=To_Hall, so the pair say the same thing twice.

Worth keeping in one place because the failure never looks like a convention problem. The same half turn stands an actor facing the door they just came through, walks them backwards, arrives them with their back to what they came to look at, and aims their head away from whatever they were told to watch — four bugs that get chased separately.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.HeadingOf(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: Reads a heading back out of a placement.
member.param: A placement built as a turn about the vertical and a move.
member.returns: The heading, as the game's data measures one.
member.remarks: The inverse of , and its own inverse: a half turn undoes a half turn. It lives here so that the two can never drift apart.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Face(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Single)
member.summary: Turns towards a direction, at most so far this frame.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Heading(System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: The heading that looks along a direction.
member.param: Where they should be looking, in world space.
member.returns: A heading, in radians, as the game's data measures one.
member.remarks: The game's own convention, which is Heading::FromDirection: zero along +Z, increasing towards +X. What a heading means for the model is 's business, and only its business — a value that comes out of here and one that comes out of a scene file mean the same thing and may be compared, subtracted and handed to the same places.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.StandingOff(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Single)
member.summary: Where to stand to look at something, rather than on top of it.
member.param: The middle of what is being looked at.
Where the actor is coming from.
How far short to stop, in scene units.
member.returns: A spot on the line between the two.

remarks.para: A named spot is where the artists put it and is walked to exactly. A thing has no spot, so the aim is the middle of the object — and the middle of a picture on a wall is inside the wall. The boundary stops the actor before they get into it, so nothing looks broken; they just end up with their nose against it. Measured in R25, walking to the middle of the four paintings stops 9, 9, 13 and 35 units off them.
Never further away than the thing already is, so an actor standing closer than this does not back away from what they were sent to look at.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Flat(System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Drops the vertical, because walking is a thing done on a floor.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Wrapped(System.Single)
member.summary: Brings an angle into the range where the shorter way round is the smaller.
member.param: The angle.
member.returns: The same angle, between minus half a turn and a half turn.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.Walker.Wrap(System.Single)
member.summary: Brings an angle into the range where the shorter way round is the smaller.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkFloor
member.summary: How high the ground is under a point.

remarks.para: The walk boundary is a picture of the floor seen from above: it says where an actor may stand and nothing whatever about how high the floor is there. Nothing else did either, so a walk held whatever height the actor set off at — which is right for a flat room and wrong for every ramp, step and slope in the game.

The height comes from the room's own geometry. A scene names the object its floor is — floor=rc1_floor — and every room's general .SIF does, so this is a lookup rather than a guess. The named object's triangles are dropped into a uniform grid keyed on X and Z, and a query tests the handful in one cell.

Rooms are not single-storey. A stairwell's floor object covers the same ground twice, and a balcony over a hall covers it a third time, so "the triangle under this point" is several triangles and which one is meant depends on where the actor already is. The nearest one that is not an implausible climb wins; failing that, the nearest of any. Following the wrong storey is the one failure that looks like a bug rather than a wobble, and it is what a plain highest-or-lowest rule does at the top of every stair.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkFloor.Rise
member.summary: How far above an actor the floor may be and still be theirs, in units.
member.remarks: A step up. Gabriel is 76 units tall, so this is a little under knee height: enough for a kerb or a stair tread, not enough to reach the landing above.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkFloor.Drop
member.summary: How far below an actor the floor may be and still be theirs, in units.
member.remarks: Deliberately larger than : walking off a step is ordinary and walking up onto one is not, and an actor whose feet are a shade above the ramp they are on must not be handed the storey below.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkOverlay
member.summary: The walk boundary as something you can look at.

remarks.para: A boundary is a bitmap in its own coordinate space with a size and an offset, and every part of that is easy to get subtly wrong: an inverted row order, a swapped offset sign and a boundary half a room out all produce a mask that looks reasonable in isolation. Plan/04 makes overlay validation part of the phase's exit criteria for exactly that reason — the only way to know a boundary is right is to see it lying on the floor it describes.

Each open texel becomes a quad at the height of the floor beneath it, coloured by region so the gradient away from the walls is visible and the scriptable regions stand out from ordinary ground. Texels with no floor under them are left out: a boundary covers a rectangle and a room is not one, so a good half of most bitmaps hangs over nothing.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkOverlay.Lift

member.remarks: About a centimetre. Enough to win the depth test everywhere without the quads visibly hovering, which at this scale would read as a bug in the overlay rather than as the overlay.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkOverlay.RouteLift

member.remarks: Higher than so a route drawn over the region overlay wins the depth test against it rather than fighting with it texel by texel.

member.summary: Draws a route across the floor.
member.param: The scene's geometry, for the floor to lie on.
Which object in it is the floor; null tests all of them.
The boundary the route was found on, for its scale.
The route's corners, as returned them.
What to draw it in, each channel from zero to one.
member.returns: One patch carrying the whole route, or null when it has no points or no floor beneath it. Its region is -1: a route is not a region of the boundary.
member.remarks: A ribbon of overlapping squares sampled along the route rather than one quad per segment, because each sample takes the height of the floor under it — so the ribbon climbs a step and follows a ramp instead of sinking through either. It is drawn one texel wide, the same as the cells it crosses, so a route reads at the scale of the boundary that produced it rather than as a hairline nobody can see. It is drawn above the region overlay so the two can be shown together, which is the check worth doing: a route that leaves the green is a bug in one of them.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath
member.summary: Finds a way across a scene's walk boundary.

remarks.para: The algorithm is G-Engine's WalkerBoundary::FindPath: a breadth-first search over the boundary's texels, then two passes of conditioning to make the result look like something a person would walk. G-Engine's note on why it is not A* is worth keeping — the graph is enormous and its edges are effectively unweighted, so the heuristic buys nothing that the queue was not already giving.

The search runs on a sparse lattice first, taking every fourth texel, and halves that only when it fails. Most walks are across open floor and find their way at the coarsest setting; a doorway three texels wide is what forces the full grid. Intermediate texels are still tested when stepping between lattice nodes, so a sparse search cannot walk through a wall — it can only fail to find a gap.

Then the gradient earns its keep. Regions 0-7 measure distance from a wall, so the interior nodes of the route are nudged towards lower indices until they are comfortably clear of one, and the route is string-pulled: where three consecutive nodes have open floor between the first and the third, the middle one is not doing any work. Without both, a BFS path scrapes the walls and turns on every texel.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.Neighbours
member.summary: The order neighbours are considered in: the four sides, then the four corners.
member.remarks: The order decides which of several equally short routes comes out, so it is part of the behaviour rather than an implementation detail. This is G-Engine's order.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.InitialNodeSkip
member.summary: How many texels the first, sparsest search steps by.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.ClearOfWalls
member.summary: The region a conditioned node is happy to sit on.
member.remarks: Far enough from the wall that an actor of ordinary width clears it. Pushing all the way to zero would drag every route to the middle of the room.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.ShortcutCeiling
member.summary: The highest region a string-pulled shortcut may cross.
member.remarks: A shortcut is a straight line with no conditioning of its own, so it is held to a tighter standard than a node the search chose: 7 and 8 are close enough to a wall that cutting a corner across them clips it.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.MaxErasures
member.summary: How many nodes may be dropped from one place before moving along.
member.remarks: String pulling with no limit collapses a route to a single straight line wherever it can, which loses the shape of a room — the way a corridor bends, or a route that goes around a table rather than at it.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.Find(GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Finds a way from one point to another.
member.param: Where actors may stand.
Where the walk starts. Only X and Z are read.
Where it is trying to get to. Only X and Z are read.
member.returns: The route. Either end is snapped to the nearest open texel first, so a walk that starts inside a wall — an actor placed badly by a script — still leaves it, and a click on a wall walks up to the wall.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.Search(GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary,System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32}})

member.param: Where actors may stand.
The texel to start from.
The texel to reach.
How many texels a step covers.
Receives the route, start first, replacing whatever it held.
member.returns: True if the goal was reached.
member.remarks: A failed search still fills , with the route to whichever node came closest to the goal. That is the difference between an actor who walks as far as the locked door and one who stands still when you click past it.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.IsClear(GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Whether a straight step between two texels stays on open ground.
member.remarks: Only matters when the search is stepping several texels at a time: a lattice node on either side of a wall is no use if the wall is between them.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.Crosses(GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary,System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.Int32)
member.summary: Whether the straight line between two texels stays on open ground.
member.param: Where actors may stand.
One end.
The other.
The highest ordinary region the line may cross, or zero for any walkable one.
member.returns: True when an actor may walk it.

remarks.para: The line has to be the line. This used to walk towards the far end one texel at a time, moving diagonally while both axes differed and straight afterwards — which for anything but a pure axis or a pure diagonal is a different path from the one it is meant to be testing. From (0,0) to (10,2) it went diagonally to (2,2) and then straight along the row, so a wall standing across the middle of the real line was never sampled and the shortcut was allowed. The actor then walked the real line, through the wall.
Stepping the dominant axis one texel at a time and rounding the other is exact enough: no texel along the line is skipped, because neither axis can advance by more than one in a step.

A diagonal step must not slip between two blocked texels that meet at a corner. Both of the texels it passes between have to be open, or the line goes through the join — which is a wall with no gap in it as far as anybody looking at the room is concerned.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.Open(GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Whether one texel is open, and open enough for the caller.

member.summary: Nudges the route's interior off the walls.
member.remarks: The ends are left exactly where they were. They are where an actor is standing and where it was told to go, and moving either of those is a bug rather than a polish — an actor asked to stand on a mark has to stand on the mark.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.Downhill(GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary,System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32},System.Int32)
member.summary: The first neighbouring texel that is further from a wall, if any.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkPath.PullString(GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkBoundary,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.ValueTuple{System.Int32,System.Int32}})
member.summary: Drops nodes the route does not need.
member.remarks: Given three consecutive nodes, if the walk from the first to the third is clear then the second was an artefact of the grid. G-Engine's limit on how many may go at once is kept, and reset each time the window moves, so the route keeps the shape of the room instead of collapsing onto the longest straight line available.

member.summary: Whether a straight walk between two texels is comfortable.
member.remarks: Stricter than : a shortcut also has to keep clear of the walls, or string pulling would undo the conditioning that just moved the route off them.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.OriginalSaves
member.summary: Reads the saves the 1999 game wrote, as far as they can honestly be read.

remarks.para: A retail .gk3 save is two things. The front is a summary — who saved, when, where they were in the story, what they had scored, and a picture — in a fixed layout that G-Engine documents field by field. The rest is the original engine serialising nearly every live class in itself through RTTI, which no reimplementation reads; G-Engine writes its own data there too.

So the import takes what the summary states and recovers what follows from it: the timeblock, the location, the score, and the save's own name. Everything a point in the story implies — every score event belonging to a timeblock already behind the player — is marked earned by the same reasoning the schema-1 migration uses: the story cannot leave a timeblock until its rules are met, and marking those events is also what stops them paying out twice. What the player was carrying beyond their starting items, and the flags of the current block, are not in the summary and are not invented.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.OriginalSaves.Import(System.String,GK3Reborn.Game.SaveStore,GK3Reborn.Game.ScoreEvents)
member.summary: Imports every original save in a directory that has not been imported yet.
member.param: Where the original game kept them, usually its install root.
Where the imports go.
The score table, for what a past timeblock is worth.
member.returns: How many were imported this time.
member.remarks: Each import is filed under the original file's own name — gk3-save0004 — so importing is idempotent: a slot that exists is a save already brought across, and deleting the import is how somebody asks for it to be brought across again.

It is loaded and placed either way — there is no showing something that was never read — so this is the difference between a model that is in the room and one that is in the picture. Settable, because that is exactly what the scripts change. Anything answering "what is under the pointer" has to respect it, or the player can click on things nobody can see.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.PlacedModel.Posed
member.summary: Where each mesh group has been posed to, or null where nothing has moved it.

remarks.para: A clip does not move a model — it replaces each mesh group's own transform, and the model's placement is applied on top. So says nothing about where a character an animation has put somewhere actually is: Emilio sits in the lobby's loveseat with a placement of identity, and the whole of the displacement is in here.

Kept because anything asking a question about an object after it has been posed — what did this click land on, above all — has to ask about where it is now. The renderer owns the copy that is drawn; this is the same value, on the way past.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.PlacedModel.Head
member.summary: The head as the clips address it, when the head being drawn is refined.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.SaveGame
member.summary: A game, written down.

remarks.para: The contents are not a design decision so much as a reading of : that method already enumerates everything observable about a run, in a fixed order, because a state hash that missed something would be useless for the comparison it exists for. A save that stores less than the hash covers is a save that can be loaded into a different game than the one that was saved, so the two lists are kept deliberately identical and a test compares the hash across a round trip rather than comparing fields.

Presentation is not in here. Which screen was open, where the camera was gliding, what was half-said — none of it is state the story reads, and restoring it would mean restoring a moment rather than a position. A loaded game puts the player in the room, at the scene's own camera, with nothing in front of it.

Schema version is checked, not assumed. A save from a future build is refused by name rather than half-read; a save from a past one goes through 's migration, which is a real place to put work rather than a promise. The one migration that exists today is from nothing.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.SaveGame.CurrentSchema
member.summary: The schema this build writes.
member.remarks: Two adds the score events earned and the journal's hints. The first of those was always missing rather than newly needed: a save has always carried the player's total and never which events made it up, so loading one and doing the same thing again scored it twice. The journal made that visible, because it reads those events to know what has been done.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.SaveStore
member.summary: Where saved games live, and the only thing that writes them.

remarks.para: In the user's own profile beside the settings — %AppData%\GK3Reborn\saves on Windows, ~/.config/GK3Reborn/saves on Linux — for the same reasons the settings are: a game directory may be read-only, shared between accounts, or replaced wholesale by an update, and none of those should cost somebody their progress.

Every write is atomic. A save is written to a temporary file, flushed, and moved into place; a process that dies halfway through leaves the previous save untouched rather than a half-written one. This is the single most important property here — the plan's own words are that "failures cannot corrupt the last good save" — and it is why exists.

A save is never overwritten from a game that failed to start. Nothing here decides that; the caller does, by saving after the state is real rather than before. The autosave slot is written on arriving somewhere, which is the point at which the story is at rest.

Slots are files, and the name is the slot: autosave, quicksave, slot-01. A name is checked before it becomes a path, because a slot name reaches this from a console command and a save called ..\..\settings must not be a way to write one.

remarks.para: A saves folder beside the game, rather than buried in the player's profile where the settings live. Saves are something a player copies, backs up and sends to somebody else; a preferences file is not, and the two do not want the same home.

Falls back to the profile when the game is somewhere it cannot write — a read-only install, or a folder needing a prompt nobody is there to answer. Refusing to save at all because of where the game was put would be the worse failure.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SaveStore.Migrate(GK3Reborn.Game.SaveGame)
member.summary: Brings an older save up to the current schema.
member.param: The save as read.
member.returns: The save this build understands.
member.remarks: Each step reads a version and returns the next one, so a save two versions behind goes through both. The alternative — discovering at the first schema change that every save in the wild is unreadable — is much harder to fix then than now.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SaveStore.ToSchema2(GK3Reborn.Game.SaveGame)
member.summary: Works out what an older save can honestly be said to have achieved.
member.param: A save written before score events were recorded.
member.returns: The same save, with what is recoverable recovered.

remarks.para: Schema 1 wrote the player's total and never which events made it up. That was always a defect — loading such a save and doing the same thing again scored it twice — and the journal is what made it visible, because it reads those events to know what has been done.

What is recoverable is everything belonging to a point in the story the player is past. The story cannot advance out of a timeblock until its own rules are satisfied, so a save sitting in Day 2 has been through the whole of Day 1. Marking those events earned is also strictly protective: it is what stops the player being paid twice for them.

What is not recoverable is the block they are standing in, and nothing is invented about it. Those objectives show as unfinished until the player does them again, which costs them a little repetition and never a wrong answer — and the score itself is the number the save recorded, not one recomputed from this.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SaveStore.PictureOf(System.String)
member.summary: Where a slot's picture of the room lives.
member.param: The slot.
member.returns: The path, whether or not anything is there.
member.remarks: Beside the save rather than inside it. A saved game is JSON a person can read and a picture is not, and base64 in the middle of it would make the file unreadable to keep two things together that are perfectly happy apart. Deleting a save takes its picture with it; a picture with no save is ignored.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SaveStore.Illustrate(System.String,GK3Reborn.Formats.Bitmaps.DecodedImage)
member.summary: Keeps a picture of the room beside a save.
member.param: The slot it belongs to.
The frame, already reduced to a thumbnail.
member.returns: True when it was written.
member.remarks: Failure is silent on purpose. A save whose picture could not be written is still a save, and refusing the whole thing over a decoration would be the worse trade — which is the same reasoning that makes the picture a separate file in the first place.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SaveStore.Picture(System.String)
member.summary: The picture beside a save, if there is one.
member.param: The slot.
member.returns: The image, or null when the slot has none or it cannot be read.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneAudio
member.summary: What the room sounds like.

remarks.para: Three things put sound in a GK3 scene and they behave differently enough to be worth separating. Ambience is one looping bed that lasts as long as the room does. Effects are one-shots a script fires and forgets. Dialogue is a queue: a voice-over of three lines is three files played one after another, and the second must not start until the first has finished.

Which file a spoken line actually is comes out of the animation that carries it. A script says StartVoiceOver("0NQIB44QR1", 2); the plate resolves to E0NQIB44QR1.YAK, whose [SOUNDS] names A0NQIB44.QR1, and that is the audio. Nothing in the script mentions any of those names, which is why the library and the animations both have to be here for anybody to say a word.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneAudio.FadeSeconds
member.summary: How long a bed takes to fade when its own soundtrack does not say.
member.remarks: Most of them do say. A .STK gives each sound a FadeOutMS — R25's theme asks for three seconds — and that is the artists' own answer to how long this room should take to stop being the room you are in. This is only for the ones that leave it out: long enough to hear as a change of place rather than a cut, and about as long as walking through a door takes.

member.remarks: Its own generator rather than the game's, so that how often a room creaks does not depend on how many times anybody has clicked on anything — and seeded, so that two runs of the same scene make the same noises at the same moments. ADR 0004.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneAudio.Speaking
member.summary: Told whenever a line starts or stops, so that faces can follow it.

remarks.para: A line of dialogue is one animation: its [SOUNDS] is the recording and its [GK3] is the mouth shapes, against the same frame numbers. So whatever moves mouths needs the animation and not just the name of it, and it needs it at the moment the sound actually starts rather than when the script asked for it — a queued line may be several seconds behind the call that queued it.
Null when nothing is being said, which is how a mouth learns to close. Optional: the room may be running without faces, or without anything to draw them on.

member.remarks: Read from the animation rather than a subtitle file, because that is where GK3 keeps it: a [GK3] section of speaker and text against frame numbers. It is what a subtitle track will be drawn from.
