member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Walk(System.String,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Nullable{System.Single},System.Nullable{System.Numerics.Vector3},System.Boolean,System.Boolean,System.Nullable{System.ValueTuple{System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3}})
member.summary: Sets an actor walking to a place on the floor.
member.param: Their model name.
Where to go, in world space.
Which way to face on arrival, in radians, or null to keep the direction of travel.
What to be looking at on arrival, if not a fixed heading.
Whether to go at times the usual pace. The player's own impatience and nothing else: a script's timings are written against the pace the game walks at.

Whether a long walk may pick up the pace by itself. True for a walk the player asked for and false for one a script asked for, because a script's timings assume the pace the game was authored at and this would run out from under them.

The bounds of what the walk is to see, or null for an ordinary walk. Given one, the walk stops where the thing comes into view rather than where it was aimed — which is what WalkToSee means, and 2,120 of the corpus's approaches are one.
member.returns: How long the walk will take, or zero when there is no walking to do.

remarks.para: The route is found across the walk boundary rather than aimed straight at the destination, so an actor asked to cross a room goes round the bed rather than through it. A boundary that cannot reach the destination gives the closest it can, which is what the original does: getting as near as the floor allows beats refusing to move.
Asking again replaces the walk in progress. A script that changes its mind means it.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Sight
member.summary: The room's sight tester, built the first time anybody asks.
member.remarks: Lazily, because most scenes are loaded without anybody walking to see anything in them — a corpus sweep loads all 143 — and building it walks every triangle of the room.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Eyes(GK3Reborn.Game.PlacedModel)
member.summary: How high an actor's eyes are above their feet.
member.param: The model.
member.returns: The character's own height, or the walker's default.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.ShortenedWhenSeen(GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkRoute,GK3Reborn.Game.PlacedModel,System.ValueTuple{System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3})
member.summary: Cuts a walk short at the point where what it is going to look at comes into view.
member.param: The route as the boundary found it.
Who is walking, for how tall they are.
The bounds of what they are walking to see.
member.returns: The route, cut where the thing is first visible.

remarks.para: Each corner is tested, and three points along the leg leading to it, because a doorway is often crossed between two corners and testing only the corners walks the actor a whole leg past the moment they could see. That is the reference's own sampling.

Then one corner further, also as the reference has it: stopping on the exact frame a sliver of the thing appears round a corner reads as a character noticing something impossible, where a step or two more puts them in the open looking at it.
A route that never sees it is walked in full. That is the old behaviour, and it is the right fallback: the thing may be inside a cupboard the walk is meant to end at.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Standing(System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Drops a point onto the room's floor, when the room has one.
member.remarks: The point's own height goes in and decides which storey is meant, so a spot authored on the gallery stays on the gallery and one authored at zero in a room whose floor is at zero does not move at all.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Follow(System.String,System.Nullable{System.Numerics.Vector3})
member.summary: Writes an actor's logical position, under every name they answer to.
member.remarks: A scene places gab and calls him GABRIEL, and either name may be asked for.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Place(System.String,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Single)
member.summary: Stands an actor at a spot outright, without walking them there.
member.param: Their model name or noun.
Where to stand them, in world space.
Which way to face, as the game's data measures a heading.
member.returns: True when there was somebody of that name to move.
member.remarks: This is how a room decides where the player is standing when they walk into it. A scene places its actors at whatever its [ACTORS] section says — usually START — and then its SCENE:ENTER action moves the player to the spot that matches the door they came through. Without it, every arrival is the front door.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Turn(System.String,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Turns an actor on the spot to face something.
member.param: Their model name or noun.
What to face, in world space.
member.returns: How long the turn will take, or zero when there is nobody to turn.
member.remarks: 394 of the corpus's approaches are TurnToModel, which means turn where you stand rather than go anywhere. Walking to the thing instead puts the actor on top of whatever they were meant to be looking at.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.StopWalking
member.summary: Stops everyone where they stand.
member.remarks: For leaving the room, where a walk in progress has nowhere to arrive.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Later
member.summary: How many things are waiting to happen.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.After(System.Double,System.Action)
member.summary: Holds something back for a while.
member.param: How long to hold it.
What to do then.
member.returns: True when it was taken, false when there was nothing to wait for.

remarks.para: What makes an action's approach mean anything. The original walks the player to the thing and then runs the action's script: BUTHANE, TALK, approach=WalkTo, target=TALK_BUTHANE means go and stand there before saying a word. Running the script straight away is what made Gabriel talk to somebody from across the square, and open a door from the far side of the room.
A delay of nothing is refused rather than queued, so an action with no approach — or one whose walk found nowhere to go — still runs in the frame it was asked for.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Cancel
member.summary: Forgets everything that was waiting to happen.
member.remarks: For leaving the room. What is queued is nearly always an action script belonging to the room being left, and letting one run into the next room is how a door opens twice.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.StepLater(System.Double,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.String})

member.summary: Which of the script's standing conditions are currently met.
member.remarks: By step index, so two conditions on the same noun stay apart. What makes the jumps edge-triggered: a condition fires the frame it turns true and not again until it has turned false in between.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Behaviour.Interrupted
member.summary: Whether the clip it was waiting out was stopped for something else.
member.remarks: A script that has asked for an animation waits out its length before going on, and a continuous one — a fan — waits for ever. Either way the wait is now counting down something that is not playing any more, so the script carries on as soon as it has its model back. The original reaches the same place: stopping the animation asks the player for its next node, and a paused player runs that the moment it resumes.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Behaviour.Playing
member.summary: The animation it last asked for, which is what a cleanup is looked up by.
member.remarks: A GAS file may declare USES CLEANUP EmlLbyOpnPaper emllbyclspaper: if the script is stopped while the first is what it is doing, the second puts it right. So which animation is in effect has to be remembered — a stopped script cannot be asked what it was in the middle of afterwards.

member.summary: Where the story wants the view, or null while it has not moved it.
member.remarks: A cut arrives at once and a glide takes to get there, so during one this is somewhere between the two cameras rather than at either. The player's own camera is a separate thing: this says where the story put the view, and what happens to a player who was flying it around is the caller's decision.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Gliding
member.summary: Whether the view is on its way somewhere.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.StartAt(GK3Reborn.Rendering.Camera)
member.summary: Says where the view already is, so a glide has somewhere to leave from.
member.param: Where the scene opened.
member.remarks: Without this the first move the story makes is always a cut, however it was asked for, because there is nothing to interpolate away from. The caller knows where the scene started and this does not. It deliberately does not take note of where the story currently wants the view: a glide asked for before the first frame is still a glide, and swallowing it here would turn it into a cut.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Advance(System.Double)
member.summary: Lets time pass.
member.param: How much.
member.returns: What the world did on its own, for whoever wants to say so.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate._triggers
member.summary: The patches of floor that act on whoever walks onto them.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Tripped(System.Collections.Generic.List{System.String})
member.summary: Runs the action for any trigger the player is standing in.
member.param: What to report it as.

remarks.para: How the game says "and then you overhear them". A scene file marks out a rectangle on the floor and names a noun, and standing in it does that noun's WALK — a verb no file writes beside the rectangle because Scene::Update hard-codes it. Thirty-four rectangles across twenty-nine files, and they carry the museum's eavesdrop, the front desk of the lobby, the window into Arnaud's office and the two lectures on the Blanchefort tour.

Not edge-triggered. The original tests every frame and relies on the action's own case to stop it happening twice — the museum's is GetNounVerbCount("GET_CLOSE", "WALK")==0 and its script increments that before it waits on anything. Firing only on the way in would instead lose the ones written to happen again, so the rule here is the reference's: while something is playing, nothing new is started.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.ShortenedAtTrigger(System.String,GK3Reborn.Game.Navigation.WalkRoute)
member.summary: Cuts a walk short where it would step onto a trigger.
member.param: Whose walk it is.
The route the boundary found.
member.returns: The route, cut at the edge of the first trigger it enters.

remarks.para: Walker::FindEarliestPathNodeInsideActiveTriggerRegion, whose own comment names the case: in the lobby on the first morning, the way to the front door goes through Jean's rectangle. Without this the player walks over the trigger, the action fires behind them, and the conversation it starts plays to somebody already at the door.

Only a walk the player asked for, and only one for the player. A script that sends somebody somewhere means all the way there — the museum's own eavesdrop ends by walking Gabriel into the rectangle it was fired by.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Entry(GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.SceneRect,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Where a segment first crosses into a rectangle.
member.param: The rectangle, on the ground plan.
The end of the segment outside it.
The end of the segment within it.
member.returns: The crossing point on X and Z, or null when the segment is degenerate.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Clip(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single@,System.Single@)
member.summary: One side of the Liang-Barsky clip.
member.param: How fast the segment approaches the edge.
How far outside the edge the segment begins.
The parameter at which it is inside so far.
The parameter at which it leaves.
member.returns: False when the segment misses the rectangle entirely.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Walked
member.summary: The verb a trigger's noun is looked up with.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate._quiet
member.summary: How many scripts were waiting before the room last started an action.
member.remarks: Minus one until it has. A room's own background scripts sit in the scheduler for as long as the room stands — the dining room and the third-floor hall each keep two parked permanently — so "any script is waiting" is not a usable answer to whether something is happening. The number of them when the room last acted is, because what an action starts is on top of that and what it started going away is the action being over.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Occupied
member.summary: Whether the story is in the middle of something.

remarks.para: ActionManager::IsActionPlaying, which is true from the moment an action starts until its script has finished waiting. Nothing here keeps a current action, so it is assembled out of four things that each cover part of one: an action held back for its approach walk, the waits an action reported when it ran, a clip the story is playing on the player, and any script still outstanding from the last action the room started itself.
The last of those is what covers wait CallSheep(…), whose length is another script rather than a number of seconds — which is most of what the triggers run.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.MoveView(System.Double)
member.summary: Takes the view wherever the story has put it.
member.remarks: The story moving the camera is a change of and nothing else, so this watches for one. Position and target are eased separately and linearly: an arc would look better and would also invent framing the artists did not author, which Plan/03 section 5 says to leave alone.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Pointing(System.String)
member.summary: Works out the view a camera key describes.
member.remarks: A close-up is looked for by three names in turn, which is the original's order: a camera the scene actually names — which is what InspectModelUsingAngle hands over — then the noun in the [INSPECT_CAMERAS] section, then the model standing behind that noun, because several rooms frame a thing only under the name of the mesh drawn there.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Framing(System.String)
member.summary: A close-up worked out from what the thing actually occupies.
member.param: What is being looked at.
member.returns: A camera framing it, or null when the room has no such thing to frame.

remarks.para: Only 111 close-ups are authored across the corpus, against the thousands of nouns a player can point at, so for most things [INSPECT_CAMERAS] has nothing to say. The view used to stay exactly where it was — and because inspecting still counted as having happened, the verb flipped to "Inspect Undo" and the player was offered a way out of something that never started.

So one is worked out instead, which is what the original does too. The box the thing occupies is measured in the room's own space, and the camera is put in front of it far enough back that the box fits the frame with a little air around it. An authored close-up still wins wherever there is one: the artists chose an angle, and this only chooses a distance.

From where the view already is, rather than from a fixed side. Cutting to the far side of a thing shows the player a face of it they were not looking at and reads as the room having turned around; approaching along the line they were already on reads as leaning in. Where the view is on top of the thing there is no line to keep, and the room's own default camera decides instead.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.CloseUpFieldOfView
member.summary: How wide a derived close-up sees, in radians.
member.remarks: Narrower than the room's sixty degrees. A close-up is a lens change as much as a move, and holding the room's own angle while standing this near flattens the thing being looked at into the wall behind it.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Occupies(System.String)
member.summary: The box a noun's geometry fills, in the room's space.
member.returns: The corners, or null when nothing in the room answers to that noun.
member.remarks: Every mesh of every model the noun names, at the transform it is standing at now rather than the one the scene first gave it — a thing being carried, opened or animated is somewhere else by the time anybody looks closely at it.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Inspectable(System.String)
member.summary: Whether anything in the room can be looked at closely.
member.param: What the player is pointing at.
member.returns: True when inspecting it would move the view.
member.remarks: Asked before the verb is offered rather than after it is chosen, so that a thing with no close-up simply has no Inspect on its menu — instead of one that does nothing and then offers to undo itself.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Narrowed(GK3Reborn.Rendering.Camera)
member.summary: Applies whatever field of view a script has asked for.
member.remarks: A story override rather than a camera's own: the scene files set one per camera and this is a script narrowing the view for a moment on top of that. Nothing asking leaves the camera exactly as the scene framed it.

member.summary: Whether the actor gives back the ground the clip covered.
member.remarks: An absolute clip never does. The original writes it as one line — allowMove = allowMove || absolute in AnimationNodes — and it follows from what absolute means: the clip says where in the room it happens, so putting the actor back where they were is undoing the only thing the clip was for. Emilio walks out of the hotel through an absolute clip, and without this he was returned to the spot he was standing on before he opened the door.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Playing.FromBehaviour
member.summary: Whether the model's own behaviour script asked for it.
member.remarks: What separates an idle from the story. One of these may be dropped or stopped for the other's sake; two clips from the story are the story contradicting itself, and the later one simply wins.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Playing.Correction(GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.ActFile,GK3Reborn.Game.PlacedModel,System.Nullable{GK3Reborn.Formats.Animation.AnimationPlacement},System.Numerics.Matrix4x4,GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.CharacterConfig)
member.summary: Where the clip's own space has to be moved to for it to play here.

remarks.para: A clip's mesh transforms replace the model's own, and the model's placement is applied on top. What that means depends entirely on what is being animated.

A prop is placed by the identity: the room's coordinates are the model's coordinates, so a clip written for that room plays exactly as authored and nothing has to be done to it. That is what the original does — it swaps the mesh transforms and stops there — and it is what the data expects: 1,635 of the game's prop clips move the thing away from where its model rests, because moving it is the whole point. A book being picked up is 59 units above the shelf; the moped that rides past RC1 crosses seventeen hundred units of it. Correcting those back to the model's rest is what left Wilkes riding past the world origin while Gabriel watched an empty square.

An actor is placed where the scene stands them, so their clip — authored wherever the animator built it, which for a walk is halfway across some other room — is shifted once, at the start, by however far its first frame sits from where the model rests. Root motion within the clip then still happens, measured from where the actor was standing. The shift is computed once and held, because recomputing it per frame would cancel exactly the movement it is meant to preserve.

An absolute clip carries its own spot and heading and is put there, whatever it belongs to. The heading is used as it stands: it is a transform, not a character's heading, and the half turn that turns one into the other — see — left RC1's fountain spraying water two hundred and fifty units from the fountain.

And because the model's placement is applied on top, the placement has to be taken back off for the clip to land where it was authored. A prop stands at the identity, so for years there was nothing to take off and nothing said there was; an actor stands wherever the scene put them or wherever they last walked to, and leaving that on moves the clip by the whole of it. That is the difference between Gabriel pouring the coffee at the counter and Gabriel pouring it somewhere out past the wall.

The reference point is the average of the mesh groups' origins. The original uses the shoes, named per character in CHARACTERS.TXT, which is not read yet; the average moves with the same rigid motion and differs only by a constant, which a difference of two averages cancels.

member.remarks: The frame is worked out from elapsed time rather than counted, so a dropped frame skips a pose instead of slowing the animation down. Fifteen frames a second is the original's rate and a large part of why its animation reads as stiff.

It is the same measure works from, so the two cannot disagree.

Which frame, with the fraction of the way to the next one. The clip records fifteen poses a second and the screen shows sixty, so a whole number here is four identical frames in a row; see .

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Playing.Turn(GK3Reborn.Game.Actors.HeadRig,System.Single)
member.summary: The rigid motion a clip is asking a refined head to make.
member.param: The head's authored vertices, which is what the clip addresses.
Which frame, with a fraction of the way to the next.
member.returns: The transform, or null when this clip does not move the head.

remarks.para: Every submesh the clip shapes on this frame is used, all at once: the fit wants as many points spread as widely as possible, and a hairline on its own is a poor lever arm for a rotation. A submesh whose vertex count disagrees with the model's is skipped rather than trusted — that is what a clip belonging to a different character looks like, and 12.9% of the corpus is filed under the wrong name.

A fit that comes back badly is not used. The corpus survey says every one of the fifty-six models with head clips is rigid — 1.0% of head width at the median of medians — so this is a guard rather than a routine path. What it guards against is the handful of clips that genuinely do deform a head: GAB_GABTE3HDOFF, the worst frame in the game at 17%, is Gabriel's head coming off. Where the fit is refused the vertex track is dropped and the head is carried by the clip's own transform track instead. It is decided once per clip rather than per frame, so a character near the threshold cannot flicker between the two answers. GK3Reborn.Tools head-solve is where the corpus's error is measured.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.WalkCycle
member.summary: A walking character's legs.

remarks.para: The clip is played for its pose and not for its ground. GK3 authors a walk as root motion — Gabriel's stride carries his hips 49.9 units along the model's −Z over 1.40 seconds — and the original lets that motion move the actor. Here owns the position, because it is what knows the route, the boundary and where the walk is supposed to end. Two things writing one position is the fault this avoids.

So the clip's forward travel is taken back out, frame by frame, and the character walks on the spot while the walker carries them. Only the forward travel. The hips also sway sideways and rise and fall — X returns to where it started every stride and Y bobs twice a stride — and removing those would flatten the walk into a glide with moving legs. What accumulates is Z, and Z is what comes out.
The pace comes from the same measurement, so the ground covered and the feet covering it agree. Get that wrong and the walk reads as a character being dragged.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.WalkCycle._steps
member.summary: The feet the stride puts down, and where it had got to when it was last asked.
member.remarks: A walk is played here rather than through — the stride is looped by frame and carries no schedule of its own — so nothing else can notice the animation's footstep nodes. Which meant that of all the things in the game that make a footstep noise, walking was the one that did not.

Everything that measures the clip rather than plays it asks this: how far the stride travels, which sets the pace the feet have to match, and whether the last frame closes back onto the first. Mixing into the answer would bend the pace towards a wrap that has not happened.

member.summary: The footstep nodes between the last frame shown and this one.
member.remarks: A range rather than an equality, because a stride is twenty frames and a frame of the game is a sixtieth of a second: at any pace above walking the loop skips frames, and a step tested for exactly would be missed. The wrap at the end of the loop is the other half of the same problem.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.WalkCycle.Step(GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink,System.Single)
member.summary: Poses the model for however long the walk has been going.
member.param: Where the poses go.
Time since the last frame.

remarks.para: Between the recorded frames, not on them. A stride is recorded at fifteen poses a second and drawn at sixty or more, so showing the recorded poses as they stand shows each of them four times and the legs arrive in four equal jumps. Every other clip in the game has gone through and been mixed since the day it was written; this one asked for whole frames, which is why walking was the one thing that still read as 1999 while the rest of a character did not.
The forward travel is taken out at the same moment of the clip that poses the meshes, or the body's offset steps while its legs slide and the feet skate.

The footsteps still go by whole frames. A footstep is an event on a numbered frame rather than a quantity to be mixed, and asking for it twice because a moment landed either side of one is a doubled sound.

member.summary: Tells a head where its owner has got to.
member.remarks: A glance is worked out from where the looker is standing, so an actor who walks while looking at something would go on aiming their head at where the thing was relative to where they set off from.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Turning.HeadingOf(System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: The heading a placement of this model amounts to.
member.remarks: The inverse of what turned it. A model built facing something other than −Z is turned by a different amount, so reading the heading back has to undo the same amount — otherwise a head is worked out against a body direction the body does not have.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SceneUpdate.Turning.Stands(System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Single)
member.summary: Where the model is standing and which way it faces, this frame.
member.param: Its position.
Its heading.

remarks.para: Read from the model every frame rather than remembered. It used to be told, by the walking loop, under whichever name the walk had been asked for — and a walk is asked for by noun as often as by model name, so MovedTo("EMILIO") never matched a head filed under eml and the update was silently dropped.

Emilio is the case that shows it. His scene gives him no position at all, so his facing began as the heading of the identity transform — which is a half turn — and nothing ever replaced it. He walked to the bench with his head pointing at the door, by exactly 180 degrees, for as long as this cached anything.

Nothing to keep in step is the point. A character is moved by walking, by an animation, by a script placing them and by an opening pose, and a cache has to be updated from all four; the model's own transform is already the answer to all four.

member.remarks: Pitch about the mesh's own sideways axis inside the yaw, which is nodding within a turn rather than turning a nodded head — what a neck does.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.ScoreEvents
member.summary: What each of the game's score events is worth.

remarks.para: ChangeScore takes the name of an event — ChangeScore("e_110a_lby_read_register") — and the points are the engine's business. Nothing in the shipped data says what one is worth: there is no such file in any of the eight barns, because the table was compiled into the original executable. So the engine carries it, restored from G-Engine's reconstruction; see Assets/Story/Scores.txt and NOTICE.

An event scores once. The same call is made every time the player does the thing, and the second time is worth nothing — which is also what makes the set of events achieved a reasonable record of what the player has done.

A name the table does not have scores nothing and is reported. The original logs "Illegal score name" and carries on, which is right: a typo in a script must not stop the game, and it must not silently award points either.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.ScriptHost
member.summary: Owns the loaded scripts and runs them, including when they call each other.

remarks.para: CallSheep appears 640 times across the corpus and Call another 190, so a virtual machine that cannot follow a call from one script into another cannot follow the game's control flow at all. This is what closes that gap: a repository of scripts by name, plus the API functions that jump between them.

Calls run to completion inline rather than being scheduled. The original waits on them — wait CallSheep(…) is the common form — and running the callee immediately is the same observable order for everything that does not depend on real elapsed time. Recursion is bounded, because the data can and does call in circles.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ScriptHost.#ctor(GK3Reborn.Game.Gk3SheepApi,System.Int64,System.Int32)
member.summary: Creates a host.
member.param: The API surface, which this extends with the calling functions.
Instruction budget for a single thread.
How deep script-to-script calls may nest.

member.summary: Diagnostics raised while running.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.ScriptHost.Scheduler
member.summary: Somewhere to leave a script that is waiting for something, if anywhere.
member.remarks: Without one, a blocked thread is told everything it waited on has finished and carried straight on, which is what this did from the beginning and what every tool still wants: a sweep of the corpus has no clock and no reason to want one. With one, the script waits, and the pacing it was written with is the pacing it gets.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.ScriptHost.Within(System.Action)
member.summary: Runs something, and says which scripts it called into.
member.remarks: The list is held before it is pushed, so that popping it in a finally and returning it are the same list without a field in between.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.ScriptHost._global
member.summary: The script CallGlobal reaches into, once one has said it is.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.ScriptHost._nested
member.summary: The scripts each running function has called, innermost last.
member.remarks: wait CallSheep("rc1102p", "LookMop") means "carry on when that function is over", and how long that takes is not knowable in advance: the function may itself wait on a timer, a line of dialogue or an animation. So the wait is on the thread rather than on a duration, and this is where a caller finds the threads it started. A fifth of every statement in the action corpus is one of these, and treating them as instant is what let RC1 show Wilkes's moped and hide it again in the same frame.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Settings
member.summary: What the player has chosen, and where it is kept.

remarks.para: Every one of these has somewhere real to go. The audio levels are the mixer's buses, which nothing had ever set; the picture quality is the ray-tracing ladder; the walking pace is what a double-click multiplies. A setting with no destination is a promise the interface cannot keep, so there are none here.

Kept in the user's own profile rather than beside the executable. A game directory may be read-only, shared between accounts, or replaced wholesale by an update, and none of those should cost somebody their volume levels.
Everything is clamped on the way in. A settings file is a text file somebody may edit, and a hand-typed volume of forty is not a reason to fail to start.

Somebody who wants the 1999 outline should be able to have it with the rest of the enhancement left on.

Off, or with no terrain data installed, every scene keeps the 1999 sky painting exactly as shipped.

remarks.para: Only the head. A character's body deforms and is addressed by vertex index, so it cannot be refined without invalidating that character's clips; the head is rigid and can. See .
Two by default, which is where a twenty-triangle hairdo stops reading as a polygon. Zero is a real answer for somebody who wants the 1999 outline.

member.remarks: The stride is played faster by the same amount, or the feet slide. One means a double-click does nothing, which is a legitimate answer for somebody who wants the pace the game was authored at.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.Settings.EasterEggs
member.summary: Whether the game's easter-egg content is switched on.

remarks.para: EGG is one of the built-in cases an action file may be written against, and the original hard-codes it false with a note saying it should return true when easter eggs are enabled — the switch itself never shipped, so nothing behind the case has ever been reachable in a playing game. This is that switch. It sets the story's EGG flag, which is what the case reads and what Sidney's sixth email is written against.
Off by default, because the game as it shipped is the game as it shipped, and somebody playing GK3 for the first time should meet it that way.

member.summary: Hands the audio levels to the mixer.

remarks.para: Called whenever a level changes as well as at startup, so a slider is heard while it is being dragged rather than after the menu is closed.

Every bus is set, not only the ones something plays on today. There are nine buses and five sliders; a bus left out is a sound the player cannot turn down, and which one that is would depend on which of two near-identical names the code that plays it happened to pick. Speech is a case in point: it is played on and not on .

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.SheepScheduler
member.summary: Scripts that are waiting for something.

remarks.para: A Sheep script says wait StartAnimation("GraCs3WrdbOpen"); SetNounVerbCount(…) and means it: the second statement is not supposed to happen until the first has finished. Without anywhere to put the waiting, the engine had to pretend everything finished at once, which is the difference between a script that paces a scene and a script that fires its whole contents into one frame.

The virtual machine has always parked a thread properly — a wait block with anything outstanding leaves it — and nothing ever kept it parked. This does. It holds the thread until the time the host said its calls would take has passed, then resumes it, which may block it again on the next wait block.

A host that does not know how long a call takes says zero, and a wait on it is over immediately, exactly as before. So this changes the pacing of the scripts whose waits are measurable — a timer, a camera glide — and leaves every other script running as it did.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SheepScheduler.#ctor(GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepVirtualMachine)
member.summary: Creates a scheduler over a machine.
member.param: The machine whose threads it resumes.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SheepScheduler.Count
member.summary: How many scripts are waiting for something.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SheepScheduler.Pending
member.summary: What they are waiting on, in a stable order.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Game.SheepScheduler.Calls
member.summary: What to carry a resumed script out inside, so that anything it calls can be waited on in turn.
member.remarks: A function's second wait block is reached by being resumed, not by being started, so a wait CallSheep(...) there is issued from in here rather than from . Given the work to do; answers which scripts it started. Null leaves a resumed script's calls unwaited, which is what a host with no notion of nested scripts wants.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SheepScheduler.Park(GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepThread,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepThread})
member.summary: Takes charge of a script that has blocked.
member.param: The thread.

Scripts this one called and is waiting on, if any. A wait CallSheep(...) is over when the function it called is over, and that is not a length of time — it is another script, which may itself be waiting on an animation, a walk or a timer.
member.returns: True when it was parked rather than being already finished.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SheepScheduler.Advance(System.Double)
member.summary: Lets time pass, and carries on whatever can carry on.
member.param: How much time.
member.returns: What was resumed, for whoever wants to say so.
member.remarks: A thread that blocks again goes straight back on the list with its new wait, so a script of five waited calls takes five waits to get through rather than one.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.SheepScheduler.Outstanding(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepThread})
member.summary: Whether any of the scripts a thread called is still going.
member.remarks: Being here is what "still going" means: a thread that finished was taken off this list, and one that blocked again went back on it. A caller that waited on a function which never blocked at all sees an empty answer and carries straight on, which is the ordinary case and costs nothing.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Sidney.SidneyFiles
member.summary: What may be scanned into Sidney, and what it becomes.

remarks.para: Scanning is already an ordinary action. The noun is the inventory item, the verb is SCANNER, and the case is IN_SIDNEY_ADD_DATA; the game's own INV_ALL.NVC carries the script, which marks the item used and sets a SidScanner variable to a number. Twenty-nine items can be scanned and the numbers run from 1 to 35.

What the original did with that number lives in its executable. What it has to mean here is the file the scan produces, and that is what this table is: the item's own name, which is where the meaning actually is — PARCHMENT_1 becomes fileParchment1, and the eight names the story asks about are all accounted for.

The prints, tapes and licences do not get story-visible file names because nothing asks DoesSidneyFileExist about one. They are still files: they appear in the store, the analysis recognises them, and the suspects screen is where they are meant to be used.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Sidney.SidneyLibrary
member.summary: Everything Sidney is told, read from the game's own text.

remarks.para: Sidney is a portable computer Grace carries, and the story runs through it: parchments are scanned into it, analysed, and translated, and the results are what let the next scene happen. It is not decoration and it cannot be skipped.

Almost all of it is data. ESIDNEY.TXT holds the menus, the screen names, and — the part that matters — the actual output of every analysis, keyed by what was analysed: AnalyzeParch1, ExtractParch1, Parch1French. What the engine has to supply is not the words but the machine: which files exist, which operation applies to which, what each one unlocks, and what the story is allowed to ask about afterwards. That is what this is.

Files are named by the story. DoesSidneyFileExist("fileParchment1") is a real condition in R31210A.NVC, and there are eight such names in the whole game. Scanning is an ordinary action — the noun is the inventory item, the verb is SCANNER, and the game's own action files carry the scripts — so what Sidney adds is the mapping from the item that was scanned to the file it becomes.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Sidney.SidneyMachine
member.summary: Sidney, running.

remarks.para: The words are the game's — see — and this is the machine underneath them: which file is open, which operations apply to it, what each one says, and which of them the story is allowed to notice afterwards.

What the story notices. Only two things reach the game's own conditions: DoesSidneyFileExist, which is answered from , and the flags an analysis sets when it completes. Everything else here — the text, the order the menus come in, which operation is offered — is presentation over that, and a player who never opens the analyze screen is only blocked where the story says so.

Operations are offered when they apply. The original left every menu item enabled and answered "Not implemented yet" or an unhelpful note for the ones that did not fit the open file. Here a file offers what it can do, which is the same information without making the player find it by exhaustion — docs/screens.md's rule that the interface should never have to be learned.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Sidney.SidneyMap
member.summary: Sidney's map: entering points on it and finding what they make.

remarks.para: The map is SIDNEYBIGMAP.BMP, a labelled survey of the Rennes-le-Château country with the Paris meridian drawn down it, and the puzzle is the one the books are about: mark the churches and the ruins, and see that they fall on a line, a rectangle, or a circle. ESIDNEY.TXT carries every answer the machine can give — that a line meets the meridian at Arques, that four points are "linked perfectly by a circle" — and this decides which of them applies.

The geometry is measured, not scripted. The original could have checked the player's points against a hardcoded list and printed the matching note; doing it by fitting means a player who marks four other points that genuinely lie on a circle is told so, and one who marks the right places sloppily still is. The tolerances are in map pixels and generous, because the player is clicking a village on a picture.

Coordinates are approximate and say so. The circle note quotes the coordinates of its centre, and Sidney's map carries no georeference anywhere in the game's data — the GPS.TXT entries belong to the handheld device in three outdoor scenes, not to this. What is used here is a linear fit anchored on the meridian the map draws and on the region's own extent, which puts a click within about a minute of arc. Good enough to read out; not good enough to navigate by, and the doc says so.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Sidney.SidneySearch
member.summary: Sidney's search: 391 pages of encyclopedia and the words that reach them.

remarks.para: Grace looks things up. SIDSEARCH.TXT lists 393 subjects, each naming a page and the spellings that should find it — "arcadia, et in arcadia, sheperds, shepherd" — and the pages themselves are small HTML documents in the archives, cross-linked to each other. Between them they are the game's own research material, and the puzzle that needs them is real: what the player types is checked against those spellings.

The markup is read rather than rendered. These are 1998 HTML pages using perhaps eight tags between them, and what the interface needs from one is a sequence of headings, paragraphs, rules and links. Anything a browser would do beyond that — tables, images, styling — is not in these files. Unknown tags are dropped rather than shown, because a stray <FONT> in the middle of a sentence about Rennes-le-Château is worse than no formatting at all.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.SoundtrackProgram
member.summary: Runs a .STK — the little program a room's sound is written as.

remarks.para: A soundtrack is not a piece of music. It is a list walked in order and then walked again: wait a second, play the room's theme, wait five to ten seconds, play one of three moods, and round again with a different wait each time. That is what keeps a hotel room from sounding like a loop, and playing only its first sound — which is what happened before this — gives a room its tone and none of its variety. 97 files, 5,755 steps, 125 sounds across the corpus.

The program decides; it does not play. What to start and when is arithmetic and a random draw, and both are worth testing without a sound device — so the caller passes in something that starts a sound and answers how long it lasts, and that is the whole of the coupling.

A looping sound ends the walk. Not a special case bolted on: a soundtrack meant to be continuous is written as an introduction followed by something that loops, and there is no way past that node. Everything after it in the file is unreachable, as the original has it.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.StartingItems
member.summary: What the two of them are carrying when a new game begins.

remarks.para: Nothing in the shipped data gives these out. No barn holds a list of starting items and no scene script hands one over, because the table was compiled into the original executable the same way the score table was — G-Engine hardcodes it too, with a comment saying it ought to be data-driven and that its author could not find where. So the engine carries it; see Assets/Story/Pockets.txt and NOTICE.

It is not a convenience. Prince James's card is where the number Gabriel dials comes from, so a player starting with empty pockets cannot use the pay phone, and Day 1 10am cannot be finished at all. Reported exactly that way.

Given once, when a game starts, and never on the way into a room — a player who has put the wallet down somewhere should not find it back in their pocket at the next door. Loading a save does not call this either: what a save holds is what was being carried.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Story.Introductions
member.summary: Who the player has been introduced to.

remarks.para: A question the original never had to answer, because it drew no label under the pointer. This one does, and a scene names its people by their surnames — BUTHANE, BUCHELLI, WILKES — so a label that reads them back names every suspect in the game the moment the player first sees one. It is the leak the second-floor doors had, in a place where there is no room number to fall back on.

Every condition is the game's own. They are copied out of the [LOGIC] sections of the action files — MET_BUTHANE, MET_WILKES, INTRODUCED_EMILIO — and evaluated exactly as an action's case is, against the same host. Which is what bounds the list: a character the shipped data never asks "have we met" about is not in it and keeps their name. See Assets/Story/Introductions.txt, which says which file each line came from.

Anyone not listed is treated as known. That is the safe way round: a name shown early is a small spoiler, and a name withheld from somebody the player has been talking to for two days is a bug they cannot work around.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Story.Journal
member.summary: The quest log.

remarks.para: The original game has none, and the port is not obliged to reproduce that. What it reproduces instead is 1999's problem: a player who has done everything they can think of, with no way to find out what the game is waiting for, and an evening lost to walking between the same four rooms. Plan/03 section 3 asks for an interface easier than the original's, and knowing where you are in a story is most of what that means.

Two levels, and the player chooses which. The journal says what to do and never how — see . A player who is stuck asks for a hint, and gets one line of the walkthrough at a time. Nothing from the walkthrough is ever shown unasked, because several of these puzzles are the best things in the game.

Nothing here is state. What is done is read from the score events the story has already recorded, so the journal cannot drift out of step with the game and there is nothing to migrate when it changes. The one thing it does own is which hints have been asked for, which is a player's own business and is saved with the game.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Story.TimeblockRules
member.summary: When a point in the story is over.

remarks.para: The game advances the clock when the player has done everything a timeblock requires, checked on every change of location. Nothing in the shipped data holds these rules: no script in the eight barns calls SetTime or SetLocationTime at all, because the original carried them inside its executable. What they are is written down in the design document the game shipped with, TIMEBLOCKBIBLE.TXT, one "Completion Rules" list per timeblock.

Adapted from G-Engine's Assets/Timeblocks.shp by Clark Kromenaker (https://github.com/kromenak/gengine), GNU General Public License version 3. See NOTICE. Its form there is a Sheep script the engine compiles at startup, and that is not the form here: a compiled Sheep script is a .shp, every .shp in existence is original game data, and this repository refuses that extension in .gitignore and again in the CI check. Carrying the rules as source in an assembly that cannot hold the file was a contradiction; carrying them as code is not, and it is checked by the compiler besides.

Every condition below reads the same the Sheep functions of the same name read — GetNounVerbCount is , GetFlag is — so the rules still ask the game the questions the game's own scripts ask, and stay checkable against the corpus.
Nothing here changes the clock. Deciding and acting are separate so that a rule can be asked what it thinks without moving the story; is what applies the answer.

member.summary: The walkthrough, read as data.

remarks.para: A tab-separated file of location, action and points, under a heading per point in the story. It has two jobs and they pull in opposite directions.

It is the source of the journal's hints. A player who is stuck asks for one and gets a line of this, which is why nothing here is ever shown unasked: every line is a spoiler, and several are the answer to a puzzle the game expects the player to enjoy working out. What the journal shows by default is written separately — see Quests.txt — and says what to do without saying how.

And it is a test. Every action it names is something the shipped scripts have to allow at that point in the story, so reading it against the corpus finds the places where they do not, before a player finds them by being unable to finish the game.

member.summary: Reads a walkthrough.
member.param: Its contents.
member.returns: The steps.

remarks.para: Four shapes of line, told apart by how many tabs are on them and whether the last field is a score. Three fields is a location, an action and its points. Two is either an action and its points, continuing at the location above, or a location and an action that scores nothing — which is why the score is matched rather than counted to. One field is a step in its own right that names neither, and is usually the sentence telling the player where to walk.

A heading is Day 2: 10 AM - 12 PM (Gabriel), and the code the rest of the engine uses falls straight out of it: the day, the first hour, and which half of the day it is. Nothing before the first heading is a step, which is what skips the column titles at the top of the file.

member.param: Where they first stop agreeing.
member.returns: True when every total is the sum of everything before it.
member.remarks: The file's own check on the parse. Each scored line prints what it is worth and what the player has by then, so a step read twice or missed shows up as a total that no longer follows — which is a great deal easier to find than the wrong hint appearing in the journal three days into the story.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.Sunlight
member.summary: The sun, for the scenes the artists lit without one.

remarks.para: Most exteriors ship a scenekey — the artists' own sun — but it carries the two hundred unit range 3ds Max left in the file with its attenuation switched off, and that range is honoured on lightmapped surfaces (see GpuLight.RangeOf for why it must be). So the authored sun reaches the characters and nothing else: on the ray-traced tiers the ground under them had no key light at all, nothing outdoors cast a shadow, and ground cut with real cobble relief read as flat, because relief is legible only under grazing directional light.

So outdoors the scenekey is replaced with this: a single warm sun far enough away to be effectively directional and unattenuated for real, so it reaches the ground, aimed by the timeblock's own hour rather than by where one morning's artist parked it. It subtends about half a degree — the real sun's size — so its ray-traced shadows have the real penumbra. The sky-bounce fills stay, interiors are left exactly alone, and so is any exterior at night.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Sunlight.Distance
member.summary: How far away the sun stands, in scene units.
member.remarks: Far enough that its direction is the same across the largest exterior — RC1 spans about three thousand units — and its light does not measurably fall off across one.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Game.Sunlight.Disc
member.summary: The emitter's radius, sized so the disc subtends half a degree.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Sunlight.IsAuthoredSun(GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.AuthoredLight,System.Numerics.Vector3,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: Whether an authored light is the artists' own sun.
member.param: The light as the scene asset declares it.
One corner of the loaded geometry.
The other.
member.returns: True for a scenekey: distant, unattenuated, and shadow-casting.
member.remarks: Recognised by shape rather than name, the same shape GpuLight.IsDistantKey keys on: the attenuation switch off, and a stored range that cannot reach the geometry. Measured from the bounding box, not its centre, and for the same reason the renderer measures it that way: RC1's evening square is ringed by street lamps with the switch off and a couple of hundred units of range, and against the centre of a three-thousand-unit town the far corner's lamps read as distant. Against the box a lamp standing in the scene is at distance zero, always. The sky-bounce lights share the sun's shape but not its shadows, and stay: they are the blue of the sky on whatever faces up, which the replacement does not provide.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Game.Sunlight.For(GK3Reborn.Game.Timeblock,System.Numerics.Vector3)
member.summary: The sun for a point in the story, or null where there should not be one.
member.param: When it is.
The middle of the scene, which the sun is placed relative to.
member.returns: The light, or null at night.
member.remarks: The elevation follows the hour: low and warm in the morning, high and near white before noon, sinking and warming again through the afternoon. The azimuth swings from one side of the map to the other across the day. None of it is astronomy — the game's world has no agreed compass — but a morning in the village now looks like a morning, and by evening the shadows have crossed the square.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Game.TimeblockRange
member.summary: The span of the story an asset applies to, as written in its own name.

remarks.para: GK3 files say when they are for. A location's action files are R25_ALL.NVC, R25_1ALL.NVC, R25_23ALL.NVC and R25202P.NVC: every timeblock, all of day one, days two and three, and that afternoon alone. The scene file lists all of them and the engine is expected to load only the ones that apply, so the name is not decoration — it is the condition.

The grammar, from G-Engine's Timeblock::ParseTimeblockRange: three letters of location, an optional underscore, then either ALL preceded by the digits of the days it covers, or a timeblock code optionally followed by a second one giving the end of a range — HAL110A04P runs from day one at ten in the morning to four that afternoon, the end borrowing its day from the start.

A name that does not parse covers nothing, which is the original's behaviour and the safe direction: loading an action file at the wrong point in the story puts verbs on objects that should not have them yet.

member.param: First timeblock it applies to.

member.summary: Whether the click just reported was the second of a pair.

remarks.para: Reported as well as the click rather than instead of it, because the two mean the same thing and differ only in urgency: a double-click is "do that, and get on with it". Swallowing the first click to see whether a second arrives would put a delay on every single click in the game to serve the rarer case.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Camera
member.summary: A view onto the scene.

remarks.para: Left-handed, because GK3's world is. Its scenes were authored for Direct3D, where +X is right, +Y is up and +Z is forward, and the reference implementation builds its view the same way — see RenderTransforms.h, VIEW_HAND VIEW_LH, and the comment there that negating the side axis is what would make the world appear right-handed. Putting that world through a right-handed look-at renders every scene as its own mirror image. It is nearly invisible — a mirrored room is still a plausible room — until something in it carries writing, which is why it surfaced as the numbers on the hotel doors reading backwards.

Uses a reversed-Y projection. Vulkan's clip space has Y pointing down, the opposite of the convention assumes, so without the flip everything renders upside down — a mistake easy to misread as a broken model rather than a broken matrix.

The framing helper exists because GK3's models are in their own units and sit wherever the original artists left them: some are centred on the origin, others are placed at their position within a scene. Deriving the view from the actual bounds means a model is visible without anyone having to know which case it is.

member.summary: The ray a pixel of the rendered image looks along.
member.param: Column, from the left edge of the image.
Row, from the top edge of the image.
Image width in pixels.

member.returns: A ray from the camera through the middle of that pixel.
member.remarks: The basis is the left-handed one the view matrix uses — screen right is cross(up, forward), not the other way about — so a ray built here lands on what the pixel actually shows rather than on its mirror image. The Y flip the projection carries for Vulkan's clip space does not appear here: this works in view space, where up is up, and the row is counted from the top because that is how an image is indexed and where a mouse position comes from.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Rendering.FreeCamera
member.summary: A camera the player can fly around a scene with.

remarks.para: Not how the game will present a scene — GK3 cuts between fixed viewpoints rather than letting the player roam. It exists because being able to move through a scene is the only practical way to check that geometry, textures and lighting are right everywhere rather than only where a room camera happens to point.
Speed scales with the scene's size. GK3's units put a character at about 70 tall and a street scene in the thousands, so a fixed speed is either unusably slow in one and uncontrollable in the other.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Rendering.HeadlessSceneSink
member.summary: Somewhere to put a scene when there is nothing to draw it with.
member.remarks: Loading a scene and drawing it are separate jobs, and only the second needs a graphics device. This takes everything the loader produces, measures it and throws it away, so the whole of loading — the geometry, the bakes, every texture, the props and the people — can be exercised on a build agent with no GPU. That is what makes "every scene loads headlessly" a thing a command can answer rather than a thing somebody checks by looking.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink
member.summary: Somewhere a loaded scene can be put.

remarks.para: Assembling a scene means reading half a dozen file formats and deciding which of them apply; putting it on a GPU means buffers, descriptor sets and a specific graphics API. Those are separate jobs, and this interface is the seam between them: loading talks to this, and only the backend implements it.

The seam is enforced rather than assumed — the layering tests forbid anything under Game from naming the Vulkan backend, which is what pushed this interface into existence rather than letting the loader write to the backend directly.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink.Add(GK3Reborn.Formats.Models.ModFile,System.Nullable{System.Numerics.Matrix4x4},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyDictionary{System.Int32,System.Numerics.Matrix4x4})

Where to place it, or null for its authored position.

Extra rotations for particular meshes, applied about each mesh's own origin before it is placed on the model. GK3's people have no skeleton — a character is a dozen separate meshes, each with its own transform — so this is how a head turns.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink.SetVisible(GK3Reborn.Rendering.ModelPlacement,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Draws a model, or stops drawing it.
member.param: The handle its returned.
Whether it is drawn.

remarks.para: GK3 scenes declare models hidden and scripts call ShowModel to bring them out. Both are ordinary staging: RC1 keeps Wilkes's moped out of sight until the scripted moment it rides past, at which point the scene shows it, plays its clip, has Gabriel watch it and hides it again.

Hiding must take the model out of the traced world as well as out of the picture. A model that is not drawn but is still traced lies its shadow on the floor, which is a stranger thing to look at than the model would have been.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink.Repaint(GK3Reborn.Rendering.ModelPlacement,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Paints one of a standing model's textures with something else.
member.param: The handle its returned.
The texture the model was built with, such as GAB_FACE.
What to draw instead, or null to put the model's own back.

remarks.para: What makes a character's face move. GK3's heads have no facial geometry — a head is one mesh with one bitmap on it — so talking, blinking and raising an eyebrow are all the same operation: draw a different picture on the same triangles.

By texture rather than by submesh, because that is the thing the caller actually knows. A face is "wherever this model draws GAB_FACE"; which submesh of which mesh group that happens to be is the model's business and varies per character.

The replacement must have been given to the sink already. Normal maps stay with the original texture's name: a repainted face is the same surface with a different picture on it, and its bumps have not changed.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink.TurnMesh(GK3Reborn.Rendering.ModelPlacement,System.Int32,System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: Moves one mesh of a model that is already standing.
member.param: The handle its returned.
Which of the model's meshes.
A rotation about the mesh's own origin, replacing whatever it was placed with.
member.remarks: What makes a glance a movement rather than a pose. A character has no skeleton, so there is nothing else to animate: the head is a mesh, and turning it is putting it somewhere else between one frame and the next.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink.PoseMesh(GK3Reborn.Rendering.ModelPlacement,System.Int32,System.Numerics.Matrix4x4)
member.summary: Puts one mesh of a model where an animation says it goes.
member.param: The handle its returned.
Which of the model's meshes.
Where the mesh sits in the model's own space, replacing the one the model was built with.
member.remarks: Distinct from , which applies a rotation on top of the mesh's own transform. A vertex animation stores the transform outright, and getting there through a rotation would mean inverting the model's own basis every frame to cancel it out again.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink.ShapeMesh(GK3Reborn.Rendering.ModelPlacement,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Numerics.Vector3})

member.param: The handle its returned.
Which of the model's meshes.
Which submesh within that mesh.
Every vertex, in mesh space, in the model's own order.

remarks.para: What makes a character animate rather than slide. GK3's characters have no skeleton, so a clip stores where every vertex is on every frame and playing one means putting them there.

Positions only. Normals stay as the model authored them, which is what the original does — it swaps the position stream and leaves the rest — so lighting on a deformed character is as right or wrong as it was in 1999.
A count that does not match the submesh is ignored rather than partly applied. A clip aimed at the wrong model would otherwise rewrite whatever it happened to overlap.

Where it is now, replacing where it was placed.

remarks.para: An actor walking. Every mesh moves together, keeping whatever has done to any of them, because a head that is turned stays turned while its owner crosses the room.
The same reasoning as turning a head: GK3's characters have no skeleton, so there is nothing to animate but where their meshes are.

member.param: The colour texture names.
member.remarks: The loader names these for outdoor scenes: ground and rock running past the floor= object into verges and roadside, which the displaced material classes already describe and the floor-only rule left flat. Called after , which resets both sets for the room.

member.summary: Draws one of the room's own named objects, or stops drawing it.
member.param: The object's name, as the geometry file records it.
Whether it is drawn.
member.returns: True when the room has an object by that name.
member.remarks: Not the same as , which is about a model the scene loaded from a file of its own. This is about the room: a curtain, a door, a van, all of which are runs of surfaces inside one mesh with a name over them. Scripts show and hide those 287 times across the corpus, and until this existed every one of those calls was recorded and dropped.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.ISceneSink.AddScene(GK3Reborn.Formats.Scenes.BspFile,GK3Reborn.Formats.Lightmaps.MulFile,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlySet{System.String},System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlySet{System.Int32})

member.param: The parsed scene.
Its lightmaps, in surface order, if any.
Names of objects inside the geometry that must not be drawn, such as hit-test volumes.
The object the scene calls its floor, whose surfaces may have their relief cut into the geometry rather than only sampled by the shader, or null to displace nothing.
Individual surfaces that must not be drawn, by their index in the geometry.

remarks.para: Hiding by surface exists because hiding by name is too coarse for the thing that needed it. pou_trees01 is two trees and a painted strip of distant hillside in one object: the trees can be replaced by modelled ones and the strip cannot, and there was no way to say so. Nineteen objects across the corpus are shaped like that, and each of them kept its flat trees because one surface in it was a backdrop.
Indices rather than names because a surface has no name — the name belongs to the object it is part of, which is exactly the granularity this is escaping.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Lighting.LightEstimator
member.summary: Recovers light sources from baked lighting.

remarks.para: The useful observation is that a distant light is a *linear* problem. Lambertian brightness from a directional source is I = dot(n, d), so given many surfaces with known normals and measured brightness, the direction and intensity fall out of a three-by-three least-squares solve. No iteration, no initial guess, no local minima.

Point lights are not linear, because brightness depends on distance as well as angle. They are estimated more coarsely, by clustering bright surfaces and placing a source in front of each cluster — good enough to seed a rig a human then corrects, which is all ADR 0002 asks of it.
Nothing here is trusted on its own. Every estimate carries a confidence derived from how well it explains the samples, and low-confidence output is review queue rather than content.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Lighting.LightEstimator.FitDirectional(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GK3Reborn.Rendering.Lighting.LitSurface})
member.summary: Fits a single directional light to a set of lit surfaces.
member.param: Surfaces with their measured brightness.
member.returns: The estimate, or null when the samples cannot constrain one.
member.remarks: Minimising the squared error between dot(n, d) and measured brightness gives the normal equations (sum n nᵀ) d = sum I n. Surfaces are weighted by area, so a large wall counts for more than a doorknob.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Lighting.LightEstimator.FitPointLights(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{GK3Reborn.Rendering.Lighting.LitSurface},System.Single,System.Int32)
member.summary: Proposes point lights by clustering the brightest surfaces.
member.param: Surfaces with their measured brightness.
How close two surfaces must be to share a light.
Cap on how many lights to propose.
member.returns: The estimates, brightest first.
member.remarks: A cluster of bright surfaces implies a source somewhere in front of them, so the light is placed off the cluster's centroid along its average normal at a distance scaled by the cluster's own extent. This is a seed, not a solution: it gets the light into roughly the right place so a human can move it rather than create it.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Rendering.LightmapAtlas
member.summary: Packs a scene's per-surface lightmaps into one texture.

remarks.para: A scene has one lightmap per surface — 925 of them in R25 alone — and binding each as its own texture would mean a descriptor set and a draw call per surface, plus one device allocation per lightmap. Drivers guarantee only a few thousand allocations in total, so a handful of scenes would exhaust them.
Packing them instead lets surfaces sharing a diffuse texture be drawn together, which is what makes a scene a few dozen draws rather than a thousand.

Tiles are separated by a one-texel gutter and their UVs inset by half a texel. Without that, bilinear filtering at a tile's edge reaches into its neighbour, and a wall picks up the lighting of whatever surface happened to be packed beside it — a bug that only appears at glancing angles and is very hard to attribute after the fact.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition
member.summary: The PBR description of one original material.

remarks.para: The 1999 assets carry a diffuse texture and little else. Everything a physically based renderer needs — roughness, metalness, specular response, normal detail — has to be inferred from the texture, the surface's name and its role in the scene. Those inferences are guesses, and some will be wrong in ways only visible in motion under real lighting: a stone floor that reads as wet, a brass fitting with no highlight at all.

So every channel is correctable through the same edit layer the lighting rigs use. Fix the value in the material's edits file, and the correction survives every future rerun of the inference pass. See ADR 0006.

member.summary: Logical id of the base color texture.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.BaseColorTint
member.summary: Multiplier over the base color texture.

member.summary: Roughness, 0 (mirror) to 1 (fully diffuse).

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.Metallic
member.summary: Metalness, 0 (dielectric) to 1 (conductor).

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.SpecularReflectance
member.summary: Specular reflectance at normal incidence for dielectrics. 0.5 is the neutral default.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.NormalStrength
member.summary: Strength of the normal map, where one exists.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.NormalTexture
member.summary: The surface's normal map, named for the colour texture it belongs to.
member.remarks: Null where there is none, which is most of them: 324 of the game's 6,657 textures have one so far. A surface without one is given a flat map and looks exactly as it did, which is how a partial set stays a perfectly good set.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.OrmTexture
member.summary: The surface's packed occlusion, roughness and metalness.

remarks.para: Red is ambient occlusion, green is roughness, blue is metalness — the glTF packing, which is what every generator and every authoring tool already writes. Read from enhanced/orm, named for the colour texture it belongs to.
The map multiplies and rather than replacing them, which is what keeps a corrected value in the edit layer meaningful once a generated map arrives for the same surface.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.HeightTexture
member.summary: The surface's height field, for parallax and for displacement.
member.remarks: Read from enhanced/height, named for the colour texture it belongs to. Mid grey is the modelled surface and the channel runs either side of it. Two things consume it: a marched texture-coordinate offset, which deepens mortar courses and cobbles and does nothing at all to a silhouette, and — on a floor, where the silhouette is what gives a street away — real geometry. See .

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.HeightDepth
member.summary: How deep the height map goes, in world units from its floor to its ceiling.

remarks.para: A GK3 unit is roughly two and a half centimetres, so the default is a relief of about four: a cobble's crown over its gutter, a floorboard's chamfer, the depth of a mortar course. Like this is a decision recorded per material rather than a constant in the shader, because how much of a generated field to believe differs by surface.

World units, not texture coordinates. It was the latter until the corpus was measured: the game tiles one road texture over 232 units of street and one lobby floor over 32, so a single number in texture coordinates was seven times as deep on the second as on the first, and nobody had chosen that. The shader converts through the surface's own tiling, which it can read off the tangent frame it already builds.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.MaterialDefinition.Displaced
member.summary: Whether this surface's relief is cut into the geometry as well as marched by the shader.

remarks.para: Off by default, and it has to be. Every texture in the game has a generated height field, and for most of them the field is not relief at all: a grass texture's is blades, a rug's is pile, a painted backdrop's is whatever the model made of a picture of a hillside. Marching those does no harm — the offset is a few texels and it reads as texture. Moving vertices by them makes a lawn out of corrugated iron.

And it is what the triangle budget is spent on. CSE's floor object is nineteen million square units of village, of which the road is one; displacing all of it buys a cell so coarse that the high-passed field averages to nothing inside one, which is the worst of both — every triangle paid for and no relief to show for them. Turned on for the paved fifth of it, the same budget buys four units a cell.

The set that has it on is derived from the material classifier and then reviewed: stone, brick, tile, concrete, marble and wood, plus the surfaces it calls ground whose names say road, cobble, path or pavement rather than soil or sand.

member.summary: How rough and how reflective each texture is, looked up by name.

remarks.para: A read once and turned into something a renderer can ask six thousand times a frame. Three of its channels are read: how rough a surface is, how metallic it is, and how much light it throws back when looked at straight on. The first two feed the specular lobe; roughness also decides which pixels are worth tracing a reflection from and how tightly to gather one.
A texture nobody has measured is matte, which costs nothing and reflects nothing — the renderer's behaviour before any of this existed.

Everything in a generated height field is invented, and both things that read one degrade the same way when it is pushed: the march starts to reveal that the surface has no silhouette, and displaced geometry starts to lift off whatever it abuts.

That layer is the whole point of ADR 0006 — a classifier guesses, and the person looking at the scene in-engine knows better — and it was being written and never read, so every correction anybody made to a material did nothing at all. member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Rendering.Materials.SurfaceFinish
member.summary: How a surface responds to light beyond its colour.
member.param: Zero for a mirror, one for chalk. Widens the cone a reflection is gathered over.
How much light the surface throws back when looked at straight on, before the grazing angle raises it. Half is the usual dielectric value and the assumption here.

Zero for a dielectric, one for a conductor. A metal has no diffuse term at all and tints its own reflection with its base colour, which is why this is not a slider between two shading models but a switch between them — and why a classifier that guesses it wrong on a stone wall is unmistakable rather than subtle.
How much of the normal map to believe. One is as generated; everything in a generated map is invented, so this is a per-material decision rather than a constant.
How deep the height map goes, in world units from its floor to its ceiling. Clamped to , which is well past anything a generated field has any business claiming about a surface.
Whether the surface is its own light source — a lit bulb, a lamp shade with a bulb inside it, the painted view through a window.
Whether a person had a hand in these numbers, rather than a classifier alone.
Whether the height map is cut into the geometry as well as marched by the shader. Only a paved, tiled or boarded surface wants this; see .
member.remarks: An authored finish beats a generated map. Where a surface has an ORM map, the map is normally the answer — it is a measurement of that surface and the library's value is a classifier's guess at the same thing. But a correction somebody made after looking at the room in-engine outranks both, and if it did not the edit layer would be unable to fix the one class of thing it most obviously needs to: a generated roughness that is wrong for what the surface actually is.
