member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptFile.ReadLengthPrefixedString(GK3Reborn.Formats.SpanReader@)
member.summary: Reads a 16-bit length-prefixed string.
member.remarks: The field occupies two bytes of length, then that many bytes, then one further byte. Consuming only the counted bytes leaves the reader one short, and because every subsequent field then reads from one byte early, the failure appears much later as an absurd length rather than at the string itself.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptWriter
member.summary: Writes a compiled script back out in the container the game ships.

remarks.para: The inverse of , and the reason it exists is verification rather than authoring: a compiler that produces something only its own reader understands has not been checked against anything. Writing the container and reading it back is a round trip through the format's real rules — the length-prefixed strings with their trailing byte, the section table, the offsets that are relative to the header — and any of those misunderstood shows up immediately instead of in a disassembly nobody compares.
The five sections are written in the order the reader expects to find them named, each with its own twelve-byte name, its size, its count and its own offset table.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptWriter.BeforeTable
member.summary: How much of the header comes before the section table.
member.remarks: Eight bytes of magic and five 32-bit fields. The header's declared size is this plus the table, and it is what every section offset is measured from — which is checkable against the content and checks out: all 224 shipped scripts declare exactly 28 + 4 × sections.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptWriter.Write(GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptFile)
member.summary: Writes a script.
member.param: The script.
member.returns: The bytes of a .SHP file.
member.remarks: A section with nothing in it is left out rather than written empty, which is what the game does: 206 of its scripts declare no variables and carry four sections, and the 17 that do declare some carry five.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptWriter.Strings(GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptFile)
member.summary: Writes the string pool, keyed by the offsets the bytecode already carries.
member.remarks: These offsets are the only ones in the file that are read rather than skipped: GetString looks a constant up by where it starts in the pool. The compiler chose them when it interned the strings, so this lays the pool out to match rather than the other way round.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptWriter.Code(GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptFile)
member.summary: Writes the code, which is one block and has always been one block.
member.remarks: The section's "count" is a count of blocks rather than of entries, and its one offset is where that block starts — zero, in all 224 of the game's scripts. The reader refuses anything else rather than reading the first block and ignoring the rest.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepScriptWriter.Section(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int32},System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Byte})
member.summary: Wraps a body in the header every section carries.
member.param: The section's name, in twelve bytes.
Where each entry starts within the body.
The entries.
member.returns: The section.
member.remarks: Twelve bytes of name, then the header's own size written twice, then the size of the body, then the number of entries, then their offsets. The doubled size is the original's and it checks out across the corpus: every section in every shipped script declares 12 + 16 + 4 × entries in both fields.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepSignatures
member.summary: What each system function takes and returns.

remarks.para: A compiler needs this and the language reference does not carry it in a form the engine can read: the specification is a Word document, and its machine-extracted index lives in the content workspace rather than the repository because it is derived from copyrighted documentation.

The game answers the question itself. Every compiled script carries an import table giving the return type and argument types of every function it calls, so the 224 shipped scripts between them describe the signature of every function the game uses — 139 of them. Reading the catalogue out of the content is both self-contained and authoritative: it is what the original compiler actually emitted.

Disagreements are worth hearing about rather than resolving quietly. Two scripts giving one function two signatures would mean either the reader is wrong or the assumption that a name has one signature is, and both matter more than whichever one happens to win.

member.summary: How long a waited call takes.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepVirtualMachine
member.summary: Executes compiled Sheep.

remarks.para: A stack machine, matching the original's conventions rather than improving on them. Arguments are pushed in order followed by their count; a call pops the count, takes that many arguments and pushes a result — even void functions push one, because the original compiler emits a Pop after every void call and the stack would otherwise drift.

Waiting is modelled as an explicit resumable state rather than by blocking a real thread, which is what Plan/01-architecture.md section 6 requires: wait becomes a suspension the game thread can resume, not an operation that stops the engine.
Execution is bounded. A script that loops forever stops with a fault rather than hanging the caller, which matters because these scripts came from data the project does not control.

member.summary: Starts a function and runs it as far as it will go.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepVirtualMachine.Same(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Whether two function names refer to the same function.
member.remarks: A compiled script names its functions with a $ on the end — the disassembly of R25's reads Window_Open$ — and the callers routinely leave it off: CallSheep("R25_ALL","WINDOW_OPEN") is how the action files spell it. The original appends the suffix when it is missing, with the comment "some GK3 data files do this, some don't". Matching exactly instead means the call finds nothing, the thread faults, and the action appears to run and do nothing at all — which is what opening R25's window did.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepVirtualMachine.NotifyWaitsCompleted(GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepThread)
member.summary: Tells a blocked thread that everything it waited on has finished.
member.remarks: The scheduler owns this: the VM suspends a thread and takes no view on when the animation, walk or timer it waited for actually completes. Calling this makes the thread runnable again; it does not run it.
member.param: The blocked thread.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.Sheep.SheepVirtualMachine.Current
member.summary: The thread being stepped, while one is.
member.remarks: A script may ask the host to do something that depends on which script asked — Call("TwoShot") means "the function of that name in me", and there are 190 of those in the game. The host is given a name and no context, so this is the context. It nests, because a called script may call another.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.UI.FrontEnd
member.summary: The menu in front of the game: what each page holds and what choosing a row does.

remarks.para: Deliberately free of any window, renderer or device. It turns settings into rows and rows back into settings, so the whole of the front end's behaviour can be tested without drawing anything — which is the only way to check that a slider moves the thing it says it moves.

It doubles as the pause menu. The same pages serve both; the only difference is that there is a room to go back to, so the first row says Resume rather than New Game and leaving means leaving the game rather than the menu.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.UI.GameConsole
member.summary: The developer console.

remarks.para: The game's own scripting language is the command language, because it already is one: everything the story can do is a Sheep call, the calls are named in the scripts the game shipped with, and there are 139 signatures for them in the archives. Inventing a second vocabulary on top would mean maintaining a translation between two sets of verbs that mean the same things.

Which is why the completion matters rather than being a nicety. Nobody can be expected to know that the way to see the easter-egg content is SetFlag("EGG") — which is why there is now a row for it under Options, Playing — or to remember which of SetLocation and SetEgoLocation takes what. A list that narrows as you type, showing each function's return type and arguments, is the difference between a console that is usable without the source open beside it and one that is not.

Calls are parsed here rather than compiled. A console line is one call with literal arguments — there are no variables to resolve and no control flow to run — so a parser of forty lines does the whole job, and the alternative would be standing up the compiler, a script file and a thread to run one SetFlag.
Nothing here touches the clock, the renderer or the story directly. It is a buffer, a history and a list of names; what a command does is whatever the host it is given does with it.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.UI.GameHud
member.summary: The game's interface, laid out fresh every frame.

remarks.para: The brief this is written against is in docs/screens.md and comes down to one thing: a player should never have to learn the interface to use it. The original made you hold a button to raise a verb ring, pick from icons whose meaning you had to discover, and go through a separate screen to look in your own pockets. So here the noun under the pointer says what a click will do, in words, before the click happens; the full list is one right-click away and is a plain list of verbs; and the inventory is a strip along the bottom that is always visible and always one click from being used.

Nothing here is retained. It is a function from what the game is doing to a list of rectangles, so there is no widget tree to keep in step with the world and no way for the interface to be showing something that stopped being true.

Hit testing is the same layout run twice: lays the verb menu out and remembers where each row went, and reads that back. Deriving both from one pass is what keeps the thing you click and the thing you see from drifting apart.

member.name: F:GK3Reborn.UI.GameHud.Console
member.summary: The console's own ground, darker and more opaque than the rest.
member.remarks: Nearly solid on purpose. Everything else here is a label over a room the player is looking at; this is a surface being read line by line, and the room behind it is a distraction rather than context.

member.param: Where it draws.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.UI.GameHud.Scale
member.summary: How much bigger everything is than the layout was written against.

remarks.para: Every measurement here — padding, panel heights, the gap between inventory slots — is written in the units of a nineteen-pixel line, which is what F_ARIAL_T12 gives, and multiplied by this. So changing the font changes the whole interface together rather than leaving 1999-sized gaps around 2026-sized letters.

It is derived from the font rather than set, because a bitmap font has exactly one size: there is no scaling a sheet, and drawing a seventeen-pixel one at thirty-four pixels is a blurry seventeen-pixel one. Making the text bigger means picking a bigger sheet, and everything else follows from which sheet was picked.

member.summary: The developer console.

remarks.para: Across the top rather than the bottom, because the inventory strip and the captions both live along the bottom edge and a console over either of them would hide the thing a command was about to change.

The completion list hangs below the input line and is the reason the console is worth having: the command language is the game's own 139 Sheep functions, and nobody can be expected to know their names. Each row carries its prototype, so the arguments are visible before they are typed rather than after they are wrong.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.UI.GameHud.Hotspots(GK3Reborn.UI.HudState,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Every hotspot in the room at once, while the key that asks is held.
member.param: What the game is doing, including where each noun is.
Window width.
Window height.

remarks.para: A 1999 adventure game hides what can be clicked and expects the player to sweep the pointer across the furniture until something lights up. Holding a key answers the question outright, which is what Plan/03 section 3 means by an interface easier than the original's.

Laid out so that no two labels overlap. Rooms put a dozen nouns within a few degrees of each other — a desk, its drawer, the register on it, the bell beside it — and a heap of labels on the same spot answers nothing. Each is pushed down until it clears the ones already placed, in order of depth so the nearest keeps its own place and the ones behind give way. A label with nowhere left to go is dropped rather than stacked, because a wrong label is worse than a missing one.

remarks.para: It duplicated the right-click menu, which already says which of the player's things a noun will take, and it lay across the foot of the screen — exactly where the floor at the player's feet is drawn, so every click on the ground in front of you had to be tested against it first and a good many were swallowed.
Kept rather than deleted. It is the layout for a strip if one is ever wanted as something the player can turn on, and deleting it to write it again would be the worse trade.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.UI.MenuPage
member.summary: A page of menu, drawn from rectangles and text rather than from the game's own art.

remarks.para: Nothing here uses GK3's interface bitmaps. They are 640x480 art with the button labels painted into them in one language, at one size, with the pressed and hovered states baked as separate images. Drawing the interface instead means it is sharp at any resolution, it grows with the caption ladder like the rest of the interface, it can say things the original never had a button for — a volume, a walking pace — and it needs no new art to add a row.

The layout and the hit test come from one pass, in the same way does its verb menu: a row is drawn and its rectangle remembered, so what the player clicks is necessarily what they saw. The two cannot drift apart because there is only one of them.
Every measurement is in , so the whole page scales with the font the interface picked for the window. Nothing is in pixels.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenLayers
member.summary: What is in front of the room, and how the player gets out of it.

remarks.para: GK3 has a lot of modal screens — the inventory, an item held up close, the binoculars, the fingerprint kit, the driving map, Sidney — and in the original each arrived with its own way in and its own way out. Plan/03-gameplay-ui-audio.md section 3 asks for the opposite: that they "share navigation, back behavior and scaling conventions", so the player learns the way out once and it works everywhere. This is that stack.

One rule for leaving: closes whatever is on top and puts the player back where they were. It never closes two things, never lands somewhere they have not been, and is the same gesture whichever screen they are looking at.

One rule for the inventory: says whether a dedicated binding should open it right now, and the answer is yes unless the player is somewhere their pockets are not — which is only the driving map. The original made the inventory a small target to click at the edge of the screen; there is nothing to be gained by reproducing that.

Scripts can ask what is showing — IsTopLayerInventory is a real question in the data — so this is game state rather than presentation, and part of the state hash. What it is not is a widget: nothing here draws anything, and a screen being open is a fact about the game rather than about a window.

member.name: T:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter
member.summary: The screens that go in front of the room.

remarks.para: The inventory, an item held up close, the binoculars, the driving map and Sidney. In the original each arrived with its own way in and its own way out; Plan/03 section 3 asks for the opposite, so they share their chrome, their way back and their scaling, and the player learns the way out once.

Drawn rather than blitted. The house style since the interface stopped using GK3's bitmap sheets: rectangles and text, laid out fresh every frame. It costs the original's art and buys a screen that is legible at any resolution, scales with the font, and needs no second texture in a pipeline built around one. Sidney gains most — it is a computer terminal, which is what this style draws best.

Nothing here is retained, exactly like : a function from what the game is doing to a list of rectangles, with hit testing reading back the same layout pass that drew it. There is no widget tree to keep in step with the world, and no way for a screen to be showing something that stopped being true.

What a click means is a string. The painter knows where things are and the caller knows what they do — item:PARCHMENT_1, sidney:do:Analyse, close — which keeps every rule about the game out of the drawing and every rule about drawing out of the game.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter.JournalPage(GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenView,System.Numerics.Vector4,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: The quest log.
member.param: What to draw, including the journal itself.
The panel it goes in.
Where the chrome ends.
The interface's scale.

remarks.para: By day and then by point in the story, newest last. Only the block the player is in lists its objectives; the ones behind it keep their heading and their tally and give up their list. The question the journal answers is "what now", and a morning's worth of ticked lines buries it. The tally is what is left of "how far have I come", which is worth keeping and is not worth eleven lines.

Nothing here says how. The titles are written to say what, and a player who wants more asks for it: every unfinished objective carries a button that reveals one line of the walkthrough, and asking again reveals the next. Several of this game's puzzles are the best things in it, and printing the answer where nobody asked would take them away.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter.Wrapped(System.String,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Breaks a line of prose to fit a width.
member.remarks: A walkthrough line can run to three sentences and the panel is not that wide. Broken on words, and a word longer than the whole width is left to overrun rather than cut in half, because there is no such word in the file and inventing a hyphenation rule for a case that cannot happen is work spent on nothing.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter.Inspect(GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenView,System.Numerics.Vector4,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: One thing, close up, and what can be done to it.
member.remarks: The verbs are the point. An item's own actions — look at it, think about it, read it, scan it into Sidney — are written in INV_ALL.NVC and every one of them is guarded by ALL_INV, which asks whether the inventory is on top. So this is the only place they can be reached, and a close-up with nothing on it but the item's name was a screen with 619 actions behind it and no way to any of them.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter.Places(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.ValueTuple{System.String,System.String}},System.Numerics.Vector4,System.Single,System.Single,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: A list of places, for the binoculars and for a map with no art to draw.
member.remarks: What is clicked is not what is written. A row shows a place's name — "Larry Chester's House" — and carries its location code. Carrying the name instead sent the game looking for a room called Larry Chester's House, which it did once.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter.Binoculars(GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenView,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Single)
member.summary: The binoculars: the room, seen through two circles.

remarks.para: The panorama is the room itself. The binoculars narrow the view and let the player pan the camera they already have, so what this draws is a mask over the picture rather than a picture of its own — which is also what the data says they are: each thing worth seeing is a rectangle in degrees, heading across and pitch up and down.

The mask is drawn in strips. The overlay draws rectangles, so the two circles are cut out of the dark by covering each band of rows either side of them. Four pixels to a band, which is invisible against a flat mask and keeps the count bounded at any resolution — a row-per-pixel mask on a 4K display is nine thousand rectangles and the overlay holds four.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter.Span(System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Half the width of a circle at a distance from its middle.

member.name: M:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter.Driving(GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenView,System.Numerics.Vector4,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: The driving map: the game's own painting of the countryside, with the places on it.

remarks.para: Drawn from the art rather than as a list, because the map is the content — a 640-by-480 painting of the Rennes-le-Château valley — and a list of place names is a table of contents for it rather than the thing itself. Each place's marker is a lit copy of that patch of the map, so drawing one over the base is what the original does and why the markers look like part of the picture.

Scaled to fit the panel and centred, keeping its own proportions: the map is a painting and stretching it to an ultrawide window would be visible immediately. Everything on it is placed in map pixels and multiplied through, so the hit test and the picture cannot drift apart at any window size.
Falls back to a list of names when the art is not loaded — a run against archives that do not have it, or before the pictures have been handed over.

member.name: P:GK3Reborn.UI.ScreenPainter.Sizes
member.summary: How big each of the map's markers is, in the map's own pixels.
member.remarks: The pictures know their own size and the painter cannot ask them — it draws through an overlay that takes numbers, not textures — so whoever loads them says so here.

member.summary: The analyze screen: a file, what may be done to it, and what it said.
Sidney's map, its marks and whatever is laid over it.
member.remarks: The survey of the Rennes country the whole puzzle is about, with the Paris meridian down it. Clicking marks a place; four places that fall on a circle are what the story is waiting to be told. The picture is drawn at whatever size the panel affords and every mark is kept in the map's own 1,368 pixels, so the marks and the hit test cannot drift apart at any window size.

member.remarks: Not one rectangle per side: a rectangle covering a diagonal side's bounding box is a filled block, which is right for the axis-aligned grid and wrong for everything a turned shape draws.
